News.title: Brit tourist disappears while swimming in Lake Como with teenage boy as huge search launched
News.content:
LAKE HORROR Brit tourist disappears while swimming in Lake Como with teenage boy as huge search launched







Next

A BRIT tourist has disappeared while swimming in Lake Como as desperate emergency services scour the water.

The holidaymaker, 38, got into trouble while swimming alongside the 15-year-old son of a family he had taken a boat trip with near the west side of the lake.



Moments later, the teenager’s father jumped in to help, but only managed to save his son before a passing boat pulled the pair to safety in San Siro on Monday.

But the body of the 38-year-old disappeared from sight, sparking a day-long manhunt with boats and a helicopter.



Local outlets report that the man who disappeared is “of Nepalese origin”.

Firefighter divers arrived on site from Milan with the support of the Malpensa Helicopter Unit.



After conducting initial operational assessments, they deployed Remotely Operated Vehicle (ROV) equipment for an underwater searches.

Two naval units from the Dongo and Como fire departments are also collaborating.

Local fire services said: “Operations to prepare and deploy specialised equipment are currently underway.

“The search will continue tomorrow morning, with the combined use of divers and specialized equipment.”



It comes after a spate of drownings in Lake Como this summer, including the death of a nine-year-old girl.

The idyllic holiday hotspot is long, narrow, and extremely deep as it was formed by a glacier.

During hot summers, the lake is still often deceptively cold.

In 2024, Brit tourist Sam Rigby, 21, drowned after he and his girlfriend went for a swim in Lake Como.

The boat they had used to get to the lake was pushed away by strong winds, leaving the couple stranded.



Sam was found dead by rescuers while his partner was saved by a passing boat.

In 2022 another British man, Aran Chada, 51, drowned in the nearby Lake Garda while trying to save his son who was struggling to stay afloat.

His body was found 26 days later at a depth of about 316 metres.

News.title: Why befriending the notoriously erratic Trump is CRUCIAL for Burnham’s aim to bring down the cost of living for Brits
News.content:
POLITICAL FIX Why befriending the notoriously erratic Trump is CRUCIAL for Burnham’s aim to bring down the cost of living for Brits







Next

HIGH in the sky above the Atlantic Ocean, Andy Burnham seemed relaxed ahead of his crunch meeting with Donald Trump.

Kicking back in jeans on the plane over to New York tonight, the PM smiled that the two men had already “found a connection”.



But if Burnham hopes his talks with the President to be plain sailing, he should also brace for a diplomatic squall.

Many a world leader has been invited to break bread with the President only to have their head bitten off.



And while Burnham last night insisted the Special Relationship was “stronger than ever”, many points of difference are straining the UK-US alliance.

To name but a few: the Chagos surrender deal, North Sea drilling, the Iran war, immigration, sovereignty over the Falklands and AI regulation.

Perhaps Burnham will flutter those famous eyelashes and charm the notoriously erratic Trump in the same way Keir Starmer initially found favour.

He certainly seems in no mood to pick a fight with the world’s most powerful man, despite some Labour MPs goading him to have his own Love Actually moment and stick it to the President they loathe.

Burnham himself has been rather rude about his US counterpart in the past, describing him as “poisonous”.

Wriggling last night, he said: “Politicians say things throughout their career, but now the important thing is to focus on the moment you are in.”



The PM seems acutely aware that befriending Trump – no matter their differences – is crucial for his own domestic aim of bringing down the cost of living for Brits.

And so Burnham will be in lovebomb mode when he has his grip and grin moment in New York today.

The question is whether Trump rolls out the red carpet for his guest – or pulls the rug from beneath him.

News.title: How many more women must live in fear of migrants before PM wakes up to public fury exploding across UK?
News.content:
Inviting danger







Next

HOW many more women and girls must be forced to live in fear before Andy Burnham finally gets serious about tackling illegal immigration?

The horrifying catalogue of rapes, sexual assaults and brutal violence carried out by unvetted young men with no right to be in the country makes for truly sickening reading.



A succession of terrified women now say they don’t feel safe going out alone in their own neighbourhood.

Yet what is the Prime Minister’s response? To disperse more asylum seekers across rural communities.



It’s little surprise that the 350-strong village of Piddington voted to break away from Britain after being told a horde of 1,300 men would be housed in the area — meaning women living there will be outnumbered by ten to one.

But instead of listening, Women’s Minister Bridget Phillipson brushed off their valid concerns with a stupefying, out-of-touch comment.



She claimed ALL women are unsafe regardless of where they live.

She shamelessly ducked the issue of attacks by migrants on women and girls, saying domestic violence “is the culture that we have right now in our country”.

All domestic abuse is sickening. But more than 200,000 people have landed illegally on our shores since the small boats crisis began, many from countries with primitive views on women.

How many have gone on to commit violent crimes? Ms Phillipson and her colleagues either don’t know — or they refuse to tell us.



In an interview with The Sun in Piddington, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch rightly pointed out that what was once simply a border control issue has now become a major problem of safeguarding women.

Yet still we continue to roll out the red carpet to small boat migrants, providing three meals a day, a roof over their heads and even spending money.

The only way to end the climate of fear is to stop swathes of young men from entering Britain illegally in the first place.

Winging it

FOR the second time in a fortnight, a breakdown in Britain’s air traffic control has inflicted misery on long-suffering air travellers.

This time it led to 200 flights being cancelled and hundreds more delayed.



Airline chiefs are yet again counting the financial cost of the chaos from the fourth major incident in three years.

But not so National Air Traffic Services boss Martin Rolfe, who pocketed bonuses of up to £900,000 before the latest mayhem struck.

It’s time he experienced some real turbulence.

Ministers should grant him the one thing he has denied thousands of passengers — a swift departure.

News.title: Burnham will invite Trump to visit Manchester when they meet for first time TODAY
News.content:
Next

ANDY Burnham will meet Donald Trump for the first time tomorrow — and invite him to Manchester next year.

The PM wants to shore up the special relationship following a series of flashpoints with the US President in recent months.



He will stress the need to combat harmful AI just as the 2008 crash was tackled.

Mr Burnham said: “When the global financial crisis hit, the UK brought together the world’s leading economies.



“As we confront the opportunities and challenges posed by artificial intelligence, we will show that same leadership, ensuring rapidly changing technology is harnessed for good.”

It risks bringing him into further conflict with Mr Trump, right, who has rebuked calls for more tech regulation.

Yet Mr Burnham will seek to avoid clashing on other splits including Iran and the Chagos giveaway when they meet at the United Nations in New York.

Ahead of his trip with wife Marie-France van Heel, No 10 said: “He is clear we must work with our international partners to face up to the biggest challenges of our generation.”

Mr Burnham, who said in 2021 that “any politician who gave Trump the time of day should be ashamed right now”, will confirm next year’s G20 summit will take place in Manchester.

News.title: Influencer banned from Vietnam for life after ‘dangerous and sexually provocative’ acts on motorbike
News.content:
Next

A RUSSIAN influencer has been banned from Vietnam for life after posing semi-naked on a motorbike in public.

Yulia Nikitina, 35, was accused of “dangerous and sexually provocative” acts on highways around Nha Trang, a popular resort.



The “influencer-style” stunts involved Nikitina posing provocatively on her Yamaha YZF-R15 single-cylinder sport bike.

She was allegedly seen on social media lying flat on a moving motorbike, lifting her legs into the air in a so-called “scorpion” pose exposing her underwear while riding in traffic.



Vietnamese media and commenters highlighted the “sexualised nature” of her stunts, noting that the rider was wearing a short skirt and exposing her underwear while performing manoeuvres in traffic.

Racy photos show the model kneeling on the moving bike, rubbing her body over the petrol tank, bending forward and repeatedly raising, stretching and folding her legs.



Officers initially warned the influencer that she could face up to seven years in jail for “disturbing the public order”.

Instead they deported Nikitina, who was a resident of Vietnam, and banned her for life.



She told the court that the country was her “second home”, having become a popular destination for Russians during the war in Ukraine.

They fined her £860 and seized her motorcycle and iPhone 16.

According to local reports, she apologised for flaunting her “beauty”.

They added that she filmed, edited and uploaded the material to “attract attention to herself”.

The People’s Court of Region 2 in Khánh Hòa found that between January and June 2025, Nikitina committed offences on three separate occasions.



The stunts were filmed on public roads in the Cam Lâm and Nam Cam Ranh communes.

In Vietnam, such behaviour is seen as disrespectful to local culture and an insult to public decency, particularly when carried out by a foreign visitor.

Local police in the Communist state urged all residents and visitors to “strictly comply with road traffic safety laws”, warning that dangerous or offensive acts would be punished to ensure a “safe and civilised traffic environment”.

It comes as several influencers have been kicked out of asian countries for similar acts.

In 2021, Luiza Kosykh, 40, was deported from Bali posing naked on a 700-year-old sacred tree in Tabanan, Bali.



The images went viral on social media after local businesswoman Ni Luh Putu Ary Pertami Djelantik, shared the photos online.

She captioned them: “To all foreigners who disrespect our land, Bali is our home, not yours!”

Kosykh was reportedly the 59th Russian national to be deported from Bali in 2022.

Russian yoga practitioner Alina Fazleeva also faced backlash for posing naked by the same tree in 2022.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The 28-year-old and her husband performed rituals at Babakan Temple in an attempt to apologise to the spirits for their actions.



Nevertheless, the couple were still deported from Indonesia.

News.title: Rise of upstart parties who reflect peoples’ views rather than treat them with contempt is starting to look unstoppable
News.content:
Next

REMEMBER when Remainers tried to make out that Britain was a racist, xenophobic hellhole drifting off into the Mid Atlantic, far away from the EU’s terribly nice social democracies with their lofty ideals of free movement?

It never was the slightest bit accurate, but it is an image which is becoming even harder to sustain amid the rise of anti- migration parties across Europe.



The weekend’s regional elections in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, on Germany’s Baltic coast, were not just a defeat for the Christian Democrats and their leader Friedrich Merz. They were an utter humiliation.

The CDU — which is equivalent to Britain’s Conservative Party — was reduced to just 4.9 per cent of the vote, below the five per cent required for the party to take a single seat in the regional parliament.



Remarkably, this was the home region of Angela Merkel, former leader of the CDU who served as Germany’s Chancellor for 16 years.

Contrary to those who claim it is an extremist party, the right-wing Alternative For Germany — which got most votes in the elections — supports asylum for people genuinely fleeing from persecution and war, as well as Germany being open to skilled migrants.

But it proposes a much tougher line on illegal arrivals of economic migrants. It wants failed asylum seekers or migrants who commit crimes to be returned to their home countries or a third country, no questions asked.

The AfD has also demanded that the EU’s rules on free movement be reformed to stop migration from Eastern Europe.

This is exactly what David Cameron asked for in his half-hearted renegotiation of the terms of Britain’s membership of the EU ahead of the 2016 vote.

The EU is not going to be able to resist wholesale reform of its free movement and migration policies for much longer, because much of the continent is undergoing a political revolution.



In France, Marine Le Pen is looking a likely victor of next year’s presidential election, assuming she is not banned from standing. In Italy, Giorgia Meloni — who was denounced a fascist when she took office four years ago — has revived economic growth and much reduced illegal migration.

In the Netherlands, the Freedom Party, which is far further to the right than any mainstream UK political party, is now the largest party in Parliament.

Sweden, which until a few years ago had the most liberal migration policy in Europe, now has one of the harshest policies.



You don’t have to be left-wing to think it has now flipped too far the other way, expelling UK citizens who are long-established residents of Sweden.

The only exception to Europe’s rightwards turn on migration is Spain’s socialist government, which recently offered an amnesty to more than a million illegal migrants.

As a result, other EU countries have threatened to suspend the Schengen agreement on open borders. Merz seems to think he can carry on as Germany’s Chancellor, but that is going to be an uphill struggle.

Merz is only Chancellor thanks to his negotiating a “grand coalition” including the CDU and the Social Democratic Party. It is rather as if Labour and the Tories were in government together.

It isn’t going to take much for the SPD to sniff blood, pull the plug and cause the government to collapse.



The fact the CDU and SPD were prepared to form a coalition to keep the AfD out of power tells you all you need to know about politics in Germany and other EU countries.

For decades, the established parties have acted as a cartel, trying to squeeze out opposition. A shady organisation called the Society for Civil Rights, which grew out of the Green Party, has even tried to have AfD banned on the grounds its policies are unconstitutional.

It doesn’t seem to occur to such people that banning a political party with mass support would cause mass anger.



Voters would just flock to new parties which, inevitably, would appear in its image.

Ever since World War Two, the attitude towards democracy in Germany and many other European countries is that the people need to be protected against themselves. Democracy, goes the thinking, gave us Hitler.

Therefore, politics can only be allowed to operate within a narrow range of acceptable views, enforced through the European Court of Human Rights.

The establishment parties see themselves as moderates or centrists, but are they really?

Merkel was author of the most extreme migration policy of all: “Willkommenskultur”, which meant opening Germany’s border to any migrant who could reach the country.



More than a million people swiftly took advantage before she was forced into a rethink.

It didn’t seem to occur to her that there are around 7.5billion people living in countries with a lower GDP per capita than Germany, who could potentially better themselves by moving there.

How did she imagine that 84million Germans would be able to support even a tiny fraction of these people?

Open migration simply is not compatible with the generous welfare systems found in European social democracies. That ought to be obvious.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Merz, to his credit, opposed Merkel’s open-door policies but, even so, Germans are losing patience with the political establishment.



The rise of upstart parties who reflect the views of the people rather than treating them with contempt is beginning to look unstoppable.

News.title: Migrant dinghy reaches UK without being intercepted by Border Force as five detained in first breach in a year
News.content:
BORDER FEARS Migrant dinghy reaches UK without being intercepted by Border Force as five detained in first breach in a year







Next

FIVE people have been detained after a migrant boat reached Kent without being intercepted.

They were held and passed to Border Security Command when the dinghy made it to shore at Folkestone today.



All those who arrived on the boat were understood to be accounted for and detained.

Migrants crossing the Channel are usually brought to shore by Border Security Command or RNLI boats but one is said to have slipped through today.



This was the first small boat to arrive at the UK coast without a escort since September 6, 2025.

The Home Office has launched an investigation into the incident.



A spokesperson said: “This was an isolated and rare incident. Officers responded quickly.”

Kent Police were first alerted to the boat at 9.25am on Monday morning.

People in life jackets were seen being taken into the border security command compound in Dover.

This comes after a teenage asylum seeker who piloted an overcrowded, deflating mega-dinghy across the English Channel was jailed.



Chan Atak, 19, carried the record number of passengers – including 31 children as young as 14 – on the Channel crossing on July 23.

Earlier this month, a dinghy carrying 140 migrants made what is believed to be the longest crossing of the English channel yet, departing from Normandy, 170 miles from where they usually launch around Calais.

Demonstrators rocked up in their droves to block the only access road to the marina in Eastney, where it is thought the migrants were being held.

Following protests at Portsmouth and Dover the far-right Patriot Platform group have plotted to “stop the boats” by intercepting them in the English Channel.

The Sun on Sunday revealed the anti-migrant protest group is said to be considering taking out a vessel to confront would-be asylum seekers as they cross to Britain.



This would likely involve the group taking a hired boat into international waters, potentially disrupting the busiest shipping lane in the world.

News.title: RAF to give air support to Saudi Arabia as Kingdom fights Iran-backed Houthi rebels trying to seize shipping lane
News.content:
Next

THE RAF has been scrambled to help Saudi Arabia combat Houthi terrorists who are targeting ships in a key trade route.

Andy Burnham confirmed he authorised a military jet to aid the Kingdom in repelling the Iran-backed militia who are causing havoc in the Gulf.



The PM pressed the button on his major foreign policy call to help alleviate the cost of living pressures for UK families feeling the pinch of high fuel prices.

An A400M Voyager jet will depart Britain’s Cyprus base in the coming days to assist Saudi top guns with air-to-air refuelling for defensive purposes.



Speaking on the way to the United Nations in New York overnight, Mr Burnham said: “We have received a request from the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia for military support, and on the advice of the Defence Secretary and the Foreign Secretary, last night I agreed to that request for defensive air- t-o air refuelling, and that’s the agreement that we’ve given.

“And I go back to the point I made about cost of living pressures and acting to secure the interests of Britain and the wider region, because of course Saudi Arabia has been experiencing attack, is looking at potential further disruption, and we need to keep those pathways open, and hence our agreement to the request.”

It is Mr Burnham’s first major military intervention since becoming PM.

The UK will provide “defensive air-to-air refuelling” support, he said.

Houthi strikes on ships in the Bab al-Mandab strait have disrupted trade and contributed to the soaring price of oil.

The decades-long war between Houthi rebels and Saudi Arabia has reignited in recent weeks with tit-for-tat strikes between both sides.



The fighting broke out after years of relative peace near the beginning of the US-Israeli conflict with Iran in February.

Over the last few weeks, the Iranian-backed proxy has claimed key islands and territories by the Bab al-Mandab strait – a key naval chokepoint which leads to one of the most important global trade routes, the Suez Canal.

The shipping artery, reached by passing through the Red Sea, could spark global energy chaos if shut off – much like the Strait of Hormuz.



Saudi Arabia, the world’s biggest oil exporter, has also been forced to cut its shipments after Houthi strikes targeted one of its most important pipelines – rendering it useless for weeks.

The UK’s support for Saudi Arabia could begin within the next few days, The Times reports.

It is understood to be “time limited” and likely to last “for weeks”.



Mr Burnham made the comments ahead of his first meeting with Donald Trump.

The PM is expected to urge the US president to tone down his war with Iran while pointing out the far-reaching consequences on ordinary people.

He said the decision to provide the Kingdom with air support was linked to cost-of-living squeezes felt in Britain.



“I go back to the point I made about cost-of-living pressures and acting to secure the interests of Britain and the wider region,” he said.

“Because of course Saudi Arabia has been experiencing attacks, is looking at potential further disruption, and we need to keep those pathways open, and hence our agreement to the request.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Last week, the Houthis were accused of launching a drone towards Saudi Arabia’s holy city of Mecca.

Riyadh warned the Iranian-backed terror group’s alleged attack was a “red line”.

News.title: Burnham expects to find 'common ground' with Trump in first meeting
News.content:
Asked about the state of the relationship between the UK and US, the prime minister said he believes it is "as strong as it's ever been".

Burnham has travelled to New York with his wife, Marie-France Van Heel, for a day of diplomacy and a speech to the UN General Assembly, which is expected to focus on the opportunities and dangers associated with artificial intelligence (AI).

He said: "I will be making the case for closer international cooperation on AI, a just and lasting peace in Ukraine, and renewed efforts to bring an end to the conflict in the Middle East because what happens abroad impacts each and every one of us at home."

The prime minister will also announce the start of work on a new AI and Autonomy partnership between the UK and the US, focused on protecting critical national infrastructure using AI tech.

Lib Dem leader Sir Ed Davey is expected to criticise this plan at the final day of his party's conference, saying it "doesn't come close to meeting the scale of the threat" and "only risks making us more dependent on a Trump administration in the pocket of the tech bros".

He will also call for a global pause on superintelligent AI and propose a new International AI Safety Agency.

His criticisms come after a series of stark warnings from the AI industry about the technology's possible dangers.

For a new British prime minister, the first meeting with a US president has always been a pivotal encounter, but officials are well aware of the added jeopardy of a public appearance alongside the most unpredictable president in American history.

In advance of the meeting, the UK revealed that the UK and the US have, for the first time, fired an American torpedo from a British undersea drone in a military exercise.

The torpedo, described as "heavyweight" by UK officials, is "designed to sink ships and deep diving submarines", Downing Street said.

It was launched in UK waters last week from a 12-metre long undersea drone called Excalibur, made in Plymouth.

It is the first time either the UK or the US have launched a torpedo from an uncrewed underwater vessel, rather than a crewed submarine, and is seen as a breakthrough in attempts to protect vital infrastructure such as deep sea data cables.

"Our work together already shows what can be achieved when our two countries combine our expertise and innovation," the prime minister said.

Burnham was also asked by reporters about the UK government seeking to hand over the Chagos Islands to Mauritius and pay to lease back the joint US-UK military base on Diego Garcia.

It was confirmed in April that the deal had been paused indefinitely because of Trump pulling his support.

Burnham spoke to the Mauritian prime minister, Navin Ramgoolam, on Monday.

He was asked by reporters to outline what he had told Ramgoolam, whether he supported the deal and if he had a plan to convince Trump to back it.

Burnham replied: "I said that we remain determined to secure the long-term operation of the base, which is crucial to our security and that of our allies.

"The assurance I gave was I will work towards a resolution, at the moment we don't have that, but I gave an assurance that I would commit to working towards one."

News.title: UK to provide Saudi Arabia with 'defensive' military support, says Burnham
News.content:
'Defensive support is described by UK officials as activity which could include aiding Saudi air force jets shooting down incoming Houthi missiles and drones.

The singular Voyager aircraft is part of a core fleet of nine - eight military registered and another civilian registered - on the Royal Air Force (RAF)'s books.

The RAF also has five others available for military recall if needed.

Speaking to reporters travelling with him on the way to the United Nations General Assembly in New York, Burnham linked cost of living pressures to the decision.

"I go back to the point I made about cost-of-living pressures and acting to secure the interests of Britain and the wider region," he said.

"Because of course Saudi Arabia has been experiencing attacks, is looking at potential further disruption, and we need to keep those pathways open, and hence our agreement to the request."

Shipping routes through the Red Sea are a vital artery of the world economy.

The Houthis recently seized control of the strategic port city of Mokha and Perim Island, a gateway to the Red Sea - a key shipping route used by Saudi Arabia.

As "military support" goes, Britain's offer of a single Voyager refuelling aircraft is at the lighter end of the spectrum. Some may even see this as a performative gesture to an ally in trouble.

Saudi Arabia is struggling to fend off attacks by Yemen's Houthis who seem to have an inexhaustible supply of drones and missiles to fire at their large and vulnerable Saudi neighbour to the north.

British officials have said this offer is, as they put it, "time limited", perhaps for just a few weeks.

But Yemen has been at war, on and off, since 2014 and this latest upsurge in fighting is made more complicated by the fact the Houthis are backed by Iran which is in its own on-off war with the US.

The risk for Britain here is limited but wars have a habit of drawing nations in with a steadily increasing involvement. That may well suit the Saudis but it is unlikely to please most people in Britain.

In a BBC interview last week, Nato Secretary-General Mark Rutte hinted that European support for Saudi Arabia was also likely.

He said: "I would not be surprised if some phone calls were taking place between European allies, 'hey, how are we going to deal with this?'.

"Let's see what happens, and if Nato can help, we will always be helpful."

Energy Minister Martin McCluskey last week told MPs that the UK was "providing air defence support" to Saudi Arabia through the defence partnership that they have, although would not be drawn on questions of operational military activity.

In January 2024, the UK joined the US in launching air strikes against Houthi targets across Yemen.

Then-Prime Minister Rishi Sunak said the UK "acted in self-defence" following the Houthis' targeting of ships, including a Royal Navy warship.

He also said the strikes were "necessary, proportionate, and targeted" to protect lives and commercial shipping.

Further joint air strikes from the UK and US followed in 2024, external.

News.title: Airlines criticise air traffic control as second glitch causes more disruption
News.content:
Airlines have criticised the UK's air traffic control system after a second technical problem in two weeks caused major disruption to UK flights.

EasyJet said Monday's incident "once again calls into question the resilience" of the service, while Wizz Air said there was a "national confidence crisis" in National Air Traffic Services (Nats), which runs the UK's air traffic.

Nats said a "connectivity issue" at Prestwick was behind the disruption across Scotland, Northern Ireland and northern England - and had "nothing to do" with a separate software defect at Swanwick earlier this month.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said further issues today "cause even greater concern" about the UK's air traffic control.

When asked by reporters whether he would look to fire the head of Nats, Burnham said "these are clearly serious issues and they need to be fully investigated".

He added that the transport secretary was taking the issues "extremely seriously" and initially it's a matter for her "to get to the bottom of... and why there has been a recurrence."

The underlying issue causing Monday's disruption has since been resolved, with Nats saying it was running at "full capacity", although officials warned of knock-on effects.

A spokesperson said they were now "focused on working with our customers to recover their residual delays and help get their operations back to normal".

More than 150 flights were cancelled at UK airports on Monday - including 140 departures and 137 arrivals, according to aviation analytics company Cirium.

Easyjet was the worst affected airline, with 48 of its 670 scheduled departures cancelled, while British Airways has seen 13 cancellations from its 513 scheduled departures.

The UK Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) said passengers who had flights disrupted were "unlikely" to be entitled to compensation.

It said the technical issue is "likely to be considered the result of 'extraordinary circumstances' under passenger rights rules", meaning that "although passengers should be looked after by airlines, they are unlikely to be entitled to compensation for delays or cancellations that were directly caused by the incident".

An independent review by the CAA into the resilience of the UK's air traffic control system is under way and the results will be published "within six months", it said.

News.title: Lithuania ready to 'fight back' but has evacuation plans in face of Russia threats, PM tells BBC
News.content:
Lithuania's prime minister has told the BBC his country has made evacuation plans in the face of threats from Russia, but added they "will not surrender" if attacked.

Prime Minister Mindaugas SinkeviÄius told Newsnight that Lithuanians feel "constantly threatened" by Russia, in part because of drones entering the nation's airspace.

He told Newsnight if his country was attacked, "we will fight back... we will engage". But he said there were plans for a "variety of scenarios" and used an example of getting elderly citizens out of cities "smoothly" and avoiding traffic jams.

Lithuania, a Nato member, shares a land border with the Russian enclave of Kaliningad.

"We're thinking about a variety of scenarios, not all of them are being discussed very much publicly," SinkeviÄius told the BBC.

"We face concrete threats, not on a daily basis, but we're experiencing them and it's a true reality for us."

SinkeviÄius also said the UK needed a "shift in the mindset" in terms of its approach to defence, but noted that Lithuania was "closer to the border and closer to [the] threat".

It comes just a week after Nato fighter pilots shot down a drone that entered Lithuania's airspace.

Though the origins of the drone have not been confirmed, Lithuanian Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas told Newshour that it came from the direction of Belarus, Lithuania's neighbour and a key Russian ally.

The UK's Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said: "Thanks to the swift and professional actions of Lithuanian and Italian forces, Nato once again demonstrated our readiness to protect our airspace.

"We stand united, around the clock, in defence of every inch of Nato territory."

Moscow did not comment on the incident.

News.title: Flights at major US airports delayed after cable cut by construction workers
News.content:
Hundreds of flights have been delayed at major airports in the US after construction workers accidentally cut a cable needed for air traffic control.

Ground stops and delays were issued on Monday afternoon for airports in New York, Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Massachusetts.

Hours later, US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the cable had been repaired and airports would resume normal operations, though delays were still expected.

The major east coast disruption came ahead of the UN General Assembly (UNGA) in New York City on Tuesday, which is expected to be attended by scores of world leaders arriving into New York-area airports.

That includes UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who managed to board his flight before the delays began and arrived as planned.

The delays happened after the damaged cable impacted the Terminal Radar Approach Control system, which is used to guide planes during takeoff and landing, transport officials said.

New Jersey public transportation agency NJ Transit told CBS News, the BBC's US partner, that its construction workers had accidentally severed the line and that markers had been wrongly placed at the digging site.

The BBC has reached out to NJ Transit for comment.

Duffy earlier said the damage was caused by workers from Amtrak, the US national operator of intercity railroad service, who were doing the construction work. This "caused a telecom outage" which forced the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to ground flights, Duffy posted on X.

An Amtrak spokesperson said in a statement, reported by US media, that the incident involved a NJ Transit contractor. Telecommunications company Verizon, which owns the cable, also said it was not responsible.

The severed cable was actually a backup network, and the error was only discovered after the primary circuit failed, according to the head of the FAA, Bryan Bedford.

Newark Liberty International Airport in New Jersey - one of the three major airports that services New York City - was the most heavily impacted by today's air traffic control disruptions, according to flight-tracking website FlightAware.

It reported that 267 departing flights were delayed today, while a further 257 flights destined for Newark were also delayed.

John F Kennedy International Airport and LaGuardia Airport, both in New York, were also affected, as was Philadelphia International Airport.

One passenger, Douglas Tewnion, said he boarded a flight to New York from Edinburgh and that his plane had been diverted to Boston, Massachusetts instead.

He told the BBC that, two hours after his flight was due into New York, he and the other passengers were still "sitting on the same plane, on the tarmac at Boston with no information".

Though "everyone is in good spirits", Tewnion said "it's just a pain" to see two more hours waiting added onto a lengthy flight.

Additional reporting by Ione Wells

News.title: Watch: Police raid organised crime targets in Teesside
News.content:
Cleveland Police have carried out one of their biggest raids on organised crime targets in years.

About 130 officers were involved in the operation which saw 17 people arrested in the Middlesbrough area.

The raids are part of a response to a crash on the nearby A66 last month, which resulted in the death of two officers in a police pursuit.

Five men also died when their Volkswagen Passat went the wrong way down the road and hit a Cleveland Police armed response vehicle heading in the opposite direction.

The BBC's Stuart Whincup was with the police as they carried out the arrests.

Read more about the raids in this story.

News.title: 'My army dream was ended by childhood eye surgery'
News.content:
Lewis Jackson cannot remember a time when he did not want to join the army and continue a family tradition of military service going back to World War One. That dream was shattered, though, when his application was rejected on medical grounds.

"Serving my country has always been a dream of mine and I never considered that I'd do anything else," said the 21-year-old.

Jackson, from Cirencester, was turned down by the Army because he had cataract surgery at the age of three.

A Ministry of Defence (MoD) spokesperson said: "Service in the Armed Forces is physically demanding, so it's right that we have sensible health and recruitment policies which maintain operational effectiveness but don't unnecessarily exclude people."

The BBC has spoken to potential recruits and professionals who question whether the rules are too strict while some applicants said they had been prevented from joining because of medical conditions they regard as minor or no longer relevant.

News.title: Martha's Rule rolled out at every A&E department in England
News.content:
The NHS is expanding Martha's Rule to all hospital emergency departments in England to help patients and families challenge staff and seek second opinions about their care if they want.

It is named after Martha Mills, who died aged 13 at King's College Hospital in London in 2021 after developing blood poisoning or sepsis. Her family's concerns were not listened to, which later prompted her parents, Merope and Paul, to change that culture by creating the rule.

Patients, loved ones and staff in A&E units will be able to call a dedicated phone number to trigger an urgent review if a patient's condition is deteriorating and they are concerned this is not being listened to.

The nationwide expansion starts now and should be complete by March 2028, following a successful trial at seven trusts. It is already being rolled out across all inpatient wards.

News.title: Manchester to host world leaders at G20 summit in 2027
News.content:
World leaders, including Donald Trump, will head to Manchester next year for the G20 leaders' summit.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who is the former mayor of Greater Manchester, said he was "really pleased" he would be welcoming the US president to the city.

The G20 summit, an annual gathering of the world's biggest economies, will take place on 27 and 28 November 2027 at the Manchester Central Convention Centre. It will be the largest summit ever held in the city.

Manchester was chosen earlier this year, prior to Burnham becoming prime minister. Downing Street said preparations will now step up, with hundreds of local people expected to be involved.

In June, as it looked likely Burnham would become prime minister, Trump called him "the mayor of a town".

Burnham told reporters that in the first phone call between the pair, he told the president: "Manchester isn't 'some town'â¦this is Manchester". He said the "right thing to do" was to laugh about it and "move beyond it".

When he was mayor, Burnham told the Manchester Evening News, external that he "wouldn't welcome" a visit from the American president.

But on his way to New York, where he will meet Trump for the first time on Tuesday, he said "politicians say things throughout their career, but now the important thing is to focus on the moment you are in".

Speaking to the BBC, Councillor Garry Bridges, the new leader of Manchester City Council, said an event like this would have been "unthinkable a couple of years ago" and that he hoped it would change Trump's perception of Manchester.

The UK has hosted the G20 before, in 2009 in London. The cost of the security operation at the time was estimated at Â£7.2m.

As well as the summit in Manchester, there will be events across the country next year as the UK takes on the G20 presidency.

The presidency is currently held by the United States, with this year's summit taking place in Miami in December.

The G20 brings together 19 of the world's largest economies, plus representatives from the European Union and the African Union.

It represents about two-thirds of the world's entire population and more than 85% of the world's wealth.

The annual event was first set up in 1999 with the aim of promoting financial stability and cooperation.

News.title: Vet prescription fees capped under rule changes
News.content:
Written prescription fees from vets will be capped at Â£21 as part of a raft of changes that practices will be legally required to bring in over the coming months.

Vets must also tell clients if cheaper medicine is available online, write price estimates ahead of treatment, and publish price lists for services as part of the rule updates.

The official competition watchdog has brought the measures into force after its investigation into the sector found prices had been rising at nearly twice the rate of inflation.

However, critics say the measures will hit independent vets hardest and will benefit the six firms that own more than two-thirds of practices.

The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) made its remedies for the sector legally binding as of Tuesday and vets have up to 12 months to bring all the changes in.

As well as capping prescription fees, other changes include:

Vet practices must publish a "comprehensive" price list for standard services â including consultations, common procedures, and cremation options

A written estimate must be provided in advance for any treatment expected to cost Â£500 or more, including aftercare costs, plus an itemised bill. Emergencies are the only exception to this

Vet businesses must make clear whether they are part of a group or an independent business

To help pet owners compare local practices, price and ownership information will be made available through the Royal College of Veterinary Surgeons' "Find a Vet" service, which will share the data with third-party comparison sites.

The timelines for when vets need to bring in the fixes depends on the exact regulation and the group's size. The CMA sets it out here., external

"The changes that are being required are changes that will help inform pet owners about prices," said CMA panel chair Martin Coleman.

News.title: Schools not ready for AI and 'crying out' for government guidance, report warns
News.content:
Schools are "crying out" for guidance from government on how pupils and teachers can use AI safely and effectively, a new report has warned.

Sir Anthony Seldon, former head teacher and author on AI in education, says the technology is being used more and more frequently, but that its introduction has been "chaotic and anarchic".

His report calls for the government to roll out a national framework for adopting AI in education in England, including training teachers on how to use it, which schools should use to develop their own "AI strategies" by September next year.

The government says its changes to the curriculum in England will give children digital skills and help them spot disinformation.

Sir Anthony's report, co-authored with venture capitalist Tim Bunting, says schools have not been prepared for AI's arrival.

Sir Anthony co-founded the group AI in Education, which was set up in 2023 to help educational institutions navigate AI safely.

His report argues that getting a grip of AI requires the same level of national urgency as wars and epidemics, and requires a taskforce modelled on the one which helped to roll out the Covid vaccine.

News.title: Scientists discover why Kent meningitis outbreak was so severe
News.content:
"This investigation shows just how quickly and dramatically these bacteria can change," says Dr Charlene Rodrigues, consultant in Pathogen Genomics at UKHSA.

"The fact this outbreak variant was able to spread to so many young people was due to the social environment, a place where lots of close social mixing takes place."

Speaking exclusively to the BBC, she said bacteria are known to undergo changes like this, known as horizontal gene transfer.

Such changes can make infections more severe, and may mean they get past the immune system because people haven't encountered them before.

These events, while rare and unpredictable, could happen again, so experts "should not take their eye off the ball", she added.

Scientists say speed and severity of the Kent outbreak was very unusual. It was described as "unprecedented" and "explosive" at the time, with so many infections happening in one place and over a very short period.

Two people died - a 21-year-old University of Kent student and Juliette Kenny, a sixth-form pupil at Queen Elizabeth's Grammar School in Faversham.

The outbreak is thought to have started in a nightclub called Club Chemistry in the city centre, which was popular with university students.

It's likely one person brought the infection in with them, and then it spread that evening.

Meningitis is passed through close contact - including kissing and sharing drinks or vapes.

Dr Rodrigues suspects the very same genetic changes that made the strain so dangerous may also explain why the outbreak was short-lived and did not continue to spread.

People were generally too sick to be silent carriers who can pass it on unknowingly to others.

Following the Kent outbreak, a one-off menB vaccination programme was launched to protect young people heading to university this autumn.

In July, the Joint Committee on Vaccination and Immunisation (JCVI) also recommended that teenagers should be offered the jab on the NHS around the age of 15, with catch-up programmes for those who would otherwise miss out.

News.title: New right to bereavement leave to cover step and half relatives
News.content:
Following a consultation, the government has now set out exactly who the new right will apply to.

It said including step, half, adoptive, foster and kinship care relationships â where family or friends take care of a child when their parents are not able to - would "bring the UK's laws into the 21st century".

Welcoming the move, the chief executive of the Kinship charity, Lucy Peake, said: "Kinship families grieve the loss of a loved one just like any other family, and this right to take time off work will help ensure they are treated fairly alongside other bereaved families."

Meanwhile, the right also covers women and their partners who experience a pregnancy loss, including miscarriage, terminations and unsuccessful IVF embryo transfers.

It will also apply to the other biological parent, or intended parents in a surrogacy arrangement.

Employees will be able to take the leave flexibly within 56 weeks of the loss, rather than as a full block.

The CBI, which represents UK businesses, said many employers already provide compassionate leave in these circumstances and it would engage with the government and unions to ensure the details work in practice.

However, the government said "there needs to be a safety net beyond this discretion".

Minister for the Future of Work, Kate Dearden, said: "No one should have to fight for time to grieve.

"These changes back people going through some of the hardest moments of life, whoever they are and wherever they work."

Miscarriage UK described the announcement as "an important step in recognising pregnancy loss as a bereavement".

Chief Executive Vicki Robinson said she hoped it would "provide a baseline for employers to go further", with the charity calling for bereavement leave to be paid.

Bereavement support charity Sue Ryder has also called for the right to paid leave, saying bereavement can have a significant financial impact.

News.title: Seventeen arrested in Teesside organised crime raids
News.content:
Police have carried out a series of early morning raids targeting those suspected of being involved in organised crime.

Cleveland Police said 17 people had been arrested during the operation - involving about 130 officers including some from the National Crime Agency - across South Bank, Grangetown and Eston, near Middlesbrough, on Monday.

It is part of a high-profile response to a crash on the nearby A66 last month which came at the end of a police pursuit and left two officers dead.

Five men also died when their Volkswagen Passat went the wrong way down the road and hit a Cleveland Police armed response vehicle heading in the opposite direction.

The force said Monday's raids had seen people arrested on suspicion of various offences including drugs and assault.

A convoy of about a dozen vans started the operation shortly after 08:00 BST, with roads temporarily blocked by patrol cars.

Officers used battering rams to force entry to several properties as parents walked past with their children on the school run.

News.title: Two pilot whales dead after mass stranding
News.content:
Two pilot whales have died after a distressed pod was spotted off the Northumberland coast.

British Divers Marine Life Rescue (BDMLR) said it had been alerted to a group of about 40 whales near to the shore at Amble at 15:00 BST on Sunday.

It said the whales had been "behaving in a distressed manner typically seen prior to a stranding event".

Due to the tides, attempts to refloat the animals had been unsuccessful, the charity said, and rescue teams were forced to withdraw.

Whales are highly social mammals and are well known for stranding in groups because they travel in large, close-knit communities which rely on constant communication.

There are a range of theories for why beachings occur. Some experts say the animals can become disorientated after following fish they hunt to the shore.

Others believe that one individual can mistakenly lead whole groups to shore.

News.title: Young people aren't snowflakes - mental distress is rising, says head of official review
News.content:
Accusations that the young are a snowflake generation are wrong, the head of an independent review into mental health, ADHD and autism has told the BBC.

Prof Peter Fonagy said in an exclusive interview that there had been a real rise in mental distress among children and young people, with anxiety, depression, self-harm and eating disorders the most common.

He said it was "harder to be young" now given the economic and employment uncertainty young people face, coupled with the challenges presented by social media.

His review was ordered nine months ago by Wes Streeting after the then-health secretary claimed in an interview that young people were over-diagnosed and "written off".

It is likely to feed into government policies on everything from NHS services and benefits to support for young people who are not in education, employment or training.

Fonagy said he chose to speak to the BBC ahead of the publication, which is expected later this week, because he was concerned the debate around ADHD and autism would "obscure" the wider issue of mental health.

More than 100 experts and families with experience of mental health problems have worked on the review with Fonagy, a clinical psychologist and adviser to NHS England.

He said it will conclude that the rise in mental health problems since the 1990s was real, with about one in four 16 to 24-year-olds now struggling.

The data on this is contested as some sources rely on self-reporting, while sceptics argue greater awareness and reduced stigma around mental health mean more people are coming forward.

Some have also questioned whether society was now over-medicalising distress in people's lives â giving people diagnoses when what they are facing is temporary stress that they should learn to cope with.

Last year, the BBC found that many GPs had concerns about over-diagnosis and felt normal life stresses were being over-medicalised.

NHS figures, external show the number of children and young people in contact with mental health services in England has risen by 50% in the past five years.

Democratic officials and strategists across the country are raising concerns that a significant cash shortage could prevent the party from capitalizing on favorable political conditions in the November midterms.

According to ad-tracking data from AdImpact, Republicans are scheduled to spend $682 million on advertising from Monday through Election Day across all House and Senate races nationwide. By contrast, Democrats have reserved $491 million, giving the GOP a clear financial advantage in key battlegrounds.

The funding disparity is particularly noticeable in specific high-profile races.

In the Texas Senate contest, Republicans are on track to outspend Democrats by more than 8-to-1 through Election Day. In New Hampshire, GOP groups have booked $24 million in ad time compared to $15 million for Democrats. And in an upstate New York House race held by Republican Representative Mike Lawler, GOP reserves total $14.3 million compared to $1.7 million from Democrats.

The financial gap has forced Democratic leaders to step up fundraising efforts, traveling to donor-rich areas like New York to solicit emergency funding. Insiders increasingly anticipate that billionaire Michael Bloomberg may step in with major financial support late in the race, as reported by CNN.

open image in gallery Democratic officials and strategists nationwide warn that a growing funding deficit could prevent the party from capitalizing on a favorable political environment in the midterms ( Getty Images )

Inside the House Democratic caucus, leadership has increased pressure on members to contribute.

During a recent internal strategy meeting, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and his team announced an additional $2 million commitment, while individual lawmakers pledged amounts ranging from $10,000 to $250,000. Representative Susie Lee suggested tying committee assignments to financial contributions.

“If you want to see a gavel in your hand, you should be feeling some pain and putting some money in and helping us get the majority,” Lee said.

By contrast, a closed-door meeting hosted by Vice President JD Vance for House Republicans generated roughly $20 million, a person briefed on the fundraising totals told CNN.

open image in gallery House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and his team announced an additional $2 million commitment during a recent internal strategy meeting ( Getty )

Despite the spending gap, senior Democrats express confidence in their ability to win, citing economic concerns and low public approval ratings for Donald Trump.

“We will have the money necessary to defend all of our battleground incumbents and at the same period of time, make sure we flip enough seats to take back the House of Representatives and more,” Jeffries told the outlet. “Republicans are desperate right now.”

However, local campaign officials warn that unmatched spending could alter outcomes.

“Unless more resources come in in support for House Democrats, we will ultimately leave seats on the table,” Mike Smith, leader of the primary House Democratic super PAC, told CNN.

Ikebana, the Japanese art of arranging flowers, is a form of expression that dates back more than 500 years. It continues to blossom, quietly, not only with traditionalists but also with newcomers who find its blend of creativity and mindfulness to be restorative.

Ikebana can be a bit like solving a puzzle, except there’s no fixed answer. Because each flower, and human individual, is different, there are multiple solutions.

“There’s a ‘detox’ purifying factor, and a healing,” says Hiroyuki Okada, 40, who began taking lessons in ikebana about seven years ago. He now teaches Ikenobo, the oldest of three major ikebana schools.

Okada, who also teaches backflips to anyone who wants to learn, usually wears silver chains and jeans, but he wears a nice kimono when he formally demonstrates his arrangements. He considers himself typical of those drawn to ikebana today, people looking for joy, purpose, or solace from the daily grind or pain of modern life.

“In arranging (flowers), you are dealing with the life that is there, the beauty, of course, but you find what’s in your heart,” said Okada. “You come face to face with yourself.”

The Kyoto-based Ikenobo school, which is rooted in Buddhism, now has chapters around the world.

Okada's previous job at a nonprofit involved talking to people from around the world, and he realized how different — and alike — people were. When he switched to his current job, at a flower shop, he decided to take up a pursuit that was Japanese, so he could explore that aspect of himself, and one that could be done for a long time, alone.

Observing how flowers and plants grow is part of the art

Ikebana involves interacting with nature, although on a small scale — usually in a little vase.

“It is about the relationship of the creator with the flowers,” said Senko Ikenobo, headmaster-designate of the Ikenobo school.

Her family dates back generations to the originators of the art. Her father is the current headmaster.

Jeannette Haviland-Jones, professor of social psychology at Rutgers University, says studies have shown “that flowers and even flower scents promote happiness in people. We suggested a coevolutionary theory for this in which flowers became the ‘pets’ of the plant world.”

Besides a flower's beauty and fragrance, the feel of its petals and leaves to the touch is crucial, like petting a kitten or a puppy, according to Okada.

Ikebana can be for everyone

There are toddlers who do Ikenobo, copying their moms, and there are devoted centenarians. The headmaster-designate says she has seen ikebana help women who are juggling work and motherhood, or taking care of aging parents.

Ikebana has a healing effect similar to that of yoga, meditation or play, says Mayu Shimizu, who works for an online educational service and has been taking lessons from Okada for about three years.

“I like this moment of nothingness when you are concentrating on the flowers before you,” she says. “My mind feels clearer. I feel more at peace, and gentle.”

Flowers portray the stages of human life and connect people

One traditional Ikenobo arrangement is shoka shofutai, which attempts to arrange the flowers, leaves and branches as they might look in nature, reaching toward sunlight or bending in the wind. The vase, sometimes crafted from wood or pottery, also becomes part of the arrangement's vision.

Yet the overall look is pure and simple, expressing the life cycle of flowers — from blossoming through withering — through three main elements:

— Shin, the tallest element, is arranged first, representing one's core, reaching up toward the sky.

— Soe, which is trimmed to about two-thirds the height of the shin and is placed at the side, expresses the flower’s individuality. The leaves might be slightly faded, representing the later stages of life.

— Tai, the third element, is the future. Choose a blossom or fresh small leaves — things that are being born.

There are also freer, spinoff styles that look more like casual, Western-style bouquets than the stoic, textbook-oriented shoka shofutai. That may feel easier, and more fun, for beginners.

Just as ikebana connects a person with flowers, those who practice the art say it’s also about the passing of the art over generations, connecting people.

___

Yuri Kageyama is on Threads: https://www.threads.com/@yurikageyama

The U.S. and China have made uneven progress in fulfilling the trade commitments announced after their two leaders met in Beijing in May.

As U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping sit down in Washington this week, the question is whether their second face-to-face meeting this year can jolt their governments into moving forward on issues ranging from exports of beef and Boeing aircraft to artificial intelligence.

Modest progress is likely, but analysts don't expect any major breakthroughs from Xi's visit, which begins Wednesday.

“Instead, the main deliverable really is that the trip is happening, and the symbolism and the optics of that,” said Sara Schuman, the former senior U.S. negotiator for China trade and an adjunct fellow with the Washington-based Center for a New American Security.

The two countries agreed in May on a framework of “constructive strategic stability,” under which they would seek to prevent disagreements from escalating. One hope is to find areas of cooperation, even if fundamental differences remain.

Positive signals on a Board of Trade

Much of the speculation about this week's meeting has been on the possible launch of a Board of Trade, together with reciprocal tariff reductions on $30 billion of goods in each direction. Both steps were agreed to in May.

A Chinese Commerce Ministry spokesperson said earlier this month that the two sides hope to implement the tariff reductions “at an early date.” Analysts expect an announcement, though some think it will fall short of $30 billion.

About 10 product categories are under discussion, but there are disagreements over the scope of the initiative, experts at the World Economic Forum wrote last week.

The tariff cuts would be limited to nonsensitive items. Analysts said that could include toys, holiday decorations and other low-end factory products from China. For American farmers, Chinese tariffs could be lowered on agricultural exports to China.

“I think for the president, he wants to be able to demonstrate, just before the midterms, that this approach is working and that it benefits voters,” Schuman said, referring to U.S. congressional elections in November.

Chinese farm purchases may fall short

The White House said in May that China had agreed to buy at least $17 billion annually in American agricultural products, on top of an earlier pledge to buy 25 million metric tons of soybeans a year.

That would bring China's total yearly farm purchases from the U.S. to about $30 billion, according to Luke Lindberg, the U.S. undersecretary of agriculture for trade.

It's unclear if that level will be reached. The U.S. Department of Agriculture forecast last month that China would import $21.5 billion of American farm goods in the 12-month period starting Oct. 1.

The two sides also agreed in May to work actively to reduce barriers to dairy, seafood and potted bonsai exports from China, and beef and poultry from the U.S.

China has renewed registrations for American beef plants, but negotiators are working on technical issues to clear U.S. shipments at Chinese ports, said Joe Schuele of the U.S. Meat Export Federation.

“Hopefully it will get worked out soon,” he said.

Boeing is still waiting for orders

China, a major commercial aviation market, promised to buy 200 Boeing planes in May. Four months later, those sales have yet to materialize.

Boeing CEO Kelly Ortberg said last week that Chinese airlines would announce the orders on their schedule.

“We're progressing nicely,” he told analysts. “And I'm confident that we will be receiving orders.”

The Chinese have been concerned about access to aircraft parts, said Craig Allen, a nonresident fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute.

AI is finally getting attention

Little came of an agreement to set up a dialogue on AI until a recent flurry of activity spurred by industry fears about it being misused.

“AI is now on people’s minds,” said Alvin Graylin, a senior fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute.

But while the world's two leading AI nations share concerns over risks, they also see each other as competitors, hindering cooperation.

“They see little reason to collaborate in areas where they believe a competitive advantage is key, regardless of what they say about wanting to get along,” said Ja Ian Chong, a political scientist at the National University of Singapore.

A smaller step would be setting up a channel for crisis communications.

“Given how low the trust is between these two countries, it’s really important that people know who their counterparts are and can call them when there’s a crisis,” said Schuman, the former trade negotiator.

Little hope for a Board of Investment

An agreement to form a Board of Investment, also announced in May, has proved to be a more difficult proposition than the one on trade.

Though Trump welcomes new factories in the United States, Chinese investment is drawing scrutiny from the U.S. Congress over security and strategic concerns in an era of U.S.-China competition.

China is likewise cautious about exporting its technology to the U.S. and unsure whether it is safe to invest in the country, said Kurt Tong, a former U.S. diplomat now with The Asia Group consultancy.

“It kind of sets up a parameter on how far the relationship might be able to improve, given the levels of suspicion between the U.S. and China,” he said.

___

Tang reported from Washington. AP journalists Rio Yamat in Las Vegas and Chan Ho-him in Hong Kong contributed to this report.

An unincorporated mountain outpost deep in northern California's Feather River Canyon has been put on the market for $4.75 million as its long-time owner prepares to leave after more than five decades.

Belden, an 87-year-old historic gold rush settlement in Plumas County, is currently owned by Ivan Coffman. The former mason from Fresno, Coffman bought the property in 1989 after decades spent mining the local waters.

He is now selling the entire compound, which includes a two-story resort and lodge, restaurant, bar, general store, mechanics garage, schoolhouse and colorful rental cabins.

The decision to sell comes after a series of personal shifts and tragedies for Coffman, as reported by SFGate. The Dixie Fire in 2021 burned surrounding hillsides and destroyed the nearby town of Greenville, but Belden survived because Coffman’s son and several employees stayed behind to combat the flames.

Coffman’s son died earlier this year due to health complications, prompting Coffman to finally put the property up for sale.

open image in gallery Belden, a remote mountain settlement deep in Northern California’s Feather River Canyon, is up for sale for $4.75 million, as its owner of more than five decades prepares to move on ( Google Maps )

“Oh, I guess all the people you meet over the years,” Coffman told SFGate when asked what he loved most about the place. “And you know, as time goes on, you look back on a lot of things.”

Coffman originally stumbled upon Belden during a week off from his masonry work in 1970. Following a major flood that shifted the riverbed, he discovered rich deposits of gold nuggets at the junction where Yellow Creek enters the Feather River.

“That year, we had a terrific flood that washed a huge bar of gravel off down into this hole, and that’s what left all that gold layin’ there,” Coffman said. “It’d been hidden for all them years.”

open image in gallery A former mason, Ivan Coffman built his life in the Feather River Canyon after stumbling upon a riverbed filled with gold nuggets in 1970 ( Getty Images )

During that single trip, Coffman recovered roughly 50 ounces of gold — worth about $35 an ounce at the time, compared to modern values of around $4,400 an ounce. He called his business partner to say he was extending his trip and never returned to his masonry career, expanding instead into jewelry making, private lending and eventually real estate.

Belden’s history dates back to the California Gold Rush, when it operated as a bustling camp of roughly 1,000 residents. As gold mining waned, the area transitioned into a logging and railroad outpost before turning to tourism and river fishing.

Mid-20th-century dam construction along the Feather River altered the local ecology and reduced fish populations, driving the area into economic decline.

open image in gallery Belden narrowly survived the 2021 Dixie Fire, which charred the surrounding terrain and completely destroyed the nearby community of Greenville ( AFP via Getty Images )

By the time Coffman purchased Belden in 1989, a 1970s fire had left most of its original structures in ruins. Coffman rebuilt the property, transforming it into an off-grid haven for travelers, Pacific Crest Trail hikers and motorcyclists.

Author Cheryl Strayed highlighted her arrival at the compound in her 2013 memoir “Wild,” describing her relief at reaching the remote resort during her trek. In recent years, the secluded location has also gained popularity as an all-night music festival venue, according to SFGate.

Despite its tiny permanent population of 15, the property operates as a self-contained community off Highway 70. The main lodge houses an array of vintage items, including historical taxidermy, art and an antique slot machine.

open image in gallery Belden’s central lodge features a collection of vintage items, including local artwork, historical taxidermy and an antique slot machine ( Google Maps )

Josie Litchfield, a friend helping Coffman market the listing, noted his enduring role as the host of the property.

“Who wants to be the next mayor of Belden Town?” Litchfield wrote in an email regarding the listing.

Coffman remains known for his casual hospitality toward passersby, frequently opening the closed lodge to assist travelers. During a recent visit, he offered a free bottle of water to a cancer survivor who required bottled water due to treatment.

“Well, even though we’re not open now, I can grab you a bottle of water if you need something right now,” Coffman told the visitor, refusing payment. “I’ll just give it to you, how’s that?”

News.content:

Flight operations are resuming across major East Coast airports after telecommunications lines damaged in a construction accident were repaired on Monday evening, according to federal officials.

The outage was triggered when the primary communications circuit failed at the Federal Aviation Administration's Philadelphia Terminal Radar Approach Control, or TRACON, facility and controllers discovered a backup fiber optic line had also been severed in New Jersey.

The facility handles radar and radio guidance for the region’s airspace, forcing the FAA to order ground stops that halted incoming traffic at New York’s John F. Kennedy, LaGuardia and Newark Liberty airports, as well as Philadelphia International, Boston Logan and Teterboro Airport.

The outage grounded over 1,000 flights nationwide and delayed more than 5,600 others on Monday, hitting Newark and Philadelphia the hardest.

Officials said the severed fiber optic cable was located at a rail construction site between New Brunswick and Newark, a critical corridor carrying telecommunications data for regional air traffic management.

Newark is a major United Airlines hub, while Philadelphia (pictured) is an American Airlines hub ( Getty Images )

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy wrote on X that an “Amtrak construction crew accidentally cut into a fiber line in New Jersey, which caused a telecom outage and forced FAA to pause flights in the Northeast.”

In his post, Duffy said that flights were resuming at LaGuardia and Philadelphia, while incoming traffic to Newark Liberty, John F. Kennedy and Teterboro remained paused.

“This incident underscores the need for additional funding to modernize aging infrastructure and prevent disruptions like this in the future,” Duffy wrote.

Responsibility for the severed fiber line prompted conflicting statements on Monday, as reported by the Associated Press.

Duffy initially blamed an Amtrak construction crew for cutting the wire. However, Amtrak denied involvement, with representatives pointing toward a New Jersey Transit construction crew operating in the area between Newark and New Brunswick. Officials with NJ Transit said they were investigating whether contractor crews or telecom utility markings were at fault.

The outage came as 130 world leaders and dozens of ministers were arriving in New York for the annual high-level meeting of the United Nations General Assembly.

Travelers stranded across the region posted updates on social media as the delays grew.

“Man, worst possible day for all New York City airports — JFK, LaGuardia, AND Newark — to go down,” Matthew Boyle posted on X as he was preparing to board a flight from Washington, D.C. to New York that was delayed just before boarding. “Beginning of the UNGA high-level week, and apparently FAA problems shutting all three down. (As I was about to board a flight from DC to NY, they delayed it just before we got on plane). Insane.”

Another user by the handle OkadikeOnyeisi wrote on X that the ground stops create “an enormous logistical challenge for airlines, passengers, security teams, and diplomatic delegations” during “an especially sensitive time, with the UN General Assembly bringing hundreds of world leaders and international delegations into New York.”

The outages also prompted concern among travelers regarding heightened security measures.

“I took a flight from Austin to JFK yesterday that had additional TSA check at the gate itself,” X user Michael Scaglione posted. “They assured us it was random, but another person flying told me her flight from Maine to NYC also had additional TSA check at the gate there. “They are lying. Something’s going on.”

The Philadelphia TRACON facility has faced lingering scrutiny regarding its infrastructure. In May 2025, the same air traffic operation guiding flights around Newark suffered repeated communication blackouts. Telecommunications outages also disrupted controller radar displays at Philadelphia TRACON last year.

Congress previously approved $12.5 billion to modernize aging air traffic management infrastructure and expand controller hiring to resolve chronic system vulnerabilities.

The outage at the major U.S. airports comes as the United Kingdom is dealing with its own flight issues.

A “connectivity issue” at NATS Prestwick control center in Scotland grounded flights across Edinburgh, Leeds Bradford, Belfast and Manchester on Monday, disrupting thousands of travelers.

News.content:
