Sports.title: Red Bull admits Verstappen's mysterious car issue cannot be fully fixed until 2027
Sports.content:
During several weekends this season, Verstappen has complained that the Red Bull Formula 1 car gets worse over the course of a session or race. It usually happens at the rear axle, including during qualifying at Monza, where Verstappen called the RB22 "a car made of paper".

Notably, the four-time world champion added that he has been complaining about this internally for years. According to Verstappen, Red Bull has been struggling with car degradation during a session for multiple seasons, which is remarkable given that the 2026 car is completely new following the overhaul of the technical regulations.

It raises the question of why the problem is so persistent and whether Red Bull now finally understands what is behind it.

When Autosport puts those questions to Red Bull team principal Laurent Mekies, the Frenchman replied: "I don't think we are going to explain what it is and how we are going to fix it. But I think Max is right [in saying] that there is an element of car performance degradation that is happening through a session and through a race.

"He's also right in saying that it's not a new issue. We are not sleeping on it. We have been trying to tackle that in different ways.

"I consider it a complex issue. Otherwise, we would get to the bottom of it. But everyone is very constructive about it and we are trying to make small steps at the time to be able to finally get to the bottom of it."

Verstappen said at Monza that the Red Bull car is “made of paper” after he suffered from “car degradation” during qualifying Photo by: Alex Bierens de Haan / Getty Images

As for those small steps, Mekies says several lessons were learned on the Saturday in Monza, when Verstappen voiced his frustration, and Red Bull tried to put those lessons into practice in Madrid. The problem did not occur during F1’s first visit to the Madring, or at least not to the same extent.

"We had a couple of positive steps in that regard this weekend," Mekies said. "It will never be the full picture, but we certainly have, through pain, made progress into our understanding. We don't have all the solutions on the car yet, but I trust that we are in the right way. It will not be fast, so it's something that will probably take us through next year."

In doing so, Mekies acknowledges what Verstappen had already hinted at earlier: some problems simply cannot be fixed this season and require bigger changes to the design and chassis for 2027.

The fact that Red Bull is limited in what it can do for the remainder of this year is partly because the budget cap will come into play at some point and because the focus behind the scenes has already shifted to 2027, but also because certain changes simply cannot be made to the RB22.

Mekies therefore acknowledges that the issue could occur more often in the remaining races this year, although he does not want to go into further detail about exactly what is behind it.

"I'm not going to give any more details here. But as I said, it's true that there are some aspects of the car performance that sometimes don't stay at the optimum level. And that’s serious lap time," he said.

If Verstappen does not win a Grand Prix this season, it will be the first year since 2015 without a race win Photo by: Sam Bagnall / Sutton Images via Getty Images

"So, it's something we [need to get on top of]. There is no doubt that we have everyone trying to improve that for the future."

For this year, Verstappen already knows that there is little left for him to fight for. The Dutchman acknowledged early on that he is not a factor in the title fight and can only hope for a race win.

Should he fail to achieve that, it would be the first time since 2015, when Verstappen was still driving for Toro Rosso – now Racing Bulls. Since his promotion to Red Bull in May 2016, the Dutchman has won at least one grand prix every year.

Sports.title: Mercedes aims to end pole drought with upcoming Malaysia F1 upgrades
Sports.content:
Mercedes has confirmed its next big Formula 1 car upgrade will arrive at the forthcoming grand prix in Malaysia, where it hopes to get back into contention for pole.

The Silver Arrows is the runaway leader of the 2026 championship with a 145-point advantage over second-placed Ferrari, despite its last major upgrade package being Montreal in May.

Mercedes has instead preferred to fit minor race-specific updates whereas its nearest challengers Ferrari and McLaren have been significantly more aggressive with developments.

So although Mercedes won the first six grands prix, it has since won four of the last eight as McLaren and Ferrari have closed their respective gaps taking two wins each in that time.

But the German outfit is hoping to reestablish its dominance during the Malaysian weekend on 2-4 October, the race after Baku, as the Asian country replaces Bahrain to make its F1 return.

Speaking on the Nu Silver Arrows Radio Show podcast, trackside engineering director Andrew Shovlin said: “We haven't got much new coming to Baku, but actually that's a circuit that's more about drag than downforce.

“So the car was good in Monza, hopefully it will work well in Baku. But, you need a car that can have a good straight line speed.

Toto Wolff, Mercedes, James Allison, Mercedes, Andrew Shovlin, Mercedes Photo by: Sam Bloxham / LAT Images via Getty Images

“There's other things, though, you need in Baku, like the sort of street circuit nature, almost that Monaco-esque being able to deal with the low speed, keeping all the wheels on the ground.

“And then the updates, well, they're going to come Malaysia onwards and hopefully we'll make a decent step.

“I don't think we're going to be out front by miles, but hopefully we'll be back into a position where we can really go into qualifying, knowing that we're fighting for pole.”

Although Mercedes has won the last two races - Monza and Madrid - via the dominant Kimi Antonelli, it hasn’t actually claimed pole since the Italian went quickest at Spa in July.

So that is a run of four, three of which saw McLaren’s Lando Norris take pole, marking a far cry from the start of 2026 where the Silver Arrows took pole for each of the opening 10 rounds.

“Early in the season, we tended to go thinking, we have a car that if we do a really good job, it should be on pole,” added Shovlin.

“We should be fighting for a race win. Whereas now the margin between finishing first and finishing sixth is one or two tenths and it's difficult to predict because Monza is a unique track.

“It needs a car that's quite slippy with low drag and then new circuit like Madring couldn't be more different. But we just focus on getting the most out of the car and if we win, awesome.”

Sports.title: Cadillac F1 owners Mark Walter and TWG Global face class-action lawsuit
Sports.content:
Cadillac Formula 1 shareholder Mark Walter has officially become the subject of a class-action lawsuit, while a concurrent investigation into potential fraud between his insurance companies is ongoing.

The class-action lawsuit was filed in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida, and the complaint alleges that Walter used his firms - TWG Global, alongside Delaware Life Insurance and Group 1001 - to execute a scheme aimed at concealing federal investigations and diverting billions of dollars from policyholders' funds.

The lawsuit claims that insurance companies affiliated with Walter used money from annuity policyholders to finance a broader business network.

This network enabled the mogul to acquire stakes in sports franchises like the Los Angeles Dodgers and the Los Angeles Lakers, before expanding into motorsport through TWG Motorsport (a division of TWG Global) by acquiring Andretti Global and partnering with General Motors to launch the Cadillac F1 team.

Media outlets report that instead of maintaining low-risk investments, the insurers funneled approximately 42% of their assets - around $17 billion - into Walter’s private network of business interests.

The lawsuit was brought by 67-year-old Florida resident Ira Rosner, represented by law firm Robbins Geller Rudman & Dowd, who alleges that the insurance companies intentionally withheld key financial disclosures.

Valtteri Bottas, Cadillac Racing Photo by: Alex Bierens de Haan / LAT Images via Getty Images

USA Today reported receiving a response from a spokesperson for Group 1001 Insurance, who acknowledged awareness of the suit while emphasizing: "No court has ruled that Group 1001 Insurance or Delaware Life Insurance Company did anything wrong, and we intend to defend the case vigorously, consistent with our long track record of serving policyholders with integrity."

TWG Global plays a vital role in Cadillac F1's organizational structure, acting as both an investing partner and an operational entity for the team.

While the civil lawsuit does not directly halt track operations and no criminal charges have been filed against executives, the controversy raises questions about the future of Walter's sports holdings. Walter recently agreed to sell his stakes in both the Lakers and Premier League side Chelsea - the latter case a combined 25% holding with Todd Boehly, for which the pair have received almost $1 billion from private equity firm Clearlake.

Just this past August, amid rising scrutiny over Walter's business practices, the team's parent company took a firm stance on Cadillac F1's future, issuing a statement to deny any plans to offload its Formula 1 assets.

"TWG is not considering a sale of the Cadillac team or any other part of TWG Motorsport," the company stated categorically during the Dutch Grand Prix.

Sports.title: How Antonelli's luxury problem is causing Wolff and Mercedes grey hairs
Sports.content:
For better or for worse, there seems to be no slowing down Kimi Antonelli.

Just ask Pete Bonnington, who channelled his inner schoolteacher in Madrid as he relentlessly had to remind the 20-year-old Italian to pay attention to track limits.

Having benefited from an earlier virtual safety car on a circuit where overtaking proved impossible, all Antonelli had to do was to keep it clean until the finish line, with Max Verstappen and Lando Norris resigned to following him home.

Bonnington and Mercedes had already suffered a scare earlier in the race with what almost sounded like a prank call from the young Italian.

Antonelli: "Check the car!"

Bonnington: "Which corner?"

Antonelli: "No I didn't touch any wall, but the steering feels weird..."

But with five laps to go, despite little genuine pressure from behind, Antonelli did tag one of the many concrete walls lining the challenging Madring circuit. "I touched the wall on the entry to Turn 7," Antonelli yelled.

Despite being in control, it was another race where Antonelli had been dangerously flirting with the track limits, much to the dismay of his father Marco and team boss Toto Wolff. There's just no slowing Antonelli down.

"I just discussed it with his father and we were joking: 'What an idiot!'. No, that's just Kimi,” the Mercedes boss said after the race. “The white lines, we had to drum it into his head that he shouldn't go over the white lines. Even in Monza, he still went over the white lines and [risked] the car. And the same with track limits.

"At a certain stage, I said to him: 'Don't you see out of the car? Do we need to sit you that high up so that you have [avoid] those track limit things? We had a laugh about it.

"And today, six laps to the end or whatever it was, he says: 'Check the car, I just brushed the wall.' What?! He's causing us grey hair. But maybe he's like this and maybe that's what's making him so quick."

Wolff added: "He had to hit the wall again because he wants to go fast. Sometimes for me, he's an inch too cool."

Kimi Antonelli is giving Toto Wolff a few grey hairs Photo by: Anni Graf - Formula 1 via Getty Images

Antonelli's flat-out approach appears to be a trait that Wolff and Mercedes are going to have to live with for now, at least until it goes wrong one day. Could that day come when Antonelli starts thinking about the big prize at the end as he careens towards a maiden world championship?

Wolff is adamant that won't be the case, despite Antonelli being by far the youngest driver to ever be in that position. "I promise you he's not thinking about it," Wolff insisted. "The way this kid is able to compartmentalise and be the young kid and then get into the car and be the mature racing driver...

"If Kimi says to himself: 'I'm not thinking about the championship', then he's not thinking about the championship. We are also trying, the parents and myself, the team is saying: 'You know, this is not finished.'

"There are black swan events. They can come and you're losing something out of your hands when you didn't think it was possible to lose. So, he's not going to think about it. We're too grown up and mature for this. We think about worst-case scenarios. He doesn't think about it."

Building on the lessons of a troubled debut year in 2025, Antonelli feels he has the right support system around him to carry him through to the finish line, whether that be in Abu Dhabi or at an impromptu home race in Imola near his native Bologna.

Kimi Antonelli has a strong support network in the paddock Photo by: Sam Bloxham / LAT Images via Getty Images

"I’m lucky to have really good people around me," Antonelli explained. "I have an incredible team that supports me, a great family. Especially my dad is the one who keeps me on the ground. Especially when he sees that I might lose a little bit the way, he doesn’t [hesitate] to tell me off or to just tell me to come back to the ground.

"On my side, as I said many times, I just try to do my best every race, trying to really drive as fast as I can whenever I go in the car. And then we’ll see where we end up at the end of the year. But definitely I don’t want to over-complicate things or just drive worrying about championship or results. Just driving, doing my best."

Driving as fast as he can all the time, is certainly working for Antonelli right now. As far as his team is concerned, almost to a fault.

Sports.title: Former Mercedes F1 tech chief Elliott joins Alpine as CTO
Sports.content:
Alpine has appointed Mike Elliott as chief technical officer of its Formula 1 team, further bolstering the Enstone-based team's technical structure.

Alpine announced on Thursday that Elliott will "oversee the technical and engineering functions at the team's factory at Enstone" in what is a newly created position as CTO.

For the 52-year-old Briton, it presents a return to Enstone after serving as the team's principal aerodynamicist in its Renault and Lotus days.

Elliott then went on to join Mercedes as its head of aerodynamics, helping the team make a head start on the 2014 regulations. Elliott rose to the position of technical director and chief technical officer, trading positions with James Allison, before leaving the Brackley squad in 2023.

"He has a proven track record in the sport, having contributed to an impressive eight constructors' and eight drivers' championships," Alpine stated.

Pierre Gasly, Alpine Photo by: Sam Bagnall / Sutton Images via Getty Images

"Elliott's arrival at Enstone strengthens the team's technical capabilities as the team looks to build on the improved performances on track and close the gap to the top four teams."

Current executive technical director David Sanchez is understood to be reporting into Elliott, who is overseeing the entire technical area of the outfit.

After sacrificing last year, Alpine has made a strong start to the 2026 regulations, fighting Racing Bulls for fifth in the constructors' championship. The 2026 campaign is Alpine's first as a customer team of Mercedes.

Sports.title: Tsunoda's in-depth look at why he failed to master Red Bull’s F1 car in 2025
Sports.content:
It seems almost unfathomable for a title contender's team-mate to end up 17th in the Formula 1 drivers’ standings, yet that’s what happened to Yuki Tsunoda alongside Max Verstappen at Red Bull in 2025.

In a way, it was unprecedented – the closest modern example perhaps was Felipe Massa lying a lowly 16th eight rounds into the 2012 season while Ferrari team-mate Fernando Alonso comfortably led the championship, but the Brazilian somewhat turned the situation around.

Equally, Tsunoda’s case was unique. Having decided to release an underperforming Sergio Perez, Red Bull picked Liam Lawson over Tsunoda for a 2025 promotion, believing the New Zealander’s lack of experience would be offset by his allegedly higher potential.

Lawson didn’t get much time to prove himself. After two grands prix in which he was eliminated in Q1 and failed to score any points, he was sent right back to Racing Bulls, with Tsunoda finally getting his chance at the main team.

At the time, the Japanese was actually quite bullish about his odds of succeeding where so many others had failed.

“People often say Red Bull cars tend to have strong front-end grip. I personally love cars that turn aggressively, and in the past, I adapted my driving style to that kind of set-up,” Tsunoda said ahead of his Red Bull debut.

Liam Lawson, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Red Bull Content Pool

“Racing Bulls traditionally had cars that understeered a bit more, which was challenging for me at first, but I got used to it, and it eventually became my norm. Now, the key will be adjusting to Red Bull’s characteristics again, but considering my past experience, I’m not too worried about it.”

Perhaps he should have been. While Verstappen won eight grands prix – more than anyone, including 2025 champion Lando Norris – Tsunoda failed to take a single podium finish, with his highest result an underwhelming sixth in Baku; he scored 30 points to his team-mate’s 385 over their time together.

In 27 qualifying sessions (sprints included), Tsunoda made it to Q3 eight times, was out in Q2 on nine occasions, and was eliminated as early as Q1 on 10 occurrences. He outqualified his team-mate just once and was 0.6s slower on average.

So, what was the problem with Red Bull’s RB21 F1 car? To some extent, Tsunoda remains at a loss to explain it.

“Normally I'm able to understand the car, what I'm driving, what kind of characteristic,” Tsunoda detailed on the Beyond The Grid podcast, “but it feels like even after Abu Dhabi, I didn't know what kind of car I was driving. I still don't understand what was the issue and what things made me very struggle to learn about this car and get used to the car.

“I thought confidence was there, but some race I just somehow lost the confidence. I still don't understand the car, to be honest.”

Yuki Tsunoda, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Mark Thompson / Getty Images

Still, Tsunoda has fascinating insight to provide. He openly admits he refrained from tweaking his driving style, believing that’s just what works for him. However, he did end up trying out Verstappen’s set-ups – and that experiment just failed.

“One thing about myself: I have big enough ego to not change my driving style,” Tsunoda admitted. “I know what I'm doing in terms of driving and I believe in myself. So, I never try to change my driving style to another driver’s, even though the driver is competitive and fast.

“Obviously for Max, it's a different case. He's a world champion, he proves a lot of things and I still learn a lot of things from his driving.

“My core driving is the same. And at some time, probably the first year out of any years since I started, I thought about changing driving style and trying to do something similar to Max. But in my perspective, if I just look at data, I didn't really see a huge difference in terms of driving.

“What I did most – and what I think now was the biggest mistake last year – was to try to replicate the set-up, what he's doing; even knowing that sometimes, if I feel the car very oversteer, Max's [set-up] in theory makes the car worse, more sensitive in the direction change, or makes the car slide more.

"I tend to choose the set-up, even though I'm already struggling with oversteer. It can happen sometimes the opposite way as well: even though I'm struggling with understeer, his car is more understeer. I try to replicate that.”

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing, Yuki Tsunoda, Red Bull Racing Team Photo by: Zak Mauger / LAT Images via Getty Images

Tsunoda is not the first driver to unsuccessfully attempt to use Verstappen’s set-up. Alex Albon also struggled alongside the Dutchman, for a year and a half, in 2019-20.

Back in 2023, the Anglo-Thai reminisced in the High Performance Podcast: “[Verstappen] has quite a unique driving style, it’s not that easy to get along with. Everyone has a driving style; I would say my driving style is a bit more on the smooth side, but I like a car that has a good front end, so quite sharp, quite direct. Max does too, but his level of sharp and direct is a whole different level – it’s eye-wateringly sharp.

“To give people kind of maybe an explanation of what that might feel like, if you bump up the sensitivity [on a computer game] completely to the max and you move that mouse and it’s just darting across the screen everywhere, that’s kind of how it feels. It becomes so sharp that it makes you a little bit tense.”

This metaphor was brought up to Tsunoda, but he wasn’t convinced it was particularly relevant to the RB21. Asked if he could relate, the Japanese racer said: “Yes and no. First, the car is a lot different to when Alex was driving and I’ve never driven Alex's car.

“It's sensitive, but I didn't feel that sensitive. But at the same time, like I said, it was very up and down. Some tracks I'm driving more sensitive car than him, some tracks he was driving more sensitive. On average, probably he was driving a bit more sensitive car, more like a sharper car than me.

“What he was definitely better at was, even though the car was sensitive or even numb… In a corner, there's always one phase or one moment that the car naturally reacts to, or tries to kind of respect its own behaviour. You know what I mean? Like, always in the corner, as soon as I turn in or whatever, that car does its own thing. That can be like a sensitive, sharp rotation or, I don't know, the front slides or something. He’s able to use that and he can smell that kind of behaviour probably much faster than me. And he was able to maximise that kind of behaviour throughout the corner.

“It's not necessarily my driving style that I'm doing, but if I have that kind of moments, sharp turn-in or rotation or the front slide, I tend to force the car how I want to drive. I normally respect how the car wants to drive through the corner, or I’m able to use that kind of natural behaviour from the car. But I wasn’t able to use that ability much in the Red Bull.”

Yuki Tsunoda, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Zak Mauger / LAT Images via Getty Images

As soon as he first drove the RB21 in free practice at Suzuka, Tsunoda’s early optimism gave way to caution; he reported the car was “feeling a bit more tricky” than on the simulator.

With hindsight, it was a sign of the ordeal to come.

“Even though I said, yeah, I thought I had confidence, probably it was not enough, as much as the VCARB car that I drove for four years,” Tsunoda said. “Red Bull is still a car that was completely different, which I felt as soon as I stepped into that car in Suzuka.

“There's some confidence level I was able to build up, but to maximise that whole performance, I think that was probably something I was missing, and trying to find that confidence throughout the year.”

Tsunoda eventually found out in Qatar, at the penultimate round of the season, that he would not be retained as a race driver and would act as a reserve in 2026 – no huge surprise given his results, and the campaign had been so draining that the news actually was a relief to him.

“I still remember the moments,” he recounted. “Initially, what I got told was from Helmut [Marko, then Red Bull’s motorsport advisor].

“In the end, Helmut is the person that brought me into Formula 1, brought me even to the Red Bull junior programme. We were together since when I was 17, 18. I remember he was also pretty disappointed about that.

Yuki Tsunoda, Red Bull Racing, Helmut Marko, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Mark Thompson - Getty Images

“And when I got told, I still remember, I didn't feel that much of huge disappointment or devastated feeling.

"Obviously I was still disappointed and pretty sad that I'm not driving next year. But not as I expected because I don't know why, somehow in a way, I fought really hard. I fought more than ever in that 2025 year and even if I look back now, I don't have much regret. I gave everything.

“In a way, honestly, my heart was just saying, ‘Okay, now I can be relaxed’. Because it was so stressful, the second half of the 2025 season, where I fought hard with a lot of pressure. Like I was never able to kind of breathe out much.”

Sports.title: Formula 1 cuts grand prix distances for 2027 in latest power unit rules compromise | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Formula 1’s engine regulations have led the series to cut the length of grands prix next year.

The current maximum race distance of 305 kilometres, for all events except Monaco, has been in place for decades.

The FIA confirmed a new maximum of 290 kilometres will apply from next year. The sport’s governing body said the change is being made “in line with the refinements to the power unit regulations to be introduced in 2027 on fuel flow.”

The change has been made necessary as a result of the alterations to the 2027 engine rules which were agreed soon after this season began. After teams realised the current rules forced cars to slow significantly at most circuits to save electrical energy, teams agreed to increase the proportion of combustion power for next year.

As this change will lead to an increase in fuel flow and consumption, some teams faced having to redesign their cars for next year to a greater extent than they originally intended in order to complete existing race distances under the new rules. To avoid this, the FIA has instead agreed to shorten races.

“In line with the refinements to the power unit regulations to be introduced in 2027 on fuel flow, a reduction in the total race distance from 305km to 290km was approved, corresponding to a reduction of two or three laps,” said the FIA in a statement.”

Separately, the FIA has removed the thee-hour time limit on interrupted races. “Regarding races that are disrupted by rain or other factors, it was decided that a hard stop time would be introduced for the end of any racing activity, but that the current limitation of a race to three hours (from its start to its end – including interruptions) would be removed,” it explained. “The limit of two hours of actual racing will remain.”

“These changes were introduced to ensure that the spectators have the best possible chance to enjoy a full race if disruptions occur. It was also agreed that there would be greater flexibility to extend free practice sessions should they be interrupted.”

The FIA also approved rules granting teams greater freedom in developing their gearboxes for next year. “Following consultation with the relevant manufacturer working group, and a recommendation from the Sporting Advisory Committee, it was agreed to remove gearbox homologation for 2027 which would preserve supplier development freedom,” it said.

Sports.title: How to watch the 2026 Azerbaijan GP and why it is being held on a Saturday | TV Times
Sports.content:
There are two significant changes to the usual race weekend format for this weekend’s Azerbaijan Grand Prix.

This is the latest date the race at the Baku City Circuit has ever been held. Formula One Management confirmed it moved the date forward from the usual Sunday slot to Saturday following a request from the government and race promoters “to accommodate a national day”

Azerbaijan’s dictatorial president Ilham Aliyev designated September 27th as a ‘Remembrance Day’ in 2020 to mark the beginning of that year’s war in the Nagorno-Karabakh region. Azerbaijan expelled all ethnic Armenians from the territory in 2023. Aliyev’s ethnic cleansing drove around 100,000 people from their homes.

FOM has agreed all its track sessions will take place a day earlier than usual this weekend. That includes the trio of Formula 2 support races.

The series has added an extra feature race due to the cancellation of its rounds in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia earlier this year due to the Iran war. As it will not accompany F1 to Sepang next week for the ‘Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia’, the F2 drivers have a two-month break until their next event in Qatar, though it remains unclear whether that round or the finale in Abu Dhabi will take place.

Sports.title: Wolff tried to help Masi ‘for the good of the sport, and for us’ in 2021 | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff has revealed details of his conversations with former race director Michael Masi before his controversial call in the 2021 championship-decider.

Masi lost his job over his mishandling of the 2021 Abu Dhabi Grand Prix. He arranged a final-lap restart in contravention of the rules which led Wolff’s driver Lewis Hamilton to lose the championship to Max Verstappen.

Hamilton and Verstappen were involved in a series of controversial collisions over the course of 2021. Wolff, who previously called Masi “disrespectful” and a “liability”, said he had concerns over how the race director reacted to feedback from the drivers.

“I really tried to speak to Michael and guide him all along the year,” Wolff told High Performance. “I said ‘listen I’ve been in the sport for a long time, listen to the drivers, don’t always be stubborn in your decision making, don’t be arrogant’.”

Wolff admitted his motivation in speaking to the race director was partly to advance Mercedes’ interest.

“I tried that for the good of the sport, and obviously also for us as a team not to be vulnerable to situations that could be totally detrimental,” he said.

Masi contradicted the regulations and his past interpretation of them by arranging a final-lap restart at Yas Marina by removing the lapped cars between Hamilton and Verstappen, but not any of the others. The FIA later ruled this had been an error. Verstappen passed Hamilton immediately after the restart, clinching his first world championship and denying Hamilton a record-breaking eighth.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

Wolff said Masi’s actions were “inexcusable.”

“You could say the empathy should make me realise how he feels,” he said. “I realise how it feels.

“And I know that’s not good, and bad, but he could have thought about it all year long, when people, not only me, tried to support him in the right way.

“So sometimes you have to just realise that someone is just doing his own thing or taking his own decisions. So for me, I don’t care about it anymore.”

However he admitted he still reflects on the lost championship “every week”.

“I mainly think about it because I think Lewis deserved to be the greatest of all time with eight world championship titles,” he said. “And you can argue all along about that year.

“I think Max and Lewis were deserving champions. There were instances during the year where Max lost some points that he shouldn’t have lost. You look at the crash in Monza both of them had. So both deserving champions, but on that particular afternoon in Abu Dhabi, it was unfair.”

Following his departure from F1, Masi joined SRO Motorsports Australia last week as head of sporting operations.

Sports.title: Poll: Should F1 change its rules to make Virtual Safety Car periods fairer? | Debates and Polls
Sports.content:
The outcome of last weekend’s Spanish Grand Prix was effectively decided by Lance Stroll’s retirement on lap 15.

The Virtual Safety Car was deployed while the Aston Martin driver parked up in a run-off area. It only lasted

seconds, but as far as Lando Norris was concerned its timing could not have been worse.

Norris was leading when the VSC period began seconds after he passed the pit lane entrance. Andrea Kimi Antonelli, second, was able to pit during the VSC period, gaining a useful advantage by pitting while the race was neutralised.

Every other driver on the track had the same opportunity to pit, with one exception: Norris. The VSC period ended moments before he reached the pit lane entrance.

Afterwards Norris expressed frustration that the race’s only VSC period was timed in such a way that it gave everyone apart from him a chance to make a low-cost pit stop. While it’s certainly the case he was unlucky, should F1 try to prevent a similar situation happening again?

The Virtual Safety Car problem

In F1, like other series such as IndyCar, Safety Car periods can often have a disruptive effect on drivers’ strategies. They may occur at a more advantageous time for some drivers than others (as was the case when Norris scored his first win in Miami two years ago).

However the Virtual Safety Car, which F1 introduced in 2015, created a new kind of problem. During a classic Safety Car period, every driver has the opportunity to make a pit stop. But as a VSC period can be much shorter, it is possible that only some drivers may have the chance to pit.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

This is more likely to happen in certain circumstances. For example, when the track is very long, or if conditions are wet creating longer lap times, or when the field is tightly compressed after a start or restart.

There have only been a few cases of drivers being unable to pit during a VSC period since the rules were introduced. One notable example occured in the 2024 Brazilian Grand Prix, where all but four drivers were able to pit during a VSC period.

Possible solutions

No change

The striking thing about Norris’s misfortune on Sunday was how unusual it is. As these situations are so rare, it is not worth creating special rules to deal with them, which would create further complexity and scope for unintended consequences.

Introduce a minimum duration for VSC periods

It is unusual for VSC periods to last less than a lap in duration. When they do, it is usually only by a few seconds. Introducing a minimum length for VSC periods would ensure no driver suffers the same misfortune as Norris but make little difference to the majority of VSC deployments.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

Forbid tyre changes during VSC periods

Other series which have similar mandatory tyre change rules to F1 do not allow drivers to fulfil the requirement to change tyres during a VSC period. This is the case in Formula 2, and F1 could simply adopt the same rule. Closing the pit lane entrance during a VSC period would have the same effect, though this would prevent drivers pitting for damage repairs or other reasons.

Introduce a lower pit lane speed limit during VSC periods

Drivers are able to gain an advantage by pitting during a VSC period because the speed of the cars on track is reduced while the pit lane speed limit stays the same. Reducing the pit lane speed limit could address this, though it would have to be very low, especially at tracks where the lower 60kph speed limit is used by default, and imposing it on cars in the pit lane when the VSC is deployed could be complicated.

Abolish the Virtual Safety Car

Revert to using the classic Safety Car for all interruptions to the race. This would likely result in longer disruptions to races and compress the field more frequently.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

I say

I find the VSC preferable to the regular Safety Car because it does a better job of preserving the competition as it stands, and not significantly altering the gaps between cars. It is unfortunate that in some, limited circumstances, it does create the possibility for some drivers to suffer a significant disadvantage. Introducing a minimum duration for VSC periods would seem the easiest and fairest way to tackle the problem, which is unlikely to add significant extra delays or cause knock-on problems.

Sports.title: Antonelli ‘doing a scarily good job’, ‘beating much more experienced team mate’ – Norris | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Reigning world champion Lando Norris is highly impressed by the performance of the driver who looks set to succeed him.

Andrea Kimi Antonelli scored his eighth grand prix victory last weekend and has pulled 81 points clear of his closest rival – team mate George Russell – at the top of the championship standings.

“He’s leading by 80 points because he’s doing an incredible job,” said Norris. “He’s beating a much more experienced team-mate.”

Antonelli was still a teenager when he scored his first grand prix victory earlier this year. “He’s doing a scarily good job [having] just turned 20,” Norris continued. “Pretty phenomenal.”

Norris closed within 83 points of Antonelli by winning the two rounds either side of the summer break. But his slim hope of retaining his title faded after Antonelli won the last two rounds, leaving the McLaren driver 106 behind.

If Antonelli clinches the championship this year he will break Sebastian Vettel’s record for being the youngest ever world champion. Vettel was 23 when he won the world championship in 2010. “I think it’s cool to see someone so young doing such an incredible job and more than likely go on and win the championship,” said Norris.

“He’s been impressive since the first race this year. [He’s made] very few mistakes. He’s not driving like it’s his second year in F1, that’s for sure.

“It’s cool to see and there’s going to be many, many more years of us battling and I’m excited for more, hopefully this year.”

Sports.title: Michael Spinks Denies Larry Holmes His Marciano Moment
Sports.content:
Michael Spinks shattered Larry Holmes’ pursuit of boxing history on September 21, 1985, taking a 15 round unanimous decision at the outdoor arena of the Riviera Hotel and Casino in Las Vegas.

Holmes (48-0, 34 KOs) entered the ring needing one victory to match Rocky Marciano’s iconic 49-0 mark. Another successful title defense would equal Joe Louis’ division benchmark of 20 consecutive defenses. The 35-year-old champion walked into the ring as a 6-1 favorite against a challenger moving straight up from the 175-pound ranks.

Spinks (27-0, 19 KOs) had unified the light heavyweight division, yet history stood firmly against him. Predecessors Archie Moore, Billy Conn and Bob Foster had all tried and failed to conquer reigning heavyweight kings. Spinks tipped the scales at a lean, conditioned 200 pounds after completing an intensive program under conditioning specialist Mackie Shilstone. That regimen relied on track sprints, resistance work, and targeted caloric intake.

The conditioning strategy paid off instantly. Rather than transforming into a traditional heavyweight slugger, he transported light heavyweight agility into the sport’s biggest division.

Holmes established control in rounds one and two through his signature left jab, but Spinks quickly dismantled that timing. The challenger utilized sudden lateral dips, unpredictable head slips, and varied foot angles to vacate the center line. Holmes soon found himself pawing with the lead hand rather than snapping the punishing, rhythmic jab that carried his long title reign.

Spinks exaggerated the champion’s hesitation by constantly switching directions and firing counters from unorthodox stances. His looping overhand right came over Holmes’ habitually low lead guard. Though the blow lacked true concussive force to stagger the heavyweight champion, the persistent threat forced Holmes to freeze after jabbing instead of letting combinations fly.

The second half of the bout produced a classic scoring issue. Holmes pressed forward and scored with the heavier singular wallops, but chasing Spinks proved far different from trapping him. Holmes struggled to cut the ring off cleanly, allowing the challenger to fire quick bursts and escape along the ropes.

Spinks exploited the optics of those sequences perfectly. In the closing thirty seconds of tight frames, the challenger launched quick flurries across Holmes’ guard, shoulders and face before skipping outside. Many blows landed on leather, yet the sheer flurry gave ringside officials eye-catching closing activity.

Holmes spent the final rounds hunting for an equalizer. Lingering back trouble surely restricted his mobility, but the mental burden of chasing Marciano’s ghost also took a toll. When Spinks refused to crumble during early skirmishes, Holmes cast aside the methodical rhythm that had grounded his championship dominance.

CompuBox numbers supported the challenger’s work rate, recording 318 landed shots out of 697 attempts for Spinks, against 248 of 567 for Holmes. Neither fighter suffered serious physical trauma over the 45 minutes of action.

Judges Harold Lederman and Dave Moretti turned in cards of 143-142, while Lawrence Wallace submitted a 145-142 tally, awarding Spinks the unanimous decision. Lederman noted that his scorecard sat deadlocked through fourteen rounds, with Spinks sealing the victory by outworking the champion in the final three minutes.

The loss hit Holmes hard, and the bitter aftermath carried over to the post-fight press gathering.

“I’m 35 fighting young men, and Rocky was 25 fighting old men. To be technical, Rocky couldn’t carry my jockstrap.”

Holmes later apologized for the remark. Spinks edged Holmes again via split decision seven months down the road, yet this initial Las Vegas clash holds lasting historical importance. Spinks demonstrated that an undersized champion did not require brute force to topple a giant. Precise conditioning, persistent lateral angles, and unrelenting activity were enough to pull an elite heavyweight completely out of his comfort zone. Holmes was carrying years of accumulated resentment that finally boiled over that night in Las Vegas.

The outburst had very little to do with Michael Spinks as an individual and almost everything to do with Holmes feeling chronically disrespected throughout his entire championship reign.

First, Holmes spent seven years reigning in the inescapable shadow of Muhammad Ali. When Holmes dominated a faded Ali in 1980, the public never truly forgave him for beating their icon. Instead of receiving unconditional praise as an all-time great heavyweight, Holmes routinely faced lukewarm crowds, critical press, and constant comparisons to fighters from past eras. He felt he had carried the heavyweight division with absolute professionalism without ever receiving the adoration given to Ali or Joe Frazier.

Second, the Marciano obsession amplified that frustration tenfold. Leading into the Spinks bout, the media spotlight fixated almost entirely on Rocky Marciano’s 49-0 mark rather than Holmes’ own historic accomplishments. Marciano’s family and older sports columnists openly rooted for Holmes to lose so the record would stay untouched. To Holmes, the comparisons felt inherently unfair. He saw himself as an active champion taking on prime contenders while Marciano had built his late record against aging legends like Joe Louis, Jersey Joe Walcott, and Ezzard Charles. When the decision went against him, that perceived injustice exploded into the infamous jockstrap remark.

Third, Holmes genuinely believed he won the fight. In his mind, he had walked Spinks down, landed the heavier and more damaging punches, and dictated ring position for fifteen rounds. To lose his heavyweight title, his unblemished record, and his historic milestone on a controversial decision based on what he considered slapping flurries felt like outright theft.

Rather than processing the setback in private, Holmes walked into the press room exhausted, injured, and deeply wounded by the sudden collapse of his historical quest. The irony, as you noted, was immediate: had he shown grace in defeat, the boxing public likely would have rallied around him for dropping a razor-thin decision at age thirty-five. By lashing out at Marciano, he instantly turned public sentiment against himself and alienated the very fans who were ready to appreciate his career.

When you watch the tape without audio or crowd influence, Holmes undeniably delivered the heavier, more authoritative blows. His right hands snapped Spinks’ head back, while many of Spinks’ combinations bounced harmlessly off Holmes’ high guard, forearms, or shoulders.

In traditional championship boxing scoring, effective aggression and clean, hard punching are supposed to carry the round. Holmes was the man moving forward, controlling center ring, and delivering the thudding shots that looked like actual heavyweight punches. The wire services saw it that way too, which is why the Associated Press and United Press International both scored the fight for Holmes.

Where Holmes ran into trouble with the ringside judges was purely optic. By following Spinks without cutting the ring off, he let Spinks dictate the visual tempo. When Spinks threw a four-punch flurry in the final twenty seconds of a round, even if three hit gloves, it created the illusion of dominance right as the bell rang. The judges rewarded that busy, awkward hustle over Holmes’ patient, single-punch stalking.

Losing a world championship on shoe-shine flurries when you landed the only hard shots of the night is enough to make any champion see red. It explains entirely why Holmes was so raw at the microphone afterward, convinced he had been robbed of Marciano’s milestone by judges who favored activity over real damage.

Sports.title: Pitbull Cruz Says He’s Willing To Fight Ryan Garcia
Sports.content:
San Diego, California – Saturday night at the Pechanga Arena, Isaac “Pitbull”Cruz (29-3-2, 19 KOs) successfully defended his WBC interim super lightweight title against Nestor Bravo (24-2, 17 KOs) in an ugly fight where referee Thomas Taylor had to intervene several times to put Bravo in line to stop him from roughing up Pitbull.

Taylor gave Bravo several warnings along with a point deduction in rounds 2 and 4 to stop him from holding, shoving, and even body-slamming Isaac to the ground. Nestor also landed a few low blows that appeared intentional. He appeared unable to handle Cruz’s pressure, looking overwhelmed and unable to stop the onslaught. When he finally appeared to have settled down in round six, Pitbull landed a clean left hook that sent Bravo to the canvas for the full 10-count.

After the fight, Nestor said what made Cruz such a difficult opponent was his awkwardness and his small size. He said Pitbull was not necessarily strong but hurt him with punches he didn’t see coming due to his awkward style. Before the fight, Ryan Garcia made his prediction via X by posting that he didn’t think Pitbull would defeat Bravo.

Then, once Pitbull won, he made another post: “Bravo Pitbull proved me wrong tonight. Let’s do this in December; the offer is on the table. I can tame a lion; I’m not to concerned about taming a pitbull.”

This began a series of posts whereby Ryan made it known his seriousness for wanting the fight and that if the fight is not accepted by Cruz this time around, he won’t entertain in the future.

Isaac told the media after the press conference he wants the fight and is not afraid to move up to welterweight, “Here I am for the challenge, and I am more than ready. Whether that be December, May, or September, I don’t care about the date. The desire is there, and we will do it.” For those present at the Pechanga arena, you could feel the energy of the fans chanting Pitbull and barking for Cruz. He became a household name after being one of the few fighters to go the distance with Gervonta Davis.

Since then, he’s only become a bigger star. Recently, he joined the Eddie Reynoso camp, which holds some of the elite Mexican boxers in the sport today: fighters Rafael Espinoza, Jaime Munguia, and former undisputed supermiddleweight champion Canelo Alvarez. He’s learning not only about boxing inside the ring but outside of it as well, as he wishes to create a legacy with a superstar profile among the great Mexican fighters of all time.

Sports.title: Lorenzo “Truck” Simpson Wins WBA Intercontinental Light Heavyweight Title
Sports.content:
On Saturday night, September 19th, in the co-main event of the Skyy Myles Promotions event entitled ‘The Supper,’ Lorenzo “Truck” Simpson defeated Shawn McCalman (17-3, 8 KOs) and won the WBA Intercontinental Title.

Going into the fight, the matchup was considered to be a 50/50 bout between two hungry boxers. Winning the vacant title was important to both boxers because it’s a regional belt that provides a boost in the rankings.

In the opening round of the southpaw vs. southpaw bout, McCalman got off to a good start as he was changing levels with an active jab. Simpson put his jab on display in the second round as he landed multiple jabs to the body.

The third round saw Simpson have success in regards to closing the distance and landing the left hand. As the round was coming to a close, McCalman connected with a few body shots.

The fourth round was highlighted by a solid uppercut landed by Simpson. In the fifth round, McCalman upped his production as he got back to working the jab and targeting the body.

The majority of the second half of the bout was fought in close quarters, as the back-and-forth match went the distance.

At the conclusion of the fight, the judges had to determine if they were swayed by McCalman’s volume or Simpson’s sharp power shots.

In a very technical fight, one judge scored the bout (96-94) in favor of Shawn McCalman. However, that judge’s scorecard was overruled by the other two judges, who both scored the fight (97-93) in favor of Lorenzo Simpson.

With the victory, Lorenzo “Truck” Simpson (17-3, 10 KOs) has won a title belt, and now he feels the sky is the limit. Next on his agenda is a bout against a boxer in the top 15.

Back in January 2017, Coach Calvin Ford and Coach Kenny Ellis were in the corner when Gervonta “Tank” Davis won his first world title. Now the question is, will Lorenzo “Truck” Simpson be the next world champion to come out of the Upton Boxing Center?

Sports.title: Keith Connolly Pitches Benn-Eubank Rubber Match at 168
Sports.content:
Conor Benn choosing to leap straight from a second-round knockout loss to Ryan into a third clash against Chris Eubank Jr. at 168 pounds looks like a cash grab rather than a legitimate sporting return. Rushing into another stadium payday before the UK rivalry expires takes precedence over sensible career preservation.

The condition of Benn’s chin demands serious scrutiny after Ryan stunned him inside three minutes and finished the job at 1:25 of round two. Throwing Benn back in the ring against an established, bigger operator after a brief break represents hazardous management. Benn already absorbed punishing artillery over twenty-four rounds during their initial two bouts.

“One hundred percent. 168 pounds, no excuses. The trilogy, another stadium fight, it’ll sell out. It’ll be a tremendous event, and then there’ll be no excuses. There’ll be a winner of the one-one series between the two guys. I expect it to happen. I think it’ll make the event big. Eddie Hearn with Chris Eubank. Myself and Dana White on one side backing Conor,” said manager Keith Connolly to talkSPORT Boxing.

That soundbite benefits Eubank far more than it helps Benn. Eubank escapes the brutal boils down to lower limits and enters the ring fully fueled. Benn piling on weight up to 178.4 pounds on fight night against Ryan merely demonstrated quick fluid retention, not the ability to trade functional super middleweight muscle against a seasoned campaigner.

Carrying sluggish pounds strips away Benn’s hand speed, the single attribute that gave the older man problems. Eubank gains total freedom to march forward, walk through incoming fire, and punish Benn in the pocket without the sapping weight restrictions that limited his output in the past.

The promotional split presents an aggressive battle behind the scenes. Connolly and Dana White would back Benn, with Eddie Hearn positioned in Eubank’s corner. Hearn spent years guiding Benn’s career. Hearn knows his former fighter’s technical deficiencies, stamina thresholds, and gym habits better than anyone else in the sport.

A standard recovery program would keep Benn out of heavy sparring, followed by a controlled confidence builder. Fast-tracking the trilogy brings immense gate receipts while Benn’s marketability remains intact. His management clearly prefers mining this family feud for quick millions rather than risking him against dangerous welterweights.

Eubank secures every physical edge at 168 pounds. Benn assumes all the medical hazards, trading his future punch resistance for one last massive stadium check.

Without Riyadh Season writing blank checks, the math completely falls apart. The first two encounters only happened because Saudi money absorbed the astronomical purses, underwriting the inflated demands of both camps while keeping pay-per-view prices low. Traditional broadcast economics cannot support those figures. If the Saudis decide they have zero interest in funding a third run between two damaged fighters, no standard commercial outfit can bridge the financial void.

DAZN, Boxxer, or Sky Sports operating on standard balance sheets cannot cut ten-million-dollar checks to men coming off definitive stoppage losses. Staging a stadium event at Wembley or Tottenham Hotspur Stadium costs millions just to open the turnstiles and turn on the lights. Gate receipts and a standard UK pay-per-view split would force both men to take a massive haircut from their previous paydays. When reality hits the accountants, the money will dry up fast.

Calling it a celebrity match between nepo babies accurately identifies the true product. Stripped of elite competitive relevance, this pairing relies solely on the nostalgia of their fathers’ names. Ryan exposed Benn inside four minutes as an undersized, one-dimensional slugger with a fragile chin. Eubank has drifted for years without winning a legitimate world title, relying on domestic drama rather than championship credentials.

Neither fighter commands global pay-per-view numbers outside the British market. Without international interest, the fight turns into a regional cash grab. If Dana White and Zuffa step in to foot the bill, they will quickly discover that UK nostalgia does not move subscription needles in North America. When the Saudi money train bypasses the station, both fighters will either take a fraction of their past purses or realize their lucrative family drama has priced itself out of the market.

Sports.title: Shakur Stevenson Makes Zuffa Signing Look Worse
Sports.content:
Zuffa believed it landed pure royalty by securing Shakur Stevenson following his victory against Teofimo Lopez. The subsequent months delivered zero ring appearances, endless social media bickering, alongside an obstinate champion insisting on tailor-made parameters before stepping into the ring.

A lack of signed contracts triggered sharp public reaction.

“Zuffa have to really regret that Shakur Stevenson signing. All he has done is ruin his goodwill with the fans online and continue to be a pain in the ass to get a fight done for,” Tolboof posted on X.

The critique holds immense weight given the presence of ready internal rivals. José Valenzuela threw down an explicit challenge, handing the promotion an explosive pairing of roster talent. Stevenson discarded the possibility entirely.

Rayo delivers relentless offense, legitimate stopping power, plus an eagerness to trade in the pocket. Such an opponent forces Stevenson out of his safety zones, giving the promotional hierarchy a genuine look at their prize asset under fire. Ernesto Mercado offers another devastating threat capable of delivering the carnage Turki Alalshikh expects from these venture millions.

Stevenson ignores those dangerous tests. He spent valuable calendar time chasing Devin Haney at a catchweight limit of 144 pounds, demanding artificial terms against a larger rival. Haney relies on safety-first positioning, backfoot movement, minimal inside engagement. The brass faced grueling backroom wrangling merely to stage a bloodless fencing match devoid of crowd drama.

A collaborative company asset jumps at the Rayo encounter, establishing a fierce homegrown rivalry under the promotional banner. Stevenson prioritized stagnation, fixating on comfortable terms instead of stepping through the ropes.

Pure technical craft is obvious. The actual headache centers on functional execution for the brand. The Riyadh connection thrives on reckless courage, volatility, combatants chasing knockouts against devastating hitters. Stevenson brings retreat-first tactics, endless contract stalling, vast stretches of inactivity.

The brass presented him as their crown jewel. Stevenson spent his entire tenure turning that blockbuster signing into an overpriced promotional nightmare.

Dana White has to be feeling serious buyer’s remorse, even if he will never admit it publicly. White built his entire empire on a matchmaking philosophy that is the exact polar opposite of how Shakur Stevenson operates. In the UFC model, fighters take the hardest fights presented, stay active, and entertain the crowd. Stevenson brings the complete antithesis: high financial demands, a fence-and-retreat style that empties arenas, and an obsession with handpicking circumstances down to the exact pound.

Zuffa shelled out eight figures to make Stevenson a headline acquisition, expecting him to anchor major events. Instead, the promotion bought into months of dead air, endless social media bickering, and outright refusal to engage in in-house tests. Turning down José “Rayo” Valenzuela right out of the gate showed where Stevenson’s priorities sit. Rayo is a dangerous, aggressive hitter within the same organizational family who would have forced a firefight and given the fans real drama. Passing on that test while chasing a 144-pound handicap against Devin Haney proves Stevenson wants the safety of selective terms rather than testing himself against true offensive threats.

That calculated businessman approach is poison for a fledgling promotional brand trying to build genuine momentum. Matchmaking a risk-averse defensive specialist is difficult enough; matchmaking one who demands king’s ransom money while rejecting live punchers is an outright headache. When an elite technician refuses to take risks in the ring or at the negotiating table, the company is left paying millions just to watch its marquee investment gather dust on the shelf.

Triggering an escape clause in the contract would be the quickest way to end the bleeding, because keeping Shakur on the roster is a recipe for stagnation. If the Zuffa brass has a legal mechanism based on turned-down fight offers, inactivity periods, or failure to accept assigned dates, pulling that trigger makes absolute business sense.

The problem with holding onto a fighter like Shakur is the opportunity cost. Every month wasted trying to indulge his catchweight demands against Devin Haney is calendar space denied to fighters who actually want to scrap. Dana White built his promotional legacy by freezing out athletes who attempt to play matchmaker from their couches. In boxing, promoters constantly get trapped paying massive retainers to elite technicians who believe they are entitled to dictate every single term while taking zero operational risk.

Passing publicly on José Valenzuela was the ultimate signal. When an athlete tells his own paymasters that he refuses an in-house clash with a dangerous puncher, he ceases to be a promotional asset and becomes an obstacle. If Zuffa cannot use him to test their own talent or build compelling company events, they are simply subsidizing an ego trip.

Cutting ties via a contractual exit would send a message to the rest of the roster that the money requires reciprocal cooperation. If Shakur wants to wait around for perfect conditions at his leisure, he can do it as a free agent on somebody else’s dime.

Sports.title: Ryan Garcia Denies Teofimo Lopez February 6 Talks
Sports.content:
Update: Ryan Garcia has denied knowing about any negotiations for a February 6 fight with Teofimo Lopez at Madison Square Garden. Ryan responded to a post repeating Chris Mannix’s report by stating, “This is not true. No discussions, at least from my side, has had that. Unless I don’t know about them, but I’m not looking to fight in NY, even though I’m not totally taking that off the table.”

That leaves open the possibility that representatives discussed the date without Ryan’s involvement, but Mannix’s description made the talks sound further along than Ryan believes they are. Between Ryan’s denial and Teofimo’s unresolved Catterall obligation, February 6 now looks more like an idea being circulated than an active fight plan.

This is not true no discussions at least from my side has had that. Unless I don’t know about them but I’m not looking to fight at in NY even tho I’m not totally taking that off the table https://t.co/t8cPLh25gm — RYAN GARCIA (@RyanGarcia) September 22, 2026

Ryan Garcia vs. Teofimo Lopez Talks Target February 6

Ryan Garcia faces a choice between taking a December date with Isaac Cruz or holding out for a clash with Teofimo Lopez. The second route is complicated by Lopez’s mandatory WBA obligation involving Jack Catterall.

Cruz called for Ryan after stopping Nestor Bravo in six rounds Saturday night in San Diego. Ryan quickly accepted and indicated that an offer would follow.

Preliminary discussions have taken place between representatives for Ryan and Lopez. Chris Mannix revealed that talks have targeted February 6, 2027, at Madison Square Garden.

“There have been conversations between the representatives of Garcia and Lopez about making a Garcia versus Lopez fight, to the point where the conversations even got to a spot where they talked about a date, which is early February. I think February 6th is the date that I was told, and the location is Madison Square Garden in New York City,” said Mannix on his channel.

Mannix prefers Ryan to skip Cruz and go directly into the Teofimo bout. That route assumes the WBA will permit Lopez to bypass Catterall, who defeated Shakhram Giyasov to secure his mandatory claim.

Matchroom has sent formal legal letters urging the sanctioning body to enforce its ruling. Eddie Hearn argues that Catterall’s status carried over with the belt from Rolando Romero to Teofimo. Team Lopez claims the directive applied strictly to Romero and no longer binds the new titleholder.

Mannix’s February target ignores the governing body timeline. Unless Ryan meets Teofimo prior to Catterall’s cited November window, Teofimo must satisfy that mandatory defense. Negotiations, a potential purse bid, a full camp, and physical recovery would make February 6 impractical.

Catterall also represents a stylistic danger for Teofimo. The British southpaw controls distance with a disciplined jab, employs lateral movement and scores with counters without retreating into a shell. He has a clear blueprint in Shakur Stevenson’s showing against Teofimo. Teofimo relies on a predictable pattern. He presses forward like an incoming tide to unleash combinations before resetting straight back. That approach gives a poised counterpuncher like Catterall clean opportunities to time him. Teofimo risks losing the belt before Ryan ever gets him in the ring.

If Teofimo chooses to vacate instead, the matchup with Ryan loses its title prestige and strips Teofimo of negotiating power. Ryan generates massive arena business on his own name. Lopez relies on Ryan to produce a career-high purse.

Waiting on Teofimo introduces ring rust for Ryan. Lengthy layoffs have disrupted Ryan’s timing throughout his career, and sanctioning body disputes rarely resolve quickly. A December fight keeps him sharp while cashing another substantial check.

Pitbull Cruz brings action appeal, yet remains vulnerable to Ryan’s weapons. The short pressure fighter moves forward behind an earmuff guard and lunges inside. Ryan possesses the straight right to split that defense and the check left hook to catch Cruz in mid-leap. That physical contrast grows sharper once Ryan hydrates up into middleweight territory on fight night.

Teofimo delivers the steeper tactical hurdle. He possesses the lateral agility to circle away from Ryan’s hook, the upper body slip to evade incoming right hands, and the counterpunching ability to punish an upright target.

Mannix viewed Cruz as a distraction on the road to Lopez. Catterall stands as the real roadblock. Ryan can face Cruz in December while Lopez sorts through his WBA mess. If Teofimo still possesses the belt when the dust clears, Madison Square Garden will still be waiting.

The WBA already shredded its own credibility by sanctioning Teofimo against Rolly Romero in the first place. Giving an immediate shot at a secondary belt to a fighter coming straight off a wide points loss to Shakur Stevenson made a mockery of the ratings. The only justification offered was the commercial value of putting two loud talkers on pay-per-view.

Now Gilberto Mendoza is caught in the trap he created. That July 9 message to Catterall, explicitly telling him he would get the winner of Rolly versus Teofimo within 180 days, puts the WBA president on the record. Matchroom’s legal team has documented proof that Catterall took the risk, beat Shakhram Giyasov, and earned his status in a sanctioned eliminator.

From a sporting standpoint, letting Teofimo bypass Catterall looks terrible. It signals that mandatory positions only exist for contenders who lack the leverage to be ignored. Teofimo arguing that his name was not on the original paperwork is classic promoter double-talk. Mandatory obligations belong to the championship belt, not the individual holding it. If a title changes hands, the new champion inherits the baggage attached to the hardware.

Despite how ugly it looks, the WBA will almost certainly look for an escape hatch if Ryan Garcia and Lopez finalize terms. Sanctioning bodies operate on percentages of total fight purses. A percentage of a Ryan Garcia pay-per-view at Madison Square Garden generates massive revenue for the WBA. A low-profile mandatory defense between Lopez and Catterall in Manchester or New York pays a tiny fraction of that amount.

Sports.title: David Benavidez Eyes Andy Ruiz for Heavyweight Debut
Sports.content:
David Benavidez is mapping out a multi-division campaign that his team hopes will culminate in a heavyweight appearance against Andy Ruiz Jr. José Benavidez Sr. laid out a scenario where David campaigns at cruiserweight against Michal Cieslak and Jai Opetaia, drops to light heavyweight for Dmitry Bivol or Artur Beterbiev, and then jumps into the heavyweight division.

“After that, we would love to make a fight with Andy Ruiz. We’re just dreaming here, daydreaming, but those are the fights that I think are very possible to make. Imagine David Benavidez and Andy Ruiz. Andy is a great fighter. My heart is with him, and he’s like family to me, but I believe he would love the same, an opportunity to fight the Mexican Monster. For us, it would be a great opportunity,” said Jose Sr. to ProBox TV.

Jumping between three weight classes demands an enormous physical toll. David would have to pack on bulk to trade punches with cruiserweights, strip off 25 pounds to make the 175-pound limit, and then rebuild his body for heavyweight. Modern fighters rarely ping-pong across weight classes because stripping away functional muscle ruins stamina, drains punch resistance, and deadens a fighter’s legs.

Targeting Ruiz reveals a desire for name recognition over actual heavyweight danger. Ruiz carries brand value, quick combinations, and strong appeal in the southwestern market. He also stands barely six feet tall and lacks the reach of legitimate heavyweights.

Ruiz returned from a two-year layoff and suffered a defeat against Damian Knyba. By the time David finishes this proposed multi-belt tour, Ruiz will be pushing 40 with extensive periods of ring rust. Facing that diminished version provides David a heavyweight victory without the terror of sharing a ring with a massive, six-foot-six puncher.

Reaching that point assumes David survives the cruiserweight division, which looks like pure fantasy. Opetaia is not a stepping stone. The Australian operates with elite lateral movement, explosive power, and precise timing. David had uncomfortable moments handling the physical pressure and punches of Oleksandr Gvozdyk at light heavyweight. Opetaia possesses far more destructive force at 200 pounds and has the tools to dismantle David before any heavyweight plans materialize.

The promotional hurdles make the blueprint even more detached from reality. Coordinating multiple sanctioning bodies, rival promoters, and separate network platforms across three weight classes takes years. David risks burning through his athletic peak waiting for theoretical fights that may never happen.

José Sr. openly called the idea daydreaming, yet floating Ruiz exposes the underlying strategy. Team Benavidez wants heavyweight credit without taking heavyweight risks, targeting an aging, undersized former champion instead of the division’s genuine giants.

Counting on Ruiz to rebuild credibility by stringing together wins over the next couple of years ignores everything he has shown inside and outside the ring. Against Jarrell Miller, Ruiz could barely muster the work rate to stay competitive, struggling through long stretches where his punch output disappeared. Following that up with a lackluster performance and a loss to Damian Knyba confirmed that the hunger, conditioning, and explosiveness that defined his upset win in 2019 are long gone. Put him in with any durable, busy heavyweight right now, and he drops another decision simply by being outworked.

The financial reality makes the idea of a comeback even more absurd. Ruiz made life-changing money from the Anthony Joshua bouts and has zero financial urgency to run through grueling training camps or take punishment. When a heavyweight has millions in the bank and only fights once every year or two, the fire never comes back. Expecting him to suddenly become active, stay disciplined, and beat legitimate contenders while David Benavidez runs a marathon through cruiserweight and light heavyweight is wishful thinking.

If this matchup ever happens, Team Benavidez will not be getting a resurgent former champion coming off a hot streak. They will be buying the shell of a recognizable name who is happy to cash one final paycheck before walking away for good. That makes the commercial payoff far smaller than José Sr. envisions, because boxing fans can easily see through a cash grab against a washed-up opponent.

Sports.title: Janibek Alimkhanuly’s Canelo Alvarez Plan Requires Statement Knockout
Sports.content:
Janibek Alimkhanuly sees the vacant WBO super middleweight title as his route to Canelo Alvarez. Winning it will not be enough. He needs a violent performance that gives boxing fans a reason to demand the unification.

“Everyone knows I’m not interested in the money. I’m ready! I’m also ready to see the news that he’s vacating the title. I just need that title. Then I have to unify with Canelo. That’s it!”

Janibek posted that message on X last Thursday following the purse bid for his ordered fight with Hamzah Sheeraz. Queensberry won with an offer of $1,001,809, but Sheeraz surrendered the WBO title shortly afterward. Janibek returned Monday with another message: “Brother, why not Janibek vs Canelo? 😎”

The WBO must first choose his opponent. Diego Pacheco and Jacob Bank are among the leading candidates, and Pacheco would make Janibek earn every bit of his new position. The 6’4″ contender has the reach, power, and natural size to test whether Janibek’s punch resistance belongs at 168.

Janibek cannot merely edge Pacheco from the outside. He would need to cut off the ring, close the distance, and stop a younger super middleweight to prove his power traveled with him.

Even then, the business case works against him. Canelo has never allowed sanctioning bodies to control his schedule. David Benavidez had an interim belt, substantial public support, and years of pressure behind him. None of it produced the fight.

Janibek offers even less commercial incentive. He is a dangerous southpaw with heavy hands and extensive amateur schooling, but he lacks a large American pay-per-view audience. That makes him a severe physical risk without the purse Canelo expects from taking one.

Canelo has defeated southpaws Billy Joe Saunders and John Ryder since his difficult 2014 fight with Erislandy Lara. Janibek presents a different version of that stance. He is more compact, hits harder, and looks for damaging counters instead of surviving through movement. Canelo must also defeat WBC champion Christian Mbilli on October 31. At 36, Canelo is nearing the final stage of his career and will favor stadium events, major paydays, and carefully selected farewell fights over collecting every available belt.

Janibek cannot force his way onto that schedule. Knocking out a credible WBO opponent would at least make leaving him off much harder to defend. Taking on Pacheco, Sadjo, or Bank for the vacant strap means Janibek must instantly solve elite 168-pounders without a warm-up bout.

The odds of both men surviving those respective hurdles to meet in a unification clash look slim. Alvarez facing Mbilli after a full year out of the ring is a risky fight for a superstar on the decline. Against Terence Crawford, Canelo looked heavy, flat-footed, and completely devoid of the sharp reaction time that once made his upper-body movement and counter-punching elite-grade.

Mbilli is the worst stylistic matchup for someone in Canelo’s state: he is relentless, throws punches in volume from awkward angles, and doesn’t care about taking shots to land his own. Canelo is not suddenly going to regain the lateral movement or snap needed to keep Mbilli off him for twelve rounds.

The division jump from 160 to 168 pounds is brutal for Janibek. At middleweight, he could intimidate opponents with power and technical skills. At super middleweight, he’ll face naturally bigger, harder-hitting, and far more seasoned opponents than anyone on his middleweight record.

Ghana News.title: Prof. Kwofie urges publishers to use indigenous knowledge systems to decolonise AI
Ghana News.content:
The Director of the Institute of Applied Science and Technology at the University of Ghana, Prof. Samuel Kojo Kwofie, has called for the integration of indigenous knowledge systems into data used to train artificial intelligence (AI) models as part of efforts to promote culturally inclusive development and decolonise AI.

Prof. Kwofie made the call when he served as a guest reviewer at the launch of “The Book Industry Programme in Ghana: From Dream to Reality and Beyond’’, authored by I.K. Appiah. The event formed part of the 23rd Ghana International Book Fair 2026, held at the National Theatre in Accra.

Prof. Kwofie urged publishers to embrace emerging AI technologies while incorporating Ghanaian knowledge systems and locally developed solutions. He noted that artificial intelligence was already influencing different stages of publishing through automation and digitalisation.

He cautioned, however, that AI should not be regarded as a replacement for human creativity and responsibility in the publishing industry. Prof. Kwofie reiterated that issues of ethics, plagiarism and cognitive ownership should underpin creative writing.

While AI could support efficiency, decrease production time, content creation and streamline various publishing processes, he said, it could not replace the role of authors and publishers.

He therefore encouraged industry stakeholders to find a balance between technological advancement and the development of indigenous capacity.

Publishing as a Driver of Knowledge

Reviewing the book, Prof. Kwofie described it as a strategic resource that could strengthen Ghana's publishing industry and create opportunities for networking, knowledge development and professional growth.

He commended I.K. Appiah for producing what he described as a well-researched and strategically written account of the Publishing Studies Programme's nearly four-decade journey.

According to him, the publication goes beyond documenting the history of the Book Industry Programme at the Department of Publishing Studies, Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST) by highlighting the achievements and impact of students and alumni who passed through the programme.

He said the book would serve as a useful resource for professionals, students and other stakeholders seeking to understand the evolution and opportunities within Ghana's publishing industry.

Prof. Kwofie emphasised the critical role publishing has played in shaping the knowledge ecosystem, noting that its influence extends across virtually every sphere of society.

He encouraged young people to consider publishing studies as a viable area of academic and professional pursuit, arguing that the book industry equips graduates with skills applicable across several sectors.

Digital Content Expanding Access to Books

The academic also highlighted the changing nature of books in the digital age, noting that publications can increasingly be produced, distributed and accessed as digital content.

He explained that readers with access to appropriate digital devices can read books without necessarily relying on traditional physical formats.

For him, this development reinforces the need for publishers and other industry players to adapt to emerging technologies while ensuring that Ghanaian knowledge and content remain relevant and accessible.

Four Decades of the Publishing Studies Programme

The Book Industry Programme in Ghana: From Dream to Reality and Beyond traces the development of the book publishing programme over approximately 40 years.

The book was authored by I.K. Appiah, a Senior Lecturer in the Department of Publishing Studies, Faculty of Art, College of Art and Built Environment (CABE), KNUST, and published by Adwinsa Publication (GH) Ltd.
