Having more test cases and being transparent about both the challenges and opportunities could help other farmers make the leap, she said.

toggle caption Madeleine Charis King/Iowa Public Radio

Tanner Faaborg, who brought the vision of 1100 Farm to the family several years ago, wants their mushroom operation to be another "proof of concept."

"It just takes someone doing something a little different to help folks realize that it is possible," he said.

His parents, Rand and Tammy, bought their 25-acre farm in the 1980s with the dream of a homesteading lifestyle, he said. The family of seven harvested and preserved produce from their garden and fruit trees. They had a wood-burning stove and raised chickens for eggs.

Rand Faaborg said they started out by raising a few market hogs for "pocket money" to supplement his income as a welder. But it didn't work out.

"I lost money," Faaborg said. "And then I saw in the paper this  of contract feeding."

Becoming a CAFO

Under contract feeding, a company provides the animals and pays for the feed while the farmer contributes the labor and covers the costs of the infrastructure.

This legal arrangement is a key component of CAFOs, which the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency defines as operations that meet certain animal number thresholds and confine them in an area without vegetation for at least 45 days out of the year.

Sponsor Message

Large CAFOs in Iowa increased from 789 in 1990 to 4,444 in 2025, according to an analysis by the Environmental Working Group, an organization that advocates for greater regulation of CAFOs. Together with small- and medium-sized operations, EWG estimates 66% of all the CAFOs in the state housed a total of 33.4 million hogs.

Rand Faaborg said contract feeding seemed like a good opportunity at the time.

The family did not put up new buildings for the enterprise at first. They retrofitted existing buildings on the farm to raise 2,000 hogs at a time.

Faaborg said once the farm scaled up and became a CAFO, it was "very profitable" but required more work than he expected on top of his day job.

"I was working 16-hour days, sometimes 24-hour days, going to work without even sleeping," he said.

toggle caption Madeleine Charis King/Iowa Public Radio

After a few years, Faaborg said they borrowed $400,000 to build two new hog barns designed to improve efficiency. They had automatic feeder lines and systems to move the manure out to an open-air holding pit.

"Fortunately, we could make cash flow until we got the buildings paid off," Faaborg said, explaining it took 12 years to get out of debt.

But raising hogs was physically demanding work and became less profitable for the family over time, Faaborg said.

"In my day job, my pay over 35 years increased tenfold, and my pay raising hogs dropped by two-thirds," he said. He believes the decrease in profits was due to the proliferation of CAFOs across the state.

A new chapter for the Faaborgs

Rand and Tammy Faaborg decided several years ago they were ready to exit the hog business. Rand said they didn't have a deep love for raising pigs, but they'd poured so much money and time into the buildings that he didn't want to see them fall into disrepair or be bulldozed.

Sponsor Message

They asked their family if they had ideas to use the buildings for something else. That's when their son Tanner Faaborg began to lay out his vision.

"We have this infrastructure," he said. "We could retrofit it, change it, and do something that is a lot healthier on us, healthier for the planet, and actually is profitable, that'll be a job creator for the family, but for the community, as well."

toggle caption Madeleine Charis King/Iowa Public Radio

Tanner Faaborg said he developed a passion for sustainability and climate change mitigation in college. He joined Urban Ambassadors, a volunteer-driven nonprofit that promotes sustainability in the Des Moines area, and was part of the steering committee for the city's climate action and adaptation plan.

But his work in Iowa's capital felt out of line with other parts of his life.

"I would come back [to the farm] and help out with pig chores and kind of living a double life that I felt terrible about," Tanner Faaborg said.

The Faaborgs raised around 8,000 hogs each year, producing roughly a million gallons of liquid manure. They stored it in an open pit until Rand Faaborg could find row-crop farmers to haul it off to spread on their fields during tight windows in the spring and fall.

While manure can provide essential crop nutrients, it's a major contributor to climate change. Manure pits and lagoons release methane, which is "28 times as potent as carbon dioxide at trapping heat in the atmosphere," according to the EPA. Excess manure in fields can also increase nitrous oxide emissions and pollute nearby bodies of water when it rains.

Tanner Faaborg said he was also bothered by the reshaping of rural Iowa by industrial animal agriculture. Near his childhood home, he pointed to long buildings surrounded by cornfields down the road.

"There used to be a house over there. Now, instead, there's turkey barns," he said. "There used to be a house over there, and now it's hog barns."

Sponsor Message

These local changes have a ripple effect, he said. The small school he attended no longer exists.

"There's just not enough people," Faaborg said. "There are small towns and rural communities that are losing population every single year, and it's really devastating."

Where Tanner Faaborg saw an opportunity for change, his brother Tyler said he needed more convincing.

Tyler Faaborg said he raised and sold around 200,000 hogs a year across three counties. But when his parents announced to the family that they were done, he said it took about a week to decide he was ready to try something different.

"I had a good job. I got paid well," he said. "But I did it for 25 years. It's really hard on your body, and Tanner just kept talking to me about it."

toggle caption Madeleine Charis King/Iowa Public Radio

The Faaborgs began working with Transfarmation in 2021, sold the last herd of hogs a year later and received a $15,000 grant from the program in 2023 to start growing mushrooms and sell products as a yearlong pilot project. The Faaborgs reported that site preparations in one of their outbuildings, supplies, branding and website development cost roughly $35,000.

As the business grows and expands with the new demonstration hub, Tyler Faaborg said they'd like to sell fresh mushrooms to a few companies. Eventually, 1100 Farm could also convert the second hog barn. But Tanner Faaborg said it would be used for something else, possibly microgreens.

Rewilding the farm

The Faaborgs said the transition from CAFO to specialty mushrooms has not always been easy, and they have a long road ahead. But there have been rewards along the way, like the conversion of a manure pit into a freshwater pond.

A Natural Resources Conservation Service grant program, part of the U.S. Department of Agriculture, partially funded the remediation, Tanner Faaborg said. Instead of being an eyesore, he said it's become a haven for frogs, ducks and other wildlife.

Sponsor Message

"It just shows that if you create the right environment, that rewilding can happen faster than you think," Faaborg said.

Rand Faaborg said the manure pit was a significant source of anxiety when he raised hogs. Sometimes he'd make contact with people who said they would take the manure but not show up, he said.

"That part of my life is gone and in exchange is just this little pond. My grandkids catch frogs," he said. "That's probably been my favorite part of it all."

toggle caption Madeleine Charis King/Iowa Public Radio

The Faaborgs also have planted native grasses and flowers to support pollinators. They're expanding their orchard and adding hundreds of trees and shrubs next to the creek that cuts across the farm to support better water quality and wildlife habitat.

Standing next to an empty grain silo that once held pig feed, Tanner Faaborg said he'd like to turn it into a space for visitors to stay overnight and wake up the next morning to sip lion's mane coffee while looking out at the farm.

The list of projects is long enough that they could take the rest of his life to complete. But he hopes the impact of 1100 Farm extends well beyond that.

World.title: Germany's leader stands his ground after his party loses in state elections
World.content:
Germany's leader stands his ground after his party loses in state elections

toggle caption Michele Tantussi/Getty Images

BERLIN — On Sunday night, Friedrich Merz should have been on his way to New York to attend the United Nations General Assembly. Instead he was at his Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party's headquarters in Berlin from where he broke the stunned silence as exit polls for two state elections showed its worst result since World War II.

State elections for parliament seats, which in turn elect a government and a governor, were held in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and in the city of Berlin. In both places, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) made significant gains since the last state elections in 2021 and 2023, receiving 38.2% in the rural northeastern state and 16.3 % in the capital. In Berlin, the far-left Die Linke came in first with 25.7% of the vote, seven percentage points ahead of the CDU.

Receiving just 4.9% of the vote in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the CDU hasn't even cleared the threshold meant to keep fringe parties out of parliament. Merz quashed talk within the press and his own party about his possible resignation despite Sunday's losses for his party just two weeks after a crushing defeat in the state of Saxony-Anhalt.

Sponsor Message

Usually, the German federal chancellor does not comment so promptly on state election results, especially for two states with relatively small electorates. But his party's crushing defeat in both states is starting to reflect poorly on Merz.

Merz conceded that the night spells "disaster" for the political center, but assured the public he'd push ahead with his federal agenda of tax and welfare reforms, describing them as "the antidote to the poison of authoritarianism."

He stressed that implementing these reforms "require backbone, steadfastness and patience" and that he will "demonstrate this" as "chancellor of our country."

toggle caption Ralf Hirschberger/AFP via Getty Images

Speaking to public broadcaster ARD, federal leader of the far-right Alternative for Germany — or AfD — Alice Weidel said the more Merz digs in his heels, the more her party benefits.

"Friedrich Merz is the wrong chancellor for the CDU," Weidel said, "and he is dragging the party down with him."

The far-right AfD also beat Merz's coalition partner, the Social Democrats (SPD), in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.

But the AfD is unlikely to find coalition partners willing to form a government so the incumbent SPD state governor, Manuela Schwesig — who came in second with 35% of the vote — is expected to find the allies she needs to remain in office.

Sponsor Message

In Berlin — which is both a city and a state whose mayor also serves as state governor — the far-left party, Die Linke, brought home its best ever result with a 25.7% share of the vote.

Its leader, Elif Eralp, pledged to make Berlin affordable again, drawing comparisons with New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

Taking to the stage as the results came in, Eralp said that Berliners will not tolerate the AfD's policies, adding "in our city, love and justice have triumphed over hate."

Eralp — whose parents fled Turkey after the coup d'etat in 1980 — pledges to introduce a rent cap and seize apartments owned by large corporate real estate developers.

But this second policy could prove contentious, even make-or-break as she enters into coalition negotiations this week.

Germany's electoral model is a combination of winner-take-all and proportional representation, meaning that parties need partners to form the parliamentary majority needed to govern.

For Eralp to take office as mayor, she needs to form a government with at least two other parties.

On a federal level, Merz — whose party co-governs with the Social Democrats — is finding that kind of consensus difficult with just one coalition partner.

Sudha David-Wilp of the think tank German Marshall Fund told NPR that despite talk of replacing him, Merz will counter any political reckoning by standing his ground.

"Merz himself has wanted to be chancellor for so long that he is probably loath to throw in the towel," David-Wilp said, "and he also knows the bar is very high to oust a chancellor in Germany."

But as an increasingly fragmented political landscape makes for unstable coalitions with parties blocking each other from implementing policy, the AfD tells the mainstream parties it's just waiting in the wings for the next federal election.

World.title: A consequential fall begins with familiar concerns and a new test for the Carney government
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

On the eve of Parliament's return to business, Mark Carney sought to manage expectations.

"We are meeting at a decisive moment for our country," the prime minister told a room full of Liberal MPs on Friday.

Near the end of his remarks, Carney told his caucus that this would be "a crucial session of the House of Commons."

"We are going to introduce some of the most consequential legislation, not just of this government, but in decades," he said.

Consequence can generally only be measured after the fact. But the prime minister's stark, ambitious foreshadowing and its promise of things to come seemed to at least meet this particular moment.

The broader moment that Canada now finds itself in has been apparent for something like 20 months — since the president of the United States started talking about Canada as the 51st state or since the president ruptured the Canadian-American relationship with the first of a series of unwarranted tariffs. But over the course of a few weeks this summer — from the collapse of trade talks with the United States in late August to last week's investment summit and Carney's address to the European Parliament — the moment has seemed to gain new urgency and momentum.

And with the political winds at his back, Carney is now touting a legislative agenda that befits the moment.

The Building Canada Strong Act, tabled on Monday, might be the new centrepiece of that agenda, but it will likely not be the end of it. New social media regulations, tabled last spring, are awaiting debate. The operations of Canada's biggest airports might be turned over to private investors. And the Carney government's second budget — and its first with a majority in the House — will land sometime later this fall.

Beyond Parliament Hill, potentially consequential events are scattered far and wide: a Quebec election on Oct. 5, a referendum in Alberta on Oct. 19, a Canada-European Union summit in Montreal on Oct. 29. The Supreme Court should deliver a ruling on the notwithstanding clause, a provincial election in British Columbia could yet be triggered and as many as six federal byelections might be called.

But on the first day of the fall sitting, the Official Opposition attempted to focus on matters most immediate.

The Conservatives want to save you money

"To the Canadian people," Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said, speaking directly to the television camera across from him, "the message of Conservatives is that we will fight to save you money."

A month ago, Poilievre had asked the prime minister to immediately reconvene Parliament so that MPs could discuss the worsening trade war with the United States. But at question period on Monday it took several rounds before Conservative MPs got to questions about the Carney government's handling of counter-tariffs.

Poilievre challenged Carney to acknowledge that the cost of living — specifically, the prices being paid for things like housing, gas and groceries — was still unacceptably high. Carney pointed to measures his government had taken to address affordability concerns — an income tax cut, a tax break for first-time home buyers, an enhanced GST credit.

WATCH | At Issue panel looks at Carney's EU pivot: At Issue | Is Carney’s Europe pivot in Canada’s best interest? | Duration closed caption 24:08 At Issue this week: Prime Minister Mark Carney moves to deepen ties with the European Union, but is it in Canada’s best interest? The Liberals try to lure foreign investment. And Stephen Harper stands behind the decision to walk away from U.S. trade talks.

Poilievre was unimpressed — all Canadians have received from the prime minister, he said, "is "big talk around the world and big bills here at home." Carney countered that Canadians knew it was the war in Ukraine, the war in Iran and a trade war that was increasing costs for Canadians.

Poilievre said it was federal policy that was to blame for consumer prices. Carney begged to differ.

It is hard to argue with the general relevance of such questions, both practically and politically. And "affordability" might yet grind away at the Carney government the way it undid Justin Trudeau's government — it might yet somehow revive Poilievre's political fortunes.

But if the history books remember the fall of 2026, it is likely to be for more dramatic matters.

A 'consequential' legislative agenda takes shape

It was not until the last intervention of Monday's question period — the lone opportunity provided to an NDP MP — that the government was asked something specific about that consequential legislative agenda.

"Well, Mr. Speaker, the real nature of this government is starting to appear," said the NDP's Don Davies, alleging that the Liberals were about to trample on the right to strike with the Building Canada Strong Act.

Patty Hajdu, the jobs minister, dismissed Davies's concerns and shortly thereafter her colleague, Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon, tabled Bill C-39, a 243-page piece of legislation that makes changes to environmental regulation, impact assessment and labour laws.

Speaking to reporters outside the House, McKinnon called it the government's "most significant piece of economic legislation yet."

Hajdu said the government was "responding to a crisis" and "doing exactly what Canadians have asked us to."

WATCH | Hajdu says C-39 will put 'guardrail' around Labour Code: Building Canada Strong Act will 'put a guardrail' around Labour Code provisions, says Hajdu | Duration 1:28 In response to a reporter who suggested that changes to the Canada Labour Code in the omnibus bill tabled by the government Monday will weaken the right to strike, Jobs and Families Minister Patty Hajdu says the bill will 'raise the bar around accountability' on both sides of negotiations.

If question period was any indication, the loudest opposition to C-39 may come from outside the House of Commons — in this case from environmental groups and organized labour.

Carney has built up an immense store of political capital over the last year and a half. And political capital exists to be spent. Carney's government has also not been particularly cautious before now.

But C-39 — and whatever else of consequence could follow this fall — might newly test how and how well this prime minister and his government respond to criticism and objections — and how well the prime minister can bring Canadians along with an agenda that won't always be easy or unanimously applauded. Not even a wartime prime minister can take the public's support for granted.

Probably no one would dispute that this is — one way or another — a consequential moment for the country. The extent of those changes remains to be debated. And the consequences for the Carney government itself remain to be seen.

World.title: U.S. shouldn't buy 'blood potash' from Belarus, Sask. premier says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe defended the province's potash industry as ethically and economically superior to other international exporters after U.S. President Donald Trump threatened to source more of his country's fertilizer from Belarus.

"Buying blood potash from Belarus is supporting Russian aggression," Moe said in a post on social media. "It’s wrong and it doesn’t make sense."

Moe's post on Monday afternoon was a response to a Trump social media post from earlier that day.

"The United States is working on ​a massive Deal with respect to the purchase of Potash ​from Belarus," Trump said on Truth Social. "The pricing would be for substantially less than we are currently paying to Canada, very good news for ​our Farmers and Ranchers."

Potash is mainly used in fertilizers. In 2024, almost a third of the world's potash production came from Canada and all of the country's 10 active potash mines are in Saskatchewan, according to Natural Resources Canada.

"More than 40 countries — Canada and its allies — have sanctions against Belarus for supporting war criminal Putin’s invasion of Ukraine," Moe said in his social media post.

"Does anyone believe Belarusian blood potash shipped through Russia is going to be more affordable, more sustainable or more ethical than potash shipped from Saskatchewan — right here in North America?"

Nutrien Ltd., The Mosaic Company, Compass Minerals, and K+S Potash Canada are responsible for all of Canada's potash production. BHP is building the Jansen potash mine in Saskatchewan and expects to start commercial production in mid-2027.

Nutrien is the largest potash fertilizer producer in Canada and one of the largest in the world. The Saskatoon-based company referred CBC to Fertilizer Canada when asked to comment on Trump's post.

U.S. farmers have used Canadian potash for decades, said Fertilizer Canada, an industry trade group, in an emailed statement to CBC News.

"Reliability, proximity, transportation infrastructure, product availability and the ability to deliver during critical application windows all matter," the statement said.

"A strong and integrated North American fertilizer supply chain helps support farm productivity, affordability and food security on both sides of the border.”

Potash is currently exempt from U.S. tariffs. Canada exported $4.2 billion of potash to the U.S. in 2025, according to Natural Resources Canada.

Last year, Nutrien announced plans to build a potash export terminal at the Port of Longview, Wash., to handle expected growth in international demand for its fertilizer products.

The exterior of the Mosaic potash mine, located near Belle Plaine, Saskatchewan, is shown on July 16, 2025. (Alexander Quon/CBC News)

University of Regina economics professor Jason Childs said exporting potash to the U.S. from Belarus could end up costing more compared to exports from Canada.

"I'm skeptical just because you've got so much more transportation to deal with," Childs said in an interview with CBC.

"Unless you come up with some wonderful deal where Belarus is going to have way lower production costs or something like that, I don't see it being that big a boon for the American farmer."

If Trump does make a deal with Belarus, it could affect the companies in Canada by lowering the overall price of potash, Childs said.

"Right now, Belarus and Russia have not really been active in the North American market. We benefited from that," Childs said.

"If they [enter] the North American market, then we're competing against another supplier and that's going to hurt our costs. That's going to hurt the price we can get for our product."

The opposition NDP called Trump's social media post "infuriating" in a statement on Monday.

"He is looking at signing a deal with an authoritarian Russian satellite state that is supporting Putin’s brutal war against the people of Ukraine," the NDP statement said.

"This is a bad idea that will only hurt families and communities on both sides of the border."

World.title: Alberta premier adamant referendum ads are not ‘neutral’ on separation question, as UCP president claims
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith is adamant she is promoting that the province stay in Canada, rejecting her own party president’s claim that the government’s advertising is “as neutral as possible” on the question.

“I'm not a neutral party in this,” Smith said at an unrelated press conference on Monday.

“I believe that we should remain, and I believe that we should do everything we can to address the things that are causing grievances [within the province]. You can't ignore them.”

In a lengthy Facebook post, UCP president Rob Smith acknowledged that many party members have “expressed disappointment” about the government’s $4-million advertising campaign on the referendum.

In his interpretation of the ad campaign, the UCP president argued the premier isn’t promoting a pro-Canada message as loudly as she is campaigning on the other questions.

He said the premier is spending $4 million to promote the message: “VOTE YES TO THE 9!!! … and, commensurately less, in a measured, limited way: Vote for ‘a sovereign Alberta within a united Canada.’”

The UCP president continued: “And [the premier] assured me … emphasized, I’d even say, that the included language and ‘promotion’ regarding this question would be as NEUTRAL as possible and not nearly as persuasive as for Questions #1-#9.”

“I’ve heard some of these ads, and I believe what Premier told me,” he said.

WATCH | Provincial government campaign urges Albertans to vote for specific answers: Alberta government referendum campaign urges Albertans to vote for specific answers | Duration closed caption 1:43 The Government of Alberta has launched its advertising campaign which encourages voters to select specific answers on the 10 questions, including the one on separation. As Travis McEwan reports, both sides of the separation argument feel the province should remain neutral.

When asked about the UCP president’s comments, the premier rejected the idea that the province’s campaign is dampening its pro-federation stance on Question 10.

“The nine questions that the government has put forward are what we were providing more information to the public on, 'cause I don't see anybody actually doing any campaigning on either side of any of those,” Smith said.

It’s not the first time the premier and UCP president have shared contradicting perspectives on the topic. In May, the two were at odds over where they stand on Alberta staying in Canada.

Lori Williams, a political scientist at Mount Royal University, said the premier and UCP president have differing strategies, with Rob Smith trying to “placate” those who are concerned that the premier is taking a pro-Canada position.

But what those contradictory messages from within the UCP could mean for party unity is “an open question,” she said.

“It's very difficult to try to hold together a party that has people with such disparate and conflicting views within it.”

Last week, the Highwood UCP association, a riding association in southern Alberta, formally urged a party vote to review Smith’s leadership.

Group board member and prominent independence supporter Tanya Clemens said she was motivated largely by the premier’s vocal support for the “stay” option in the referendum. However, she said she still respects Smith and would likely support her UCP leadership if a review was held today.

‘I have to take responsibility for my communications’: premier

On Monday, the premier was asked about the perception that federalists feel she is more aligned with separatists, while separatists feel she is a federalist.

Chuckling at the reporter’s question, Danielle Smith said, “I guess I have to take responsibility for my communications on that.”

“I understand the frustrations Alberta had after being abused for 10 years by an out-of-touch federal government, and it created a lot of anger,” she said.

“And I know that this is one of the ways that some people are wanting to express that anger and, you know, I sympathize with their position. But, I believe that Canada is working, every day, better than it has in a long time.”

WATCH | Tearful Danielle Smith reflects on referendum: 'Albertans are angry': tearful Danielle Smith reflects on referendum | Duration closed caption 4:17 Alberta Premier Danielle Smith became emotional while speaking Saturday during a virtual conference about the upcoming referendum. The event, put on by former federal Conservative leader Preston Manning, aimed to provide more information before the vote. Smith said it's important to understand the frustrations felt by Albertans, that has led to this moment.

Williams believes the premier’s strategy is to try to avoid offending those who are leaning separatist and to have the other nine referendum questions substitute for the question on separation.

But, she points out, you can’t always please everybody.

"Trying to be neutral, trying not to offend anyone, trying to please all of the people who disagree has wound up, more than once, in everybody disagreeing with her, being angry with her, and in some cases calling for her leadership,” Williams said.

Danielle Smith previously promised to travel across the province campaigning for voters to choose to stay in Canada.

“I’ve got a pretty busy travel schedule this summer. I’ll be doing town halls and meetings and talking to people about why it is I think they should vote to remain,” she told reporters at a May 22 press conference.

World.title: Another Marineland beluga has died after being moved to Chicago aquarium
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A fourth whale that was moved out of Marineland in July has died after struggling with its health since arriving at her new home in Chicago, Shedd Aquarium said Monday.

The park said 26-year-old Osiris died Monday morning. The female beluga was one of 10 that came to Shedd from Marineland, the shuttered tourist attraction in Niagara Falls, Ont.

It was part of the world's biggest collective move of captive whales. Marineland had said it was running out of money and could no longer care for its animals.

Over a series of moves beginning in July, Marineland moved 30 belugas and four dolphins to five aquariums abroad: Shedd in Chicago, SeaWorld locations in San Antonio, Texas, and San Diego, Calif., Georgia Aquarium in Atlanta and Oceanografic Valencia in Spain.

Beluga whale Tofino was one of 10 transported by a group of experts from Marineland to various aquarums earlier this summer. (Carlos Osorio/The Canadian Press)

Osiris was "not a consistent eater" but had improved recently after receiving fluids and medication, Shedd said.

"Our care team observed sudden changes this morning in both Osiris's behaviour and respiratory patterns," Shedd said in a statement.

"Respiratory rates are one of many measures we track closely and continuously, as changes can signal that an animal may need additional support. The team moved Osiris to the medical habitat, so immediate care could be provided if needed. Her condition declined rapidly, and Osiris passed away despite lifesaving efforts by our veterinary and animal care teams."

The park will conduct a necropsy to try to better understand what happened.

WATCH | Marineland's belugas relocated: Final Marineland whales moved to the U.S. | Duration closed caption 2:02 Marineland's last six beluga whales, the last of the mammals in Canadian captivity, were moved from the closed theme park and flown to the U.S. Thirty whales and four dolphins have been relocated since July.

Two other Marineland whales, Rain and Peekachu, died at Shedd within weeks of the move. One longtime Shedd resident beluga, Beethoven, also recently died.

All are being investigated, but the results have not yet returned, Shedd said.

Another Marineland beluga, Jelly Bean, died at Oceanografic in Spain last week.

The whales were cleared by veterinarians at Marineland and the other parks to move and Fisheries Minister Joanne Thompson also signed off on the relocation.

Last week, Shedd said it is concerned about the health of another recently moved whale, Secord.

"Secord has not yet been consistently taking in the amount of food teams would like to see, even as they try different feeding approaches and offer different types of herring to gauge her preference," Shedd said in a blog post last week.

Marineland originally sought to move the whales to China after securing a deal to sell all 30 of its belugas to Chimelong Ocean Kingdom, which has a Guinness Book of World Record for the largest aquarium in the world.

Thompson blocked that move, saying it was not in the best interest of the whales and inconsistent with a 2019 federal law. That law banned whale and dolphin captivity and performances, but grandfathered in Marineland's whales. It also banned breeding, which forced Marineland to separate its whales by sex.

Marineland turned to an American-led consortium to house the world's biggest pod of captive belugas, but they needed five aquariums to house them all.

There are no breeding or performing restrictions at the belugas' new homes.

Marineland's whales had struggled in recent years. Nineteen belugas and one killer whale died at the park between 2019 and 2025.

The park blames some of those deaths on the new federal laws.

World.title: Canadian investigation launched into data breach that exposed millions of IDs
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canada's privacy commissioner has launched an investigation into a data breach at IDScan.net that potentially exposed details from millions of driver's licences and other kinds of government-issued identification from Canada and the U.S.

IDScan.net provides identification verification software to several categories of businesses, from bars and casinos to car rental companies.

Earlier this month, the company published a public notice about a data security incident, stating that " an unauthorized third party may have accessed and/or copied certain customer information stored within their accounts on the IDScan.net cloud."

The company said it was notifying individuals who had potentially been affected and offered free credit monitoring services.

Two days before IDScan.net published its alert, the FBI confirmed it was looking into the reported theft of tens of millions of driver's licences belonging to people in the U.S. and Canada that were being sold on the dark net.

The bureau said it was “looking into the incident” but could not comment “due to the ongoing nature of the investigation.”

Unprecedented in size and scope

The breach could be one of the largest-ever exposures of government-issued identity documents in North America.

Zach Edwards, a threat researcher at the cybersecurity company Infoblox, told Reuters the incident was unprecedented in terms of its sweep.

"There's never been a breach of driver's licences at this scale," said Edwards, who added that he discovered his own license was part of it. Edwards said that the ongoing nature of the breach "means that this attack created legitimate national security risks for high-profile individuals."

Canada's Office of the Privacy Commissioner says it's examining the security safeguards IDScan.net had in place at the time of the breach and whether its actions to notify potentially affected Canadians were adequate.

The probe will also look at whether IDScan.net breached Canada’s federal private-sector privacy laws.

World.title: Suspect, police officer wounded in shooting outside Belleville, Ont., synagogue ID'd
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results. Police have identified the suspect in a shooting outside a synagogue Sunday night that left a police officer injured. Police said Sean Ward, 29, was armed with a shotgun and fired at an officer before a second officer arrived and returned fire. The shooting comes as members of the Jewish community gather to mark Yom Kippur. Ward is in the hospital in life-threatening condition. Investigators have identified the wounded suspect in the shooting incident that unfolded near a Belleville, Ont., synagogue Sunday night, and the local police officer who was also wounded. The suspect has been named as Sean Ward, 29, of neighbouring Quinte West. The officer, who remains in hospital in critical but stable condition, is Const. Jeff Smith. The Belleville Police Service confirmed their identities Monday in a noon-hour news conference held just outside the taped-off scene. Sons of Jacob Synagogue is located at the corner of Bleeker and Victoria avenues. Yom Kippur services were underway inside when the suspect allegedly opened fire on Smith with a shotgun while the officer was stationed outside the building, Belleville Deputy Police Chief Sheri Meeks and Kristy Denette, a spokesperson for Ontario's Special Investigations Unit (SIU), said during the news conference. Another Belleville police officer also fired their weapon. Smith had been parked outside Sons of Jacob at the request of the synagogue, its president told CBC News. "We always have police protection," Norm Weddum said of large gatherings at the synagogue, adding that the pre-emptive police protection put in place for Sunday evening had been requested as a matter of routine a week earlier. "Thank God that person was there," Weddum said of the officer. PHOTOS | The unfolding scene in Belleville: Smith, who has been with Belleville's police service since 2013, suffered serious injuries during the shootout and is recovering in an intensive care unit where he remains in critical but stable condition. "While he continues to face a significant road to recovery, his condition has stabilized and we remain hopeful and encouraged by his progress," Meeks said. The shooting is a reminder that "every day [officers] leave their homes and loved ones not knowing what they may encounter," she added. Ward is in life-threatening condition. "It's my understanding that he was very critical and but was sort of brought back to life, so to speak," Denette said. Police on Monday were at the Quinte West home Ward shares with his mother. They have not yet announced any charges against him. A former employer and neighbours tell CBC that Ward was formerly in the Canadian military in Alberta. Kingston police outside Ward's home on Monday. (CBC) Questions remain It's unclear if the shooting was targeting Smith, Sons of Jacob or the city's Jewish community. Meeks said Belleville police won't be providing any more updates on their own investigation of the incident while the SIU performs a parallel, narrowly focused investigation into the circumstances that prompted Smith and the other unnamed officer to fire their weapons. "We are in the process of securing body-worn camera footage from the officers involved and also in-car camera [footage]," Denette of the SIU said. "So until such time as we are able to review that, it's difficult for me to give you a sequence of events. "It's believed that [Ward] came in a truck and he had a shotgun and he discharged his firearm at a police officer and then that police officer returned fire and then there was a second officer who arrived and then also discharged [their] firearm. That's what we can tell you is our preliminary kind of findings." Asked about the timing of the incident during Yom Kippur and whether the evidence so far suggests it was an attack aimed at the Jewish community, Denette replied, "I'd be speculating, but ... I think that common sense would say that probably was the case." This photo of the shooting suspect, Sean Ward, was posted to his father's Facebook page in 2017. (Doug Ward/Facebook) 'Literally everyone went down' Weddum said the synagogue was ushering people inside when Yom Kippur services began at around 7 p.m. "It was boom, boom, boom," Weddum told CBC News Network of the gunshhots he heard outside. Weddum said he went to the lobby where he could hear more defined shots. "I could say, 'Oh, this is definitely … someone is shooting here,'" he said. "So that's when we ran back into the auditorium of the synagogue, closed the doors behind us so as to not leave a visible target and we hit the floor." "Literally everyone went down," he said. "I yelled for everyone to get on to the floor and the shots continued for a few more seconds, and then it was basically over." Weddum said an officer had been stationed outside the building in an unmarked car. WATCH | The synagogue president describes what he heard and saw: Member of Belleville, Ont., synagogue describes hearing shots that left 2 wounded | Duration closed caption 5:47 A police officer and a man were wounded in an exchange of gunfire Sunday near a synagogue in Belleville, Ont. Norm Weddum, president of Sons of Jacob Synagogue, was ushering in members for Yom Kippur when he heard shots and secured the building. Meeks, the deputy police chief, said that while there is no ongoing threat to public safety, the police service is increasing patrols and "maintaining a heightened police presence" throughout the city, including at places of worship. "Let me be very clear: Antisemitism, hate and violence have no place in our community," she said. "Every person deserves to feel safe when attending a place of worship, gathering with loved ones, or participating in community life. Denette said the SIU has sent four investigators and two forensic investigators to the scene, which she described as "complex." "There are dozens of bullet holes in the street behind me and some homes have been hit and there are some vehicles with shot out windows, that sort of thing. So it would have been quite the scene," she said. The scene will likely be blocked off for a couple more days, she added. Police and Ontario's Special Investigations Unit are shown Monday at the scene of the shooting that took place a half a block away from the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, Ont., on Sunday evening. A suspected and a police officer are both wounded and in the hospital. (Ian MacAlpine/The Canadian Press) Carney, Ford release statements Yom Kippur, one of the most sacred days of the Jewish calendar, began at sundown on Sunday. Prime Minister Mark Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford were among the public figures to release statements after the shooting. "Jewish people must be able to worship safely. To live free, open, proud Jewish lives. Canada’s government will do everything in our power to support law enforcement in ensuring that the perpetrator is held accountable to the fullest extent of the law," Carney said on social media. WATCH | Carney comments on the shooting: Carney calls shooting outside Belleville, Ont., synagogue 'deeply distressing' | Duration closed caption 0:30 Prime Minister Mark Carney appealed for anyone with knowledge of a shooting near a Belleville, Ont., synagogue to speak to law enforcement, saying 'hearts go out to the community' after two people, including a police officer, were injured. Sunday's shooting comes months after Carney warned that Canada was failing its Jewish community amid a surge in antisemitism. "I'm disgusted by the shooting that took place outside the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville earlier this evening as Jewish community members gathered to mark Yom Kippur," Ford said in a post. "We owe an immense debt of gratitude to this brave officer and to all the first responders who acted so quickly to keep the community safe." I’m disgusted by the shooting that took place outside the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville earlier this evening as Jewish community members gathered to mark Yom Kippur.

My thoughts are with the Jewish community in Belleville and across Ontario, who have every right to… —fordnation Belleville Mayor Neil Ellis told the CBC's Ontario Morning he was shocked by the news of the incident and commended the injured officer. "We've been rocked by this … stuff like this doesn't happen in Belleville," he said. "We are a community that's strong, and we are a community that's vibrant, and we will get through this together." "The City of Belleville is behind the Jewish community," Ellis told CBC Ottawa later Monday morning, adding that he was brought to tears when he first heard about the shooting Sunday evening. 'It's just devastating that this happened to Belleville,' Mayor Neil Ellis says. (Christian Lachance/CBC) Hopefully the SIU investigation will get to "the root cause" of the incident, the mayor added. Belleville had about 55,100 people as of the 2021 census. The broader area has about 111,200 people. The city is a hub for Hastings County and eastern Ontario’s third-biggest city, about 175 kilometres east of Toronto and 190 kilometres southwest of downtown Ottawa. Witness counts over 20 shots Chris Masterson, who lives nearby, said he was watching TV on Sunday evening when he heard three "loud pops." "There was a little bit of a pause and then I heard more shots," he said. "It was very clear it was gunshots." Masterson said he estimates there were around 25 shots back and forth before he heard a siren and someone clearly yell: "Police, stop." "I've been living here for over 10 years and nothing like this has ever happened," said another resident, Cody Bain. "It kind of makes you nervous. Makes you wonder about the future." WATCH | Neighbour says he heard shots while out for a walk: Neighbour describes hearing shots near Belleville, Ont., synagogue | Duration 1:41 Scott Granville, who lives near the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, Ont., says he was out for a walk Sunday night when he heard gunshots. 'It sounded almost like an explosion,' he said, adding that things unfolded in a matter of minutes. 'We will carry on': synagogue leader When asked what he thought the man involved in the shooting was trying to do, synagogue leader Weddum said he thought "his intentions were pretty clear." "Well, he was coming down the street with some type of a firearm, and he was headed toward a synagogue where Jewish people were having service. So I think his intentions were pretty clear," said Weddum. "It's rough. And unfortunately we can't have our services again today to complete the Yom Kippur holiday, because the building is under a lockdown right now for the investigation," he said. "But, you know, once the building is released we'll get back to having services. "We will carry on."

World.title: Denmark, Greenland set to sign security deal with U.S. on Tuesday
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Denmark, Greenland and the U.S. are to sign a deal on Greenland's security on Tuesday, an agreement Denmark says will put Arctic security under NATO's watch rather than leaving it solely to Washington ‌and Copenhagen.

The agreement, to be signed at the UN General Assembly in New York at 10:30 a.m. ET on Tuesday, has not been made public. Denmark and Greenland say the deal will benefit the Arctic island and respect its sovereignty.

The deal is expected to allow the U.S., which already has one military base in Greenland, to expand its military presence to two additional sites.

One of those sites is Narsarsuaq, whose population has dwindled to a few dozen people since ​the U.S. closed its Cold War-era Bluie West One military base there in the 1950s. The other ​is Mestersvig, a military outpost currently used by the Sirius Dog Sled Patrol, a special forces unit that enforces Danish sovereignty in the territory, according to two people familiar with the matter.

Trilateral signing ceremony planned

U.S. President Donald Trump will meet in New York on Tuesday with Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenland Prime Minister Jens-Frederik ​Nielsen for a trilateral signing ceremony, a White House official said.

A sign in Nuuk proclaims 'Greenland is not for sale!' (Tim Barsoe/Reuters)

The deal follows months of pressure from Trump, who has said the U.S. should ⁠control Greenland and at times refused to ⁠rule out using military or economic force to acquire the semi-autonomous Danish territory. His threats peaked ‌in January, triggering a diplomatic crisis within the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO), the military defence alliance, and pushing Denmark and Greenland into negotiations aimed at defusing the pressure.

The agreement "will be in a form where responsibility for security in the Arctic is not only Danish or American," Danish Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen told national broadcaster TV2 on Sunday. He said that, to a large extent, "it would be NATO that looks after the Arctic."

It remained unclear whether the deal ⁠amends an existing 1951 defence agreement that is the legal basis for the U.S. presence in Greenland.

"It appears that we are now using this crisis to try to strengthen NATO's cohesion through Greenland," said Ulrik Pram Gad, a researcher at the Danish Institute for International Studies (DIIS).

Strategic interest in Greenland

Washington's strategic interest in Greenland dates back to the Second World War. In 1941, the U.S. signed a deal with Danish envoy ‌Henrik Kauffmann, who acted without authority from his country, then under German occupation.

WATCH | Trump posts map showing U.S. flag covering North America, Greenland and Iceland: Does Iceland feel threatened by Trump's expansionist threats? | Hanomansing Tonight | Duration closed caption 3:47 Iceland summoned the U.S. ambassador after President Donald Trump posted a map showing the U.S. flag covering North America, Greenland and Iceland. Magnús Eyjólfsson, a journalist with national broadcaster RÚV, discusses how Icelanders are reacting to Trump’s expansionist rhetoric and why his recent threats to take over Greenland hit particularly close to home.

The U.S. sought the deal to keep Greenland out of German hands and secure the North Atlantic supply route between North America and Europe. Under the agreement, the U.S. built airfields, naval facilities and weather stations across the island, reaching around 5,500 military personnel by 1943, according to DIIS.

In 1946, then-U.S. president Harry Truman sought to buy the island as a strategic asset for $100 million US in gold, but Copenhagen declined ​to sell. Instead, a new agreement was signed in 1951 that gave the U.S. military extensive rights in Greenland but was tied to the existence of NATO.

"I don't think Denmark and Greenland will sign if the same NATO clause isn't included," ⁠said Gad.

Cold War presence

During the Cold War, the U.S. maintained 17 military installations and more than 10,000 personnel in Greenland. Today only Pituffik Space Base remains, with some 150 ⁠U.S. military personnel.

A NATO spokesperson said on Saturday that the alliance welcomed the new agreement, which would "help advance security, stability and co-operation in this vital region."

Rasmussen, who travelled to ⁠New York ⁠overnight, declined to discuss the contents of the agreement.

"But we have ​said from the start that we are open to accommodating the United States' legitimate security interests," he told Danish news agency Ritzau on Monday.

Trump said in a social media post on Friday the agreement gave the U.S. "permanent control over ⁠security, and all other needs, in Greenland," and that no U.S. adversary could have a base or military presence there without Washington's written approval.

Denmark has not responded to Trump's assertion, though Copenhagen earlier acknowledged it underinvested in Greenland's defence for decades and has pledged to expand its military presence on the island, including more NATO troops.

Greenland's government has sought to reassure the public about the deal.

Erik Jensen, an opposition lawmaker in Greenland, wrote on social media that he had read the draft agreement. "I feel reassured and am not worried," he said, adding that the island's foreign minister was handling the work ⁠well.

World.title: Flights resume after ground stops at major U.S. airports, including New York's JFK and ‌LaGuardia
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration resolved a telecommunications problem late in the afternoon that had snarled thousands of flights across the country, with incoming flights halted for hours at major East Coast airports.

The issue started around 9:45 a.m. ET when workers accidentally cut a telecom line in New Jersey used by the FAA. This forced a halt to incoming flights at major airports, on a day when 130 world leaders and dozens of ministers were arriving in New York for the annual high-level meeting of the United Nations General Assembly.

The FAA stopped arrivals at all three major New York-area airports as well as ​Philadelphia and Boston, and two smaller airports in the New York region. The problems were ​not fully resolved for eight hours.

Prime Minister Mark Carney was among the leaders whose flights were affected. His office said his planned flight into New York this evening was delayed, meaning he would not make it to a scheduled event. He is expected to arrive in the city later Monday night.

U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy posted on X late in the afternoon that telecom lines had been repaired and normal operations throughout the Northeast were resuming. He said it would take time to resolve existing delays and urged passengers to check the status ​of flights for which they were waiting.

Passengers at Philadelphia International Airport were left looking for alternatives after a ground stoppage halted flights in and out for hours on Sept. 21. (Alexandre Silberman/CBC News)

Fewer than a dozen flights were affected at Toronto's Pearson International Airport as a result of the ground stop in the U.S.

Officials at Pearson and at Montreal's Trudeau International Airport said they were continuing to monitor the situation, and encouraged passengers flying to or from the U.S. to contact their airlines directly for updated information.

FlightAware, a flight-tracking website, said about 7,000 flights were delayed or cancelled, including 1,400 flights at the three ⁠major New York-area airports.

More than half ⁠of all flights were cancelled at Newark, a major United Airlines hub. United said it issued ‌a travel waiver to help impacted passengers.

The issue also forced the diversion of more than 100 flights to other airports.

Flights at Philadelphia had resumed by late in the afternoon after a second ground stop was lifted. Reagan Washington National Airport also halted flights for more than an hour because of ​volume issues.

A ground stop at Boston, which stopped accepting flights because of spillover volume, was also ⁠lifted.

“The timing is absolutely horrible and I’m very sorry for the delays and cancellations,” Bedford told reporters. He stressed that safety was the top priority. “We’re going to do what ⁠is necessary to make sure the airspace is safe.”

World.title: Colombia’s war crimes tribunal warns ICC that De la Espriella supports “worst attack in history”
World.content:
Colombia’s war crimes tribunal JEP said that it would warn the United Nations and the International Criminal Court about plans of President Abelardo de la Espriella to cut its budget.

In a statement, JEP president Alejandro Ramelli raised the alarm warned about a pending proposal by far-right Senator Enrique Gomez (National Salvation) to reduce the tribunal’s budget by COP100 billion ($31.6 million), which received De la Espriella’s support.

A second proposal by another far-right party, the Democratic Center, sought to push all sentences against members of the security forces to military justice for revision.

According to Ramelli, the two bill proposals “prove the existence of a strategy to block the JEP’s functioning” and called on the international community to “put a stop to this effort to dismantle our financial system and calls for the essential resources needed for our operations to be guaranteed.”

These initiatives constitute a combined strategy of economic strangulation and the subjugation of the JEP to military criminal justice. It is the most serious attack we have ever faced against our independence and autonomy. JEP president Alejandro Ramelli

The president , who vowed to get rid of the JEP on campaign, said that the 2027 national budget “does not constitute any threat to any judge, it’s the Constitution at work.”

I do not have a policy of retaliation against the JEP. I have a duty to manage spending, demand results, and allocate the State’s limited resources to a justice system that serves everyone, not to a court that part of the country perceives—for reasons debated in Congress and in public opinion—as a system of privileges rather than an effective end to impunity. President Abelardo de la Espriella

Since March of 2018, the JEP has played a key role in clarifying crimes committed during the armed conflict that erupted in response to the insurgency of the now-defunct guerrilla group FARC.

Among other things, the JEP found that the guerrillas recruited more than 18,000 children and that the security forces assassinated more than 7,800 civilians to inflate their combat kills.

Hundreds of former guerrillas and former members of the armed forces are taking part in a transitional justice system that seeks to solve as many as possible of the hundreds of thousands of crimes committed during the decades-long armed conflict.

World.title: Colombia pulls out of international LGBT coalition
World.content:
The government of President Abelardo de la Espriella pulled Colombia out of the international Equal Rights Coalition, which promotes the rights of sexual and gender minorities around the world.

The Foreign Ministry announced its departure from the coalition in a letter addressed to the organization of which Colombia was co-president until February next year.

According to Caribe Afirmativa, a gay rights NGO that was part of the international initiative, warned that the decision was “a serious setback in foreign policy and commitments to LGBTIQ+ rights.”

We also view this action as a snub to the international community, a break from the leadership role Colombia had established, and an unequivocal political signal regarding the place the current government is willing to grant to the rights of LGBTIQ+ people. Caribe Afirmativa

De la Espriella has appointed multiple prominent far-right figures in his government and has vowed to wage a “Culture War” against what it considers “gender ideology.”

On top of this, De la Espriella and multiple of his cabinet members oppose the right of gay couples to adopt children and reportedly sacked the newly appointed planning chief because he and his gay partner had adopted a child.

World.title: Court imposes strict conditions on Colombia’s military air strikes if minors are present
World.content:
A Bogota court imposed strict conditions on Colombia’s military authorities if they want to carry out air strikes on illegal armed groups in places where victims of forced recruitment are present.

The ruling of Bogota’s 34th Family Court lifted a suspension on the strikes that had been imposed earlier this month in response to a lawsuit.

The court imposed the following conditions on air strikes to evade violating International Humanitarian Law, which prioritizes the rights of child victims of forced recruitment over the success of military operations.

Don’t assume minors are legitimate targets because they form part of an illegal armed group

Intensify the verification and cross-checking of available information on the possible presence of minors at potential targets

Explicitly include this assessment to the legal and operational assessment of the attack

Assess the foreseeable risk of an attack on the lives and integrity of the minors

Examine the existence of less harmful means, methods, timing or operational alternatives that would allow the achievement of a comparable military advantage

Rigorously apply the principles of distinction, precaution, and proportionality before authorizing and executing the operation

The court additionally ordered family welfare institute ICBF to be integrated into military operations and strengthen the pathways for disengagement, restoration of rights, comprehensive care, and reintegration of children and adolescents who are victims of recruitment, with a differentiated and territorial approach.

The court asked the Ombudsman and the Inspector General’s Office to monitor compliance of the orders issued to maximize the protection of children’s rights.

The lawsuit had been filed in a successful attempt to protect children against the violence President Abelardo de la Espriella sought to unleash on illegal armed groups that refused to demobilize.

World.title: US maintains Colombia “failed demonstrably” in fighting drug trafficking
World.content:
The United States President Donald Trump maintained that Colombia “failed demonstrably during the previous 12 months to make substantial efforts to adhere to their obligations under international counternarcotics agreements.”

In an annual reviews, Trump stressed that the South American country maintains its an unwilling drug trafficking country “solely due to the incompetence and chaos produced by the previous far-left government.”

“If, as expected, Colombia makes progress on aggressive coca eradication and dismantling its narcoterrorist networks over the coming year, I will consider lifting the country’s ‘failed demonstrably’ status,” said the US president.

President Abelardo de la Espriella “has pledged to lead an aggressive campaign against coca cultivation and cocaine production, which reached record levels under the failed socialist policies of his predecessor,” Gustavo Petro, according to Trump.

Colombia is poised to resume its place as our foremost security partner in the hemisphere, and the country’s military, police, prosecutors, and courts now finally have a worthy champion in President de la Espriella. US President Donald Trump

De la Espriella, who took office in August, informally joined the US Government’s Shield of the Americas program in an attempt to increase cooperation between Trump’s conservative and far-right allies in the region.

As part of his counternarcotics efforts, the Colombian president tried to increase air strikes on so-called “narcoterrorist” groups, but was forced to stop this by a court to protect minor forced recruitment victims.

The National Police announced a pilot aerial fumigation program, but this was also suspended by a court because of health and environmental concerns.

The State Department vowed to seek $1 billion dollar in aid, but has yet to ask Congress for these funds while allegedly dealing with the world’s highest number of deaths caused by the consumption of illicit drugs.

World.title: Colombia’s statistics chief sacked for claiming Petro did not manipulate statistics
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella sacked his statistics chief because he claimed he found no anomalies in labor statistics presented by the administration of former President Gustavo Petro.

In a press statement, De la Espriella’s press secretary said that DANE director Ricardo Valencia was sacked for claiming “that he had not found any anomalies in the DANE indicators for the month of July, figures compiled during the final month of the previous administration.”

Valencia made that claim “without any in-depth audits having been conducted beforehand,” according to the press secretary.

It is essential for the National Government to conduct a rigorous review of the information received and to ensure that the data on which strategic decisions for the country are based fully reflect the economic and social reality of Colombians. President’s Office

The former DANE director was sacked days after the President’s Office canceled another statistics press conference that are common because of the agency’s regular updates on the state of the Colombian economy

July’s labor statistics confirmed claims by the previous government that unemployment dropped to record lows after Petro raised the minimum wage.

De la Espriella has insisted that the country’s economy is in crisis contrary to evidence, which indicated Petro increased economic growth in his last half year in office.

World.title: Colombia’s social organizations and labor unions announce national strike in November
World.content:
Some 1,500 representatives of social organizations and labor unions agreed to begin organizing an anti-government national strike that should take place throughout Colombia either on November 11 or on November 20.

The organizations agreed to the mass mobilization during the National Gathering for the Defense of Life, Dignity, Democracy, Peace, Sovereignty, and Social Reforms that had been organized by labor unions in the capital Bogota.

The first and fundamental decision of the Meeting is to declare the most radical opposition to the illegitimate government of Abelardo de la Espriella because of the course it has imposed on the country—one of subordination to the interests of U.S. imperialism and alignment with the agenda of the international far right—which constitutes a direct threat to national sovereignty, democracy, and the rights won by the Colombian people, and an undeniable shift toward fascism. Social organizations and labor unions

In a statement, the organizations said that the national strike will be preceded by regional protests on October 10 and 14 that will seek to generate momentum for the national strike.

Indigenous organizations will additionally organize a Day of Indigenous, Afro and Popular Resistance on October 12.

A final date for the national strike has yet to be defined.

The organizations decided to call a strike to protest the government’s security and defense policy, the ending of peace processes with illegal armed groups and in defense of social reforms that had been implemented by former President Gustavo Petro.

The protests additionally seek to express solidarity with the people of Palestine, western Sahara, Iran, Bolivia and Venezuela, and reject US imperialism in the Americas.

We must categorically reject the interference of U.S. government officials in the formulation of domestic policies under the guise of so-called friendly aid, which in reality masks the ambition to intensify overexploitation, extractivism, territorial control, and the presence of foreign troops on our soil. Social organizations and labor unions

The organizations agreed to “prepare, through the most intense and massive agitation and propaganda campaign, a national strike.”

World.title: Judge suspends Colombia’s aerial fumigation pilot
World.content:
A Putumayo from the southern Putumayo province suspended the government’s announced resumption of the aerial spraying of coca, ordering information that would allow “a sufficiently informed decision on the merits.”

Earlier this week, the National Narcotics Council (CNE) ordered the National Police to restart the aerial fumigation of coca, the base ingredient for cocaine, “as a controlled, limited, temporary, and evaluable experimental phase, the implementation of a pilot plan for the eradication of illicit crops through aerial spraying using a manned aircraft and the formulated product Glufosinate Ammonium 200 SL.”

The National Police subsequently said that the 10km2 pilot area was located in Putumayo, a province inside the Amazon forest.

These announcements triggered a local foundation to sue the administration, claiming that the plans to do a pilot were in violation of the 2015 ban on aerial fumigation and threatened both locals and the environment.

The judge agreed and ordered the administration of President Abelardo de la Espriella to provide information on the environmental and health risk involved in the aerial spraying with glufosinate ammonium.

The potential implementation of the pilot plan before gathering and analyzing the studies, documents, and technical evidence cited by the administration itself as the basis for the decision could render the requested constitutional protection ineffective and jeopardize the possibility of reaching a sufficiently informed decision on the merits; Indeed, the combination of the announced imminence of the measure, the current lack of essential information needed to understand its territorial, social, and environmental scope, and the particular ecological sensitivity of the department of Putumayo necessitates preventive action aimed at preserving the effectiveness of this constitutional action. Putumayo court

The suspension of the aerial spraying comes days after De la Espriella promised US Secretary of State Marco Rubio that he would resume aerial fumigation, a notoriously ineffective way to get rid of coca.

World.title: Colombia announces new aerial fumigation pilot program
World.content:
Colombia’s National Narcotics Council (CNE) ordered the National Police to restart the aerial fumigation of coca, the base ingredient for cocaine.

In a resolution, the CNE ordered “as a controlled, limited, temporary, and evaluable experimental phase, the implementation of a pilot plan for the eradication of illicit crops through aerial spraying using a manned aircraft and the formulated product Glufosinate Ammonium 200 SL.”

In a public statement, the National Police’s counternarcotics unit said that the 10km2 pilot area was located in Putumayo and would not affect indigenous and afro-descendant communities, who would need to be asked permission.

The exclusion of environmental protection zones and protected areas, zones associated with bodies of water, rivers, and other environmentally sensitive areas is contemplated, as well as those territories that, in accordance with current regulations and the corresponding technical studies, must be excluded. National Police Counternarcotics

The purpose of the pilot program is to “evaluate the effectiveness of aerial spraying, as well as its application under the established technical and operational conditions, said the police.

The police stressed that “this experimental phase does not constitute the resumption, adoption, or definitive authorization of a widespread or nationwide aerial spraying program,” which was banned by the Constitutional Court in 2015.

In order to resume aerial fumigation, health and environmental authorities must sign off on the program and the police would only be allowed to use airplanes with the approval of the court and local communities.

President Abelardo de la Espriella vowed to resume aerial spraying more than 330,000 hectares while on campaign and after taking office last month as part of his hardline approach to organized crime.

Former President Ivan Duque also vowed to resume aerial spraying, but failed to comply with the norms established by the court.

World.title: Evacuations ordered in Chile as wildfires run amok
World.content:
Chile’s National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response (Senapred) Wednesday ordered the evacuation of 14 communes in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía, including Nacimiento, Purén, and Contulmo, which have all been particularly affected by the forest fires.

In messages broadcast through the Emergency Alert System (SAE), the authorities also called on residents to leave their homes to avoid further damage to their health.

It has already been a week since the first wildfires ran amok in south-central Chile despite efforts to contain them. High temperatures, dryness, and strong winds add to the plight of local people and some 5,600 firefighters deployed in the area while helping flocks in from abroad.

”We are entering this part of the week which is the most complex. Today, tomorrow, and the day after we have an alert for high temperatures in several regions of the country that has mobilized a very large effort (…) to prevent the fires from spreading,“ Interior Minister Carolina Tohá said regarding the 311 active fires, of which 89 are being fought. The Senapred also said 180 fires were under control, and 309,747 hectares have been affected.

”If the temperature rises and the wind increases we can indeed have more problems, and we already have many fires,” Spanish Lieutenant Colonel Carlos Javier Martín Traverso told AFP. Traverso’s Air Operations Section of the Military Emergency Unit (UME) arrived in Chile on Sunday to join the firefighting efforts.

Over 309,000 hectares have been consumed in the regions of Maule, Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía with the death toll standing at 24, plus 2,180 people injured as 1,180 houses were destroyed, leaving 5,560 people homeless.

There seems to be a seamless scientific consensus that fires are the result of human actions, either by intentionality or carelessness, although the drought that has hit Chile for 13 years adds to the aggressiveness of the fires.

In this scenario, President Gabriel Boric Font has announced a curfew in the areas of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía where a state of catastrophe is in force, in order to guarantee the security and tranquility of

the families affected by the crisis. Defense authorities working on the sites will determine the restriction’s schedule.

“We have 24 people dead nationwide, three are from Santa Juana and we do not want there to be even one more,” Boric told reporters after visiting the area.

The number of fatalities was updated to 24 after two bodies were determined to belong to people who had died before the fires broke out.

Meanwhile, Biobío Governor Rodrigo Díaz said he was certain about “people criminally setting fires.”

“I have reports from police, firefighters, of people who have been setting fires. I do not have indications, but certainties, we need more patrols,” he insisted in a radio interview.

“We have fire outbreaks at the southern exit of Contulmo, different places where fires were set 300 meters away from each other, I could see it, nobody told me about it. The mayor of Mulchén told me how fires were lit in the four cardinal points, I have reports from the police, the Fire Department, from people who have been setting fires. I do not have indications, but certainties, we need more patrols in the area,” he explained.

President Boric’s Regional Delegate Daniela Dresdner said eight people had been arrested for “irresponsible and suspicious attitudes with respect to the setting of fires. This was due to citizen complaints and patrols by the Navy.”

“We are asking that all these conducts be denounced and we are filing a lawsuit for all these denunciations to [be] prosecute[d],” she added.

The Biobío Regional Prosecutor’s Office called on the citizenry to e-mail all data regarding criminal behavior to fiscaliaincendios@gmail.com, including pictures, videos, audios, or written information as to the probable causes of the fires, which will be handled confidentially. (Merco Press)

World.title: Chile’s wildfires death toll reaches 24
World.content:
Chilean authorities spoke Sunday of 24 fatalities, nearly 1,000 people injured, and some 800 houses destroyed in the past five days by wildfires spreading fast in amid a highly-irregular heat wave with strong winds and temperatures above 40°C in areas 500 km south of Santiago.

The death toll reached 24 after the death of one of the injured people who had been hospitalized in Angol, Undersecretary of the Interior Manuel Monsalve explained. “The risk situation in the country remains” in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía, and in certain localities of the central region of Maule, he said. A red alert was also decreed Sunday in communes of the southern regions of Los Ríos and Los Lagos due to the appearance of new fire outbreaks. He also pointed out that 26 of the 997 people injured were in serious condition.

“I came home from work and I was already without anything, without a house. I was left on the street, with my arms crossed, now with my son, and my wife, in a tent. I have no fodder for my animals,” a resident of the town of Purén, in the Araucanía region, told Televisión Nacional de Chile (TVN).

Meanwhile, President Gabriel Boric Font attended the wake of a firefighter in the town of Coronel. ”Chile is crying with you. I am here to tell you that you are not alone, that the family of Yesenia (Muñoz, the deceased firefighter) will not be alone,” he said.

According to Chile’s National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response (Senapred), the number of fires being fought went down from 87 to 51. “We are experiencing a small window of improving weather conditions during Sunday and Monday. That means that we are not with extremely high temperatures,” Monsalve said.

Undersecretary Monsalve also told reporters that 10 people have been arrested for their responsibility in starting some of the fires for which the red alert was still maintained. Of the total number of fires, 22 occurred Sunday for a total of 283 active fires, of which 151 were under control and 71 are being fought.

Given the magnitude of the fires in size and number, international help has been summoned. “We have just sent a plane to Chile with a contingent of the Military Emergency Unit to collaborate in extinguishing and controlling the fires that are raging in the country. All our support to the Chilean people,” tweeted Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez.

Chile’s Foreign Ministry also said assistance was being coordinated with Argentina, Brazil, Ecuador, the United States, and Mexico, while Boric’s administration has declared a constitutional state of catastrophe in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío and La Araucanía, to speed up additional resources while restricting free transit and involving military forces to contain the disaster.

In 2017, another chain of fires destroyed some 460,000 hectares, left 11 people dead, nearly 6,000 injured, and more than 1,500 homes burned.

Monsalve also warned that this week high temperatures will continue, as well as the risk of low humidity and strong gusts of wind, which will make it difficult to extinguish the flames. – MercoPress

World.title: Parts of Chile under red alert for major forest fires in central region
World.content:
The Government of Chile has declared a “red alert” in the central part of the country due to the heat wave stemming from 39 major forest fires as the wave keeps spreading throughout the country, most of them in Araucania (17) but also in Bío Bío (7), Ñuble (7), Maule (4), Los Lagos (3), and one in the Santiago Metropolitan Region.
