The difference may appear small, but it continues a long decline in births that is rapidly changing the age and size of Costa Rica’s population. In 2025, Costa Rica registered 48,414 births, the lowest number recorded during the past decade. That was 23,933 fewer births than in 2016, meaning it recorded roughly one-third fewer babies last year than it did nine years earlier.

Population projections had already suggested that Costa Rica would begin seeing its total population decline around 2044. The faster-than-expected drop in fertility means that point could arrive sooner. The change is not expected to produce a sudden drop in population. Instead, Costa Rica is gradually moving toward a society with fewer children and young adults and a larger share of older residents.

A fertility rate of about 2.1 children per woman is generally considered necessary for a population to replace itself over the long term without relying on immigration. Costa Rica is now far below that level. The reasons behind the decline are not tied to one single issue. Costa Ricans are waiting longer to have their first child, families are choosing to have fewer children, and a growing number of people are deciding not to become parents at all.

The cost of housing, childcare, employment, household finances and access to support networks can also influence decisions about whether or when to have children. Women are also increasingly delaying motherhood while studying, working and pursuing other personal goals.

Researchers say these are long-term social changes rather than a temporary decline that is likely to quickly reverse. The consequences will become increasingly noticeable in areas ranging from schools to the labor market. Fewer births eventually mean fewer children entering classrooms.

Some rural communities are already dealing with falling school enrollment, and the trend could eventually lead to more school consolidations or closures in areas where there are no longer enough students. Universities will eventually face smaller groups of potential students as well and the workforce will also change.

As today’s smaller generation of children reaches adulthood, fewer young people will enter the labor market to replace workers who retire. At the same time, Costa Rica will have a growing number of older residents requiring pensions, healthcare and other services. That combination could place additional pressure on the Costa Rican Social Security Fund and the country’s pension systems because a smaller working-age population will be helping support a larger retired population.

Costa Rica is already aging quickly as people age 65 and older are projected to make up about 12% of the population in 2026. That proportion is expected to continue rising over the coming decades, while the percentage of children and working-age residents gradually declines.

The demographic change could also affect housing since smaller families and more people living alone or as couples may need different types of homes than one dominated by larger families with several children. Businesses could face changes as well, particularly employers that depend on a steady supply of younger workers.

Immigration could eventually become increasingly important in maintaining Costa Rica’s workforce as the number of locally born workers declines. Population experts do not describe the falling birth rate as an immediate crisis, but rather as a major demographic change that Costa Rica will have to prepare for.

Costa Rica still has time to adjust, particularly by improving education, employment opportunities and productivity among the working-age population it already has. But the latest fertility numbers suggest that the transition is happening faster than expected. Costa Rica is not simply experiencing a year or two with fewer babies but is moving toward a future in which there will be fewer young people, more older adults and, eventually, fewer residents overall.

World.title: Jacó Beach Is Changing as New Residents and Major Brands Move In
World.content:
For decades, Jacó’s economy has revolved around the beach. Surfing, hotels, restaurants, nightlife and weekend visitors from San José helped turn the Central Pacific town into one of Costa Rica’s best-known tourist destinations. Tourism is still central to Jacó, but something else is happening. More people are living there year-round, residential construction is growing, and national chains are investing in businesses meant to serve customers every day rather than relying only on tourists during weekends and high season.

McDonald’s is preparing to open a restaurant along Avenida Amapola on Route 34 near the Costa Nera shopping center. The company has already held two job fairs in Jacó as it recruits workers for the new location. As of September 20, the restaurant had been announced but its opening date had not been made public.

Fresh Market has already opened at Plaza Comercial Costa Nera, marking part of the supermarket chain’s push beyond the Greater Metropolitan Area. The company’s own store directory now lists the Jacó location as operating seven days a week. KFC, meanwhile, is not new to Jacó, but the chain recently moved its existing restaurant to a larger location closer to the highway. KFC said the new restaurant involved an investment of about $500,000 and was designed to better serve residents, tourists and people traveling through the Central Pacific. The operation employs about 25 people.

Coffee and bakery chain Mocapan has also chosen Jacó for its first location outside the Greater Metropolitan Area (GMA). The company invested about $200,000 in its Costa Nera restaurant, creating 16 jobs. Little Caesars is another national chain already operating in the same commercial area.

Taken individually, a hamburger restaurant, supermarket or coffee shop does not change a town. Together, however, the investments point toward something larger: companies increasingly see Jacó as a place with enough permanent customers to support businesses throughout the year. Residential construction helps explain why.

Garabito, the area that includes Jacó, recorded 106,875 square meters, or about 1.15 million square feet, of new residential construction in 2024, according to Costa Rica’s National Institute of Statistics and Census (INEC). That was the second-highest total of any municipality in the country, behind only Santa Cruz in Guanacaste.

The population has also risen sharply. Garabito had 17,229 residents in the 2011 census. By the government’s 2022 population estimate, that number had climbed to 26,672, an increase of roughly 55% in just over a decade. Jacó’s location gives it an advantage that many other Costa Rican beach communities do not have.

It is close enough to San José and the Central Valley for residents to travel back and forth regularly, particularly people who work remotely or only need to be in the capital several days a week. It also offers supermarkets, banks, restaurants, medical services, schools and other basic services that are harder to find in some smaller beach communities.

That combination has helped create a different type of real estate market. Jacó still attracts foreign buyers, vacation-home owners and investors looking for short-term rental properties, but developers are increasingly building apartments and condominiums aimed at people who expect to spend much more of the year at the coast.

INEC’s construction figures provide some of the clearest evidence that the trend extends beyond tourism. While residential construction nationally declined in 2024, Garabito remained one of Costa Rica’s largest markets for new housing. The change does not mean Jacó is about to stop being a tourist town. Visitors remain essential to hotels, restaurants, tour operators, surf businesses and nightlife.

Instead, Jacó appears to be developing two economies at the same time: the traditional tourism economy and a growing residential economy built around people who actually live there. That shift creates opportunities, but it also places more pressure on infrastructure and public services.

Garabito ranked last among Costa Rica’s 82 municipalities in the 2025 National Competitiveness Index, with security identified as a major factor holding the area back. The same report warned nationally that weaknesses in security, infrastructure and workforce skills could limit economic growth.

Jacó will therefore have to keep pace with its own expansion as more residents mean greater demand for water, roads, health care, education, public transportation, policing and reliable internet, while rapid development brings the risk of congestion and poorly planned growth.

For now, however, the commercial signs are difficult to miss. McDonald’s is preparing to open. Fresh Market is operating and KFC has invested in a larger restaurant. Mocapan has chosen Jacó for its first move outside the Central Valley. Those companies are not abandoning tourists, but they are betting that Jacó now has enough people who stay after the weekend is over.

World.title: International News: California declares State of Emergency ahead of potential record-strength El Niño
World.content:
International News: California declares State of Emergency ahead of potential record-strength El Niño

By Zoila Palma: Today, California Governor Gavin Newsom declared a statewide state of emergency as officials prepare for a potentially historic El Niño weather event that could bring severe winter storms, flooding, landslides, and coastal erosion.

The governor’s office said state resources are being mobilized to strengthen preparedness and protect vulnerable communities ahead of the expected weather impacts.

Under the emergency proclamation, state agencies are directed to stage flood-fighting supplies, including sandbags and pumps, prepare critical infrastructure, and position equipment along roads at risk of flooding and snow-related disruptions.

The California National Guard may also support flood response, search-and-rescue, engineering, and logistics operations, while environmental agencies will work to accelerate preparations for landslides and debris flows.

California Office of Emergency Services Director Caroline Thomas Jacobs said officials are taking action before severe weather arrives, ensuring that communities and first responders have the personnel, equipment, and support needed to respond to changing conditions. Newsom said the emergency declaration is intended to provide communities with additional support and families with greater confidence that the state is prepared for severe weather.

El Niño is a climate pattern involving unusually warm ocean temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific, which can influence weather patterns across the United States and other regions.

World.title: International News: US, China discuss AI safety mechanism ahead of Trump-Xi Summit
World.content:
International News: US, China discuss AI safety mechanism ahead of Trump-Xi Summit

By Zoila Palma: The United States and China are exploring the creation of a notification mechanism to report artificial intelligence incidents that could affect national security, as officials from the two countries held economic and trade discussions ahead of a planned summit between Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Sunday that senior US and Chinese officials discussed the proposed AI notification system during what he described as “successful” talks with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng in New York.

The meeting comes as Trump and Xi prepare to meet in Washington later this week, BBC reports.

Bessent emphasized the importance of transparency between the world’s two leading AI powers, arguing that potential risks linked to artificial intelligence require greater communication across borders. His comments follow recent warnings from researchers about AI’s potential dangers and calls from prominent technology figures for more cautious development of the technology.

Beyond AI safety, the discussions also covered trade issues, including plans to operationalize a process known as the Board of Trade to identify potential tariff reductions on goods.

World.title: United States of America congratulates Belize on 45th anniversary of Independence
World.content:
United States of America congratulates Belize on 45th anniversary of Independence

By Zoila Palma: Today, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio congratulated Belize on the 45th anniversary of Independence.

“On behalf of the United States of America, I extend my warmest congratulations to the people of Belize as you mark the 45th anniversary of your nation’s independence.

The United States values the enduring friendship and close collaboration between our two countries, and we commend Prime Minister John Briceño’s dedication to strengthening regional security and promoting sustainable economic growth. We look forward to continuing our partnership with Belize in building a more secure and prosperous future for both our peoples,” Rubio said.

The USA and Belize established diplomatic relations in 1981 following Belize’s Independence.

Belize remains a committed partner on U.S. regional priorities, including security, prosperity and governance, democracy and human rights, migration management, and climate change.

World.title: International News: War, AI threats and Climate crisis to dominate UN General Assembly
World.content:
International News: War, AI threats and Climate crisis to dominate UN General Assembly

By Zoila Palma: World leaders are gathering at the United Nations this week as ongoing wars, artificial intelligence risks, climate change, and global economic pressures take center stage during the annual General Assembly meeting.

Conflicts in Gaza, Ukraine, Iran, Sudan, the Democratic Republic of Congo, and Myanmar are expected to feature prominently in discussions, with leaders facing questions about how international cooperation can help end violence and address humanitarian crises.

Climate-related disasters, rising living costs, disrupted shipping routes, and growing inequalities are also expected to shape the agenda, AP reports.

Meanwhile, concerns over the potential dangers of rapidly advancing artificial intelligence have added to discussions about global security and humanity’s future.

The future of the United Nations is also expected to come under scrutiny, including proposals to reform institutions such as the Security Council, where the United States, Russia, China, Britain, and France hold veto power.

The selection of a successor to Secretary-General António Guterres, whose second term ends on December 31, 2026, is another issue drawing attention. The 81st General Assembly’s official theme is “Restoring trust, managing transformation: A United Nations that delivers for all.”

Despite the divisions and challenges facing the international community, the United Nations remains a key platform for dialogue among its 193 member states.

The high-level debate, scheduled to begin on September 22, provides an opportunity for world leaders to discuss cooperation, peace, development, and collective responses to global crises.

World.title: PM Briceño: “Build a Belize where every generation has the opportunity to thrive”
World.content:
PM Briceño: “Build a Belize where every generation has the opportunity to thrive”

By Zoila Palma: Prime Minister John Briceño has called on Belizeans to reflect on the country’s progress and remain committed to building a brighter future as Belize celebrates its 45th Independence anniversary.

“As we celebrate 45 years of Independence, let us honour how far we have come, believe boldly in how far we can go, and continue building a Belize where every generation has the opportunity to thrive,” Briceño stated.

Happy Independence Day Belize!

World.title: Leader of Opposition: “We celebrate our shared heritage”
World.content:
Leader of Opposition: “We celebrate our shared heritage”

By Zoila Palma: Today, Leader of the Opposition Tracy Panton joined in extending Independence Day wishes to all Belizeans.

“Today, we celebrate our shared heritage, the remarkable journey that brought us here, and the limitless promise of tomorrow. United by our love for Belize, strengthened by our diversity, and inspired by a common purpose, let us stand together and build a brighter, more prosperous future for every Belizean.

With courage in our hearts, hope in our vision, and unity as our greatest strength, we can move Belize forward, from strength to strength,” Panton expressed.

Panton called for our “national pride to shine brighter than ever, may progress reach every community, and may the spirit of unity guide us toward a future filled with opportunity, peace, and promise.”

Long live BELIZE!

World.title: 62 year old retiree punched twice in the mouth at Orange Walk gas station
World.content:
62 year old retiree punched twice in the mouth at Orange Walk gas station

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police in Orange Walk are investigating a reported assault in which a 62 year old retiree was allegedly punched twice in the mouth at a gas station on Friday night.

According to police information, the incident happened at around 8:45 p.m. at the 24/7 Gas Station on Belize Corozal Road.

The complainant told police that a man known to him approached while he was standing near the store.

According to the report, the complainant attempted to offer the man marijuana, but the man allegedly became aggressive and said he did not want anything.

The complainant said he stepped back, but the man allegedly approached and punched him once in the mouth.

He said that after questioning why he had been hit, the man returned and allegedly punched him a second time in the mouth.

The complainant reportedly began bleeding from his mouth and later made a report to police officers who were in the area.

He was taken to the police station and issued a medico legal form.

A doctor later classified his injuries as wounding.

Police identified the person of interest as Roberto Antunez, 36, a labourer of Orange Walk Town.

Police say charges for wounding are pending.

World.title: Central American Integration System Sec-Gen congratulates Belize on 45th Anniversary of Independence
World.content:
Central American Integration System Sec-Gen congratulates Belize on 45th Anniversary of Independence

By Zoila Palma: Today, the Secretary General of the Central American Integration System (SICA) extended congratulations to Belize on its 45th anniversary of Independence.

“On September 21, 1981, the Belizean people celebrate their history, identity, and diversity.

As a member country of the Central American Integration System (SICA), we recognize its valuable contribution to building a more united, integrated, and supportive region,” SICA said.

World.title: A Cuban zoo, and its animals, in epic battle for survival
World.content:
Two Bengal tiger cubs (Panthera tigris) rest at the National Zoo of Havana in Havana on September 15, 2026. (Photo: AFP)

HAVANA, Cuba (AFP) — Every day, veterinarians and zookeepers make their way to Cuba’s National Zoo by whatever means they can, determined to not abandon the nearly 1,000 animals in their care and help save species at risk of extinction.

Their dedication and food donations are vital to keeping alive an array of rhinos, jaguars and tigers — including an extremely rare white tiger — in the midst of a severe crisis that has left many Cubans struggling to feed themselves.

Just getting to the reserve situated 20 kilometres (12 miles) from central Havana is a headache for staff, as public transportation has come to a near standstill nine months into a US fuel blockade.

“The workers come by bicycle, pedal scooter or electric motorbike to ensure the animals have food and water every day,” said Yoel Machado, the zoo’s animal welfare manager.

Their efforts are about more than keeping the animals fed.

The 345-hectare (850-acre) park serves as a genetic reserve of international conservation importance, housing breeding populations of vulnerable or endangered species, including black and white rhinos, hippos and jaguars.

Yet the same crisis that has left workers scrambling to source meat, medicine and water has forced the zoo to curb reproduction programs and increasingly rely on handouts to sustain its animals.

During a recent visit by AFP, two Bengal tiger cubs, one an extremely rare white specimen, frolicked in their enclosure beneath the watchful gaze of their mother, oblivious to the strenuous efforts made to keep them alive.

AFP did not see any animals that appeared malnourished or ill, but Angel Cordero, the veterinarian in charge of big cats, said the tiger cubs “could be in better shape.”

He revealed he needed to ration their food to prevent it from running out.

“It’s no use giving them plenty if it only lasts three days,” he said.

Big cats need about seven kilograms (15 pounds) of meat per day per adult, but such quantities are hard to come by.

Even when it is available, recurring blackouts of up to 30 hours at a stretch make it difficult to preserve.

With fuel extremely scarce, there’s also the issue of how to distribute food in a nature reserve the size of New York’s Central Park.

For now, private donors have come to the rescue for the zoo’s various needs.

Every Monday, Ana Fernandez, a Cuban-American woman born in Tennessee who has been living in Cuba for nine years, donates meat.

“The animals shouldn’t have to suffer,” the 50-year-old said, though she added that “some days it’s not enough for all of them.”

Recently, the reserve went 23 days without electricity, which meant it also lacked running water.

The staff “didn’t just sit around waiting for things to fall from the sky,” the zoo’s director Juan Carlos Corella said.

“We looked for solutions, water trucks were brought in, and we found food for the animals almost daily,” he said, while admitting that keeping the park open has become “very difficult.”

An exodus of vets has added to the zoo’s woes.

More than a third have left for better-paying jobs elsewhere, mostly in Cuba’s burgeoning private sector.

Some wait tables in cafes while others work for private veterinary clinics.

The zoo is home to the only breeding group of black rhinos outside of Africa, as well as a large population of white rhinos, the largest herd of Grant’s zebras in the Americas and hippos that regularly bear calves.

“Here we have a high genetic value, and one of immense international importance,” Machado, the animal welfare manager, explained.

However, the crisis has forced the park to slow down its breeding programs.

The reason is simple: each new offspring requires more food, medicine, and staff.

“We can’t keep increasing the number of animals,” Machado said, adding that he preferred to ensure the current population was “as well cared for as possible.”

And yet life keeps renewing itself, regardless.

In recent months, the zoo has welcomed baby tigers, hyenas, jackals, and a black dromedary named Esperanza (Spanish for “Hope”), the first of its kind born in Cuba in three decades.

World.title: Golding makes fresh bid to overhaul Crown lands law
World.content:
A screen grab of PNP President Mark Golding addressing the public session of the party's 88th Annual Conference on Sunday.

SAVANNA-LA-MAR, Westmoreland — Following two failed attempts to introduce a private member’s bill that would reduce the qualifying period for Jamaicans illegally occupying Crown lands from 60 to 25 years, People’s National Party (PNP) President Mark Golding announced that another attempt will be made to have the bill accepted by Parliament.

Golding stated this will take place as soon as Parliament returns from its summer break which is slated for Tuesday.

“And I will seek the support of both sides of the House of Representatives to pass it into law. We want justice when it comes to land in Jamaica,” stated Golding as he delivered the main addressing the PNP’s 88th Annual Conference at Independence Park in Savanna-la-Mar on Sunday.

​According to Golding, he took the bill to Parliament in July, where two attempts were made to have it tabled before the summer recess.

“I was blocked from doing so by the Speaker of the House.”

Currently, the qualifying period to acquire ownership of Government land through adverse possession — the legal principle allowing individuals to claim ownership of land through unauthorised, continuous, and open occupation for a specific period — is 60 years.

This contrasts with the 12 years it takes for persons occupying private property to be able to make a claim.

Golding pointed out that this duration was legislated in the 1830s around the time of emancipation, when life expectancy in Jamaica was less than 60 years.

“The formerly enslaved people of Jamaica were not given any land at emancipation, and that 60-year rule was plainly intended to ensure that the people did not acquire ownership of land by possession when they left those plantations,” argued Golding.

“That is why I have prepared the legislation entitled The Crown Lands Reform Act 2026, which seeks Parliament to reduce 60 years to 25 years, subject to a fair legal process.

Golding said the proposed bill would also enable an area impacted by a disaster such as Hurricane Melissa last October, to be declared a Disaster Adjudication Area so that legitimate claims for ownership by possession or otherwise can be settled quickly and titles issued to those who can establish their entitlement.

The Opposition Leader had first made the proposal for the change in the law while on the campaign trail in the lead up to the September 2025 General Election.

At that time Golding had told a party meeting in Spanish Town, St Catherine: “When I think of all the thousands of Jamaicans who live on land, and have occupied that land for years but don’t have security of tenure, and they can’t use their investment in the property to further themselves with education, or in business or to deal with any emergency, I say time come to reform that 1833 law that says you have to be on land of government for 60 years before you can become an owner.

“And we going to drop it substantially so that the people who have been there for at least 25 years will be entitled to their titles. It’s not one or two, but tens of thousands, possibly hundreds of thousands of Jamaicans who will benefit from becoming owners of the rock because of that one piece of emancipatory legislation that we will be bringing forward”.

World.title: Hague relief
World.content:
Minister without portfolio in the Ministry of Economic Growth and Infrastructure Development, with responsibility for land titling and settlements, Robert Montague (right) hugs a resident in Cooper’s Pen on Saturday.

COOPER’S PEN, Trelawny — With residents whose houses remain standing facing a November 30 deadline to vacate the privately owned Cooper’s Pen property, the Government has begun subdividing lands at nearby Hague to create lots for those who qualify for longer-term relocation.

Permanent secretary in the Ministry of Economic Growth and Infrastructure Development Arlene Williams, addressing residents in the community on Saturday, said work had started on the Hague property, and that Government was actively preparing the site for eligible Cooper’s Pen residents.

“We have identified lands very near to here in Hague that we are actively subdividing so that persons who are there longer term will get [their] title,” Williams said.

She stressed, however, that the Hague lots would not be given away.

“Nothing is coming free, as the prime minister would have said to you,” Williams emphasised to residents, explaining that those who are employed and able to do so would be expected to purchase their lots.

Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness had previously told Cooper’s Pen residents that Government assistance would help qualified residents transition to a properly planned settlement, but that they would ultimately have to pay for the land and associated services.

The Hague arrangement applies to residents whose homes have not been demolished but who occupy the privately owned property and will have to relocate.

Meanwhile, the families whose homes were demolished on August 11 by the private owners of the property, and who have since been living in tents on the property, are being dealt with separately. They had been given until September 19 to vacate the land.

Sunday, the Ministry of Economic Growth and Infrastructure Development announced that cheques had been delivered to these displaced residents as the ministry with responsibility for housing — following directives by Holness during his visit to Cooper’s Pen last month — was coordinating a whole-of-Government intervention to assist members of the community to relocate.

Minister with responsibility for land titling and settlements, Robert Montague, alongside Williams, issued 19 humanitarian grants, valued at $9.9 million, to assist vulnerable citizens who were displaced in the eviction exercise.

The grants, ranging from $200,000 to $800,000 per family, are being provided to some of the most vulnerable residents, many of whom have been living under tents provided by the Government as emergency shelter since August 12, 2026, the ministry said.

At the handover, officials outlined the Government’s position on the relocation exercise and reiterated the November 30, 2026 deadline for the full evacuation of the site. Montague emphasised that the emergency assistance is being funded by Jamaican taxpayers.

“The cheque is not a Government cheque. It is the taxpayers of Jamaica’s cheque,” he said. “You who pay your taxes, and taxpayers from all over the country, have provided this assistance.”

Williams also reiterated that the Government is not the owner of the property and was not responsible for the demolition or displacement of the occupants.

Under legitimate terms issued by the property owners, residents remaining on the site are required to leave by November 30, 2026, while those currently occupying tents were required to relocate immediately.

Extensive work was done in engaging the occupants, the ministry said. A multi-sector team comprising representatives from Jamaica Defence Force, Jamaica Constabulary Force, HEART/NSTA Trust, the Social Development Commission (SDC), and others, provided social support to the displaced occupants including formalisation of their tax registration and national identification documents. The ministry said many households and displaced occupants had no formal identification documents or bank accounts, therefore a three-day facility was arranged with a commercial bank to allow beneficiaries to cash their cheques.

The ministry and the SDC are scheduled to return next week to assess the remaining residents and support the finalisation of the resettlement process ahead of the November 30 deadline.

Meanwhile, some of the displaced families have also been offered the option of temporary accommodation at a site prepared at Salt Marsh for two weeks.

Williams said the immediate assistance was only part of a broader Government intervention, with several agencies working together to determine the appropriate support for affected households.

She said the Government is working with residents to facilitate an orderly transition while preparations continue at Hague, underscoring that the State does not own the Cooper’s Pen property and therefore cannot permit residents to remain there beyond the period agreed with the owners.

Montague said the circumstances of residents vary, and that Government therefore had to hear their individual concerns rather than assume that one solution would meet everyone’s needs.

World.title: ‘People first’ on the agenda at 88th PNP National Conference
World.content:
Comrades gather at the 88th PNP National Conference at Independence Park in Westmoreland Sunday. (Anthony Lewis)

PEOPLE’S National Party (PNP) leader Mark Golding pledged a message of ‘people first’ at the PNP’s 88th anniversary conference public session at Independence Park in Westmoreland, Sunday.

Telling officers of the party, members of Parliament and senators, regional chairs, mayors and councillors, delegates and hundreds of Comrades what his vision is for Jamaica, Golding also thanked people of Westmoreland and all of western Jamaica for welcoming the party and standing strong through one of the hardest periods the region has ever faced.

Golding said the party didn’t gather in the traditional way at the National Arena in Kingston but came to the west, “because this is where the pain has been greatest, where the recovery has been slowest, and where the need for determined leadership is most urgent” following Hurricane Melissa last October.

He said the decision to come to the west was also strengthened by the fact that the Government’s response to the Hurricane Melissa disaster has been an “abject failure of the people”.

“There has been no coherent recovery plan, and the people have largely been abandoned,” Golding said.

“The many thousands who lost their roofs and suffered other damage have faced delayed and inadequate assistance to repair their homes, and those whose houses and businesses were destroyed have been left to fend for themselves.”

He continued, highlighting that there has been no programme to cushion rising food prices for hurricane victims, and well into the new school year the vast majority of damaged schools remain unrepaired.

“There has been no programme to support small business operators and help them get back on their feet,” he lamented, adding, “We did not come here merely to describe your suffering. We came to say what must now be done.”

Citing the need for a recovery road map for western Jamaica, Golding said Jamaica needs a public reconstruction dashboard showing every damaged school, health facility, road and public building, the money allocated, the contractor responsible, and the deadline for completion.

“The people must be able to see where the money is going and whether the work is being done,” he said.

“Second, we need a properly funded recovery facility for farmers, fisherfolk and small businesses. Assistance must reach people quickly and on reasonable terms so they can replace equipment, restore production, rehire workers, and earn again.”

He said reconstruction must make the west stronger than it was before — more resilient roofs and public buildings, better drainage, stronger electricity and water systems, and construction standards fit for a country exposed to more powerful storms.

“What has happened in the west reflects a wider national problem. Too many Jamaicans are left to struggle alone against the raging tide of high prices, unreliable public services, insecure housing, inadequate health care, and an economy in which work does not deliver a better life for the people,” Golding said.

“Jamaica does not lack talent. We do not lack hard-working people. We do not lack ideas. What we lack is governance and policies that put the people first.”

Golding said his vision for Jamaica is anchored in the core principles of the PNP. “Our policies must always seek to benefit the majority of the people; that is what putting people first means. We pursue social justice because we know that the way things are is not how they are meant to be, and better must come because positive change is not beyond us.”

At the conference Golding listed party promises, including ownership for more Jamaicans, making the country not a Jamaica of “permanent tenants and insecure occupants” but one of owners. He also promised a better life for working people — making life easier for those who work for a living by, among other things, introducing a liveable wage that takes the working poor out of poverty and is adjusted annually for inflation.

A third promise of a strong economy that builds and grows wealth and reduces inequality, was followed by public services that works for ordinary people, an honest government, and equal justice under the law.

“Last year the people made the PNP a much stronger Opposition, but they did not yet give us the Government,” he told delegates. “We must reflect and learn from both parts of that verdict.”

He added: ”We must be humble and ask why some Jamaicans who wanted change were not yet ready to place the full responsibility of government in our hands. We have listened. We are learning. And we are changing.”

World.title: Johnson Smith leading Jamaica’s delegation to 81st session of United Nations General Assembly
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade Senator Kamina Johnson Smith, shakes hands with United Nations Secretary General António Guterres on the margins of the 78th Session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York in 2023.

MINISTER of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade Senator Kamina Johnson Smith is leading Jamaica’s delegation to the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA81) where Jamaica will join international partners in advancing cooperation on development financing, peace and security, climate resilience, and reform of the multilateral system while deepening partnerships that support national and regional goals.

“Jamaica remains firmly committed to principled and effective multilateralism, because the challenges before us are shared and so too must be the solutions. At UNGA81, we will work with partners across regions to advance cooperation on peace and security, financing for development, climate resilience, and reform of the international system. We will seek to strengthen partnerships that support our efforts at sustainable and inclusive development, including building resilience. Jamaica will bring its experiences and perspectives to the table, working in a spirit of mutual respect and shared responsibility to help shape outcomes that benefit our region and other developing countries,” Johnson Smith said.

The minister’s emphasis on effective multilateralism speaks directly to the theme the Assembly has set for the 81st session, ‘Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations That Delivers for All’. Jamaica is contributing directly to that effort through its co-chairmanship of the General Assembly’s Ad Hoc Working Group on Mandate Implementation Review, held jointly with Norway by Jamaica’s permanent representative to the United Nations (UN), Ambassador Brian Wallace, helping to reshape how UN decisions are designed, implemented, and assessed.

The ministry said matters relating to financing development will remain central to Jamaica’s advocacy. The country continues to press for international financial arrangements that better recognise the unique challenges facing countries like Jamaica and provide developing states with affordable resources to invest in resilience, infrastructure, and sustainable growth. Jamaica’s experience with increasingly severe climate shocks further underscores the case for adaptation and loss-and-damage financing accessible to vulnerable countries before development gains are reversed.

Jamaica will also continue building international cooperation against transnational organised crime, gangs, and illicit weapons flows, while maintaining its strong advocacy for sustained international support for peace, stability, and development in countries like Haiti.

Throughout the high-level week, scheduled for September 21 to 28, Johnson Smith will also hold bilateral talks with other foreign ministers and heads of international organisations to strengthen existing partnerships and pursue new opportunities in trade, investment, and for technical cooperation.

World.title: Suspense means business
World.content:
Suspense

Suspense is no longer waiting for the music industry to figure out what to do with her. Nine years after winning Magnum Kings and Queens of Dancehall, the entertainer is approaching her career with a different mindset — one built as much on strategy, branding, and business as it is on talent.

At the start of 2026 the Jamaica Observer named Suspense among its artistes to watch for the year. Months later she believes she has made good on some of that promise, but she is nowhere near ready to declare the mission accomplished.

“Since the beginning of the year I’ve been putting in the work — creating new music, developing my image, connecting with my audience, and making sure people understand who Suspense is as an artiste,” she said. “I’m proud of how far I’ve come so far this year, but I wouldn’t say I’m satisfied yet.”

That hunger is central to what Suspense previously described as her “rebirth” — a period that saw her reassessing not only her music, but the way she conducts her career.

“When I said this chapter was a rebirth I really meant that I was becoming a new version of myself — not just as an artiste, but as a woman,” she explained. “Over the past eight months, I’ve been learning to trust myself more, be more intentional about the moves I make, and understand the kind of artiste and brand I want Suspense to represent.”

That has meant refusing to be confined to one sound. Suspense has experimented with reggae, rap, and house music, while maintaining her dancehall foundation. She has also taken her act beyond Jamaica, completing three tours this year — two in Canada and one in England.

“I’m not trying to fit into a box or follow what everybody else is doing,” she said. “I’m learning what works for me and building from there.”

There have been signs that the approach is paying off.

Suspense points to Too Bad, her collaboration with Nhance, as one of the year’s major wins. According to the artiste, the track has surpassed five million views on YouTube and inspired more than 42,000 uses on TikTok. She’s now banking on her follow-up single to keep that momentum going.

The track, Female Boss, produced by Countree Hype, deliberately presents a different Suspense — less aggressive than the sound on which she initially built her name, but no less confident. She says the response so far is proving that exploring her versatility is invaluable.

“The response to Female Boss has shown me that my audience wants music that feels empowering, relatable, and authentic,” she said. “It’s different and it’s proving that switching things up has its rewards. Listeners are taking on well to my new calm sound.”

World.title: ‘I have to sue schools’
World.content:
A copy of an industrial techniques textbook that was published by Everett Fraser which is being reprographed by educators.

AN educational author said he is considering taking legal action against more than 80 schools over breaches of the Copyright Act by teachers and other school administrators.

The author, Everett Fraser, said he has spent more than a decade gathering material to produce text and workbooks for students, spending millions of dollars to publish his work. However, he said he is not seeing the rewards of his labour as many teachers at several institutions are photocopying, scanning, or taking pictures of the entirety of his publications to share with their students instead of purchasing the material or adding it to the book list.

An educator himself, Fraser said the revelation came through his own investigations at some institutions, and interactions with teachers who became hostile when confronted about their actions. He called a meeting with the Ministry of Education to discuss the matter, stressing the need for teachers to be sensitised.

According to the Copyright Act of Jamaica, making unauthorised photocopies of entire books or substantial parts of them is illegal. While Section 59 of the Act states that copies of passages from published literary, dramatic or musical works can be made by or on behalf of an educational establishment for educational purposes, the law states that no more than five per cent of the material may be copied.

However, Fraser said many educators are not aware of the law.

“What I realise is that teachers are not aware of the Copyright Act, and when I tell the schools, it is a challenge; they are usually hostile. According to the Copyright Act, there are rules that govern how schools can use the material, and often, teachers, once they have purchased a book, they feel like they are entitled to do whatever they want with it, which is not the case,” said the frustrated author.

Fraser said his published works cater to students at the early childhood level, with a focus on teaching them how to read. He added that he has also published textbooks and workbooks designed to prepare students for technical subjects, including industrial technology, at the Caribbean Secondary Education Certificate (CSEC) level.

“You find cases where they are ‘reprographing’ the entire book, or they might scan the book and share it with students. When this is done, it affects me tremendously. I’ve spent millions of dollars and years of research, travelling to different countries to get material. I’ve volunteered to work in particular fields, and I’ve gone into schools to volunteer to work to get the experience to write these books. I even pay for students to do CSEC just to get people to learn, and I’m not making anything. It’s a real struggle,” he told the Jamaica Observer.

“It is affecting me tremendously because what you find is that students do not buy books because they see that they can get the material for free, and those who buy the books, for example half of the class buys the books, you find that the teacher will take pictures or share it in their private

WhatsApp groups or on their various school platforms,” he said.

The author said he understands that books can be expensive and that not every parent can afford to purchase a textbook or workbook for their child. In response, he said he heavily discounted the materials and even provided more than $80,000 worth of free copies to less fortunate students. However, those efforts have done little to address the problem.

“I remember I went to this school to introduce a book to the students, and when I stepped into the class I realised that they were doing

AutoCAD. I used a book I wrote to demonstrate some techniques, and I realised that the students knew every little. This book was being sold for $650; it was a massive reduction because the books were sitting there not selling, so I said, ‘Let me just sell them out cheap since they are not going,’ ” he recalled.

“…After showing the students the books they said they wanted some to buy. I went outside to get some more books, and by the time I stepped back into the classroom the teacher allowed the students to have their phones out, taking pictures of my book,” he told the Observer.

Fraser said at that same institution he had previously sent some books over to be sold that never were. He said further checks with a teacher at the institution revealed that the teacher had photocopied the entire book and was sharing it with students.

“I really have to act. I have a list of about 80 schools that are reprographing my work. Some schools, I try to go in and talk to them and try to at least get some change but they are not listening,” he shared.

“I love teaching, and I have a lot of knowledge. I want to give back what I have to education — and I think the way to give back to education is to share my knowledge with others by writing books — but it has reached a point now where I have decided that I’m going to have to sue schools. If I can’t make money from my work I have to sue schools and the ministry, because the ministry has failed its statutory duty to protect our intellectual property,” he reasoned.

Fraser said the problem became so bad that he pulled his books from book stores. He said he also has more than 10 books he recently completed that he refuses to publish out of fear they will also be photocopied and shared illegally.

“I think if authors were taking action we would see changes. I think we all have just accepted it, but I have decided that I am going to take action. If it means that I am only going to sell the books to 10 schools or parents, I am going to take action because this is damaging education,” he said.

World.title: TOP-SIX PUSH
World.content:
Jamaica’s Reggae Boyz footballers train at Sabina Park in Kingston in September 2025. (Photo: JFF)

INTERIM head coach Rudolph Speid says Jamaica’s Reggae Boyz cannot afford any slip-ups in the upcoming Concacaf Nations League games as they look to put themselves in a strong position for the start of the 2030 Concacaf World Cup Qualifiers.

Jamaica begin their 2026/2027 Nations League A group stage campaign this week at the National Stadium, starting with Guatemala on Friday and Honduras next Monday. They will then travel to El Salvador next Friday before ending action on October 5 away to Honduras.

It will be the national men’s first competitive fixture since the Inter-Confederation Playoffs in March which saw them miss out on this summer’s FIFA World Cup in the United States, Mexico and Canada.

The Reggae Boyz will need to finish top two in their group to advance to the quarter-finals where they will play one of Concacaf’s top four nations, Mexico, USA, Canada or Panama, which were pre-seeded.

Speid says the team is taking the Nations League seriously, knowing the results could have major implications for their route to the 2030 FIFA World Cup. Unlike this year when they earned automatic qualification as co-hosts, Mexico, USA and Canada will have to go through the qualifying process this time around.

“At this particular time, if you look on all the teams, we are currently seventh in Concacaf, but we need to be in the top six by the end of the year to prepare for the seedings for the World Cup qualifiers in 2030,” he said.

“So it is important that we do well in this competition because it actually decides if we get a seeded spot in the World Cup Qualifiers for 2030. If we’re not seeded, then we could go against some difficult teams.”

Speid named his 24-man squad last Friday, with the majority set to report to camp today and the others arriving by Tuesday.

A total of 14 players from Jamaica’s World Cup play-off squad in March have been retained, with the remainder made up of under-23 players, debutant centre back Miguel Freckleton and players earning recalls, including striker Javon East and full back Tayvon Gray.

Speid believes the team is strong enough to make a deep run in the competition.

“If you look at the squad, it still boasts a lot of players from March but clearly, at some point, we had to retool, so it’s a balancing act,” he said.

“But we still expect to do well because we know what we have to achieve by the end of the year. It’s a balancing act but a lot of these players are on form, doing extremely well at their club, and we think they can get us over the line.”

Questions have been raised about the absence of several players, including winger Kaheem Parris, who recently made his UEFA Champions League debut for Azerbaijan’s Sabah FK against Manchester United; and Coventry City duo Ethan Pinnock and Ephron Mason-Clarke.

There have also been questions about the number of locally based players in the squad, with only Mount Pleasant FA goalkeeper Shaquan Davis and Cavalier FC defender Christopher Ainsworth selected.

However, Speid says the door remains open to players from across the country and overseas, after scouting more than 70 players ahead of the upcoming four games.

“We’re still on the lookout for talented players, [and] I hope some come to fruition. What is most important for us is for Jamaica to really field a competitive team all the time and give players who deserve it opportunities.”

SQUAD

Goalkeepers — Andre Blake, Amal Knight, Shaquan Davis

Defenders — Damion Lowe, Richard King, Ronaldo Webster, Joel Latibeaudiere, Christopher Ainsworth, Tayvon Gray, Miguel Freckleton

Midfielders — Isaac Hayden, Kasey Palmer, Dwayne Atkinson, Karoy Anderson, Brandon Cover, Courtney Clarke

Forwards — Leon Bailey, Renaldo Cephas, Kaheim Dixon, Bailey Cadamarteri, Rumarn Burrell, Tyreece Campbell, Andre Brooks, Javon East

World.title: Britain-focused Andy Burnham starts racking up the air miles
World.content:
No. 10 said ahead of the visit that Burnham is “determined that the U.K. will play a leading role” in tackling issues confronting the world. He has already taken a more muscular approach than Starmer to Israeli settlements on the West Bank, announcing sanctions alongside France, Canada and other countries earlier this month. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said at the time that “settler terrorists” were perpetrating “ethnic cleansing.”

Burnham will also spend Tuesday pushing for closer international co-operation on AI development to manage the technology’s risks. No. 10 said AI would form a “major part” of his visit and speech to UNGA and he would “raise it across the board” in meetings in New York. It was an unexpected pivot from a leader who has devoted little time to talking about the technology.

This will be a particular challenge when meeting Trump, who has described fears about AI’s safety as a “hoax” and said the only “guardrails” needed for AI would be a “strong and smart” president.

Burnham’s spokesperson said ahead of the visit: “The prime minister is determined that the U.K. will play a leadership role in a number of different areas. The U.K. is of course a G7 nation, and you would expect us to play a leadership role across a number of different challenges facing the world at the moment.”

Others around the ruling Labour Party still aren’t sure what that will look like.

Downing Street was straining ahead of the visit to avoid portraying Britain as a “middle power” standing up to the U.S., as Carney has encouraged fellow nations to do. The U.K. has too deep-rooted a security relationship with the U.S. to turn away from it in a meaningful way.

World.title: Merkel sidesteps German conservatives’ election losses as pressure mounts on Merz
World.content:
Merkel spoke at the opening of a Bundestag exhibition on former Chancellors Konrad Adenauer and Willy Brandt, before joining Bundestag President Julia Klöckner for a discussion on Adenauer, democracy and politics. Adenauer, West Germany’s first postwar chancellor and the CDU’s first leader, helped shape the party as a broad-based Christian movement.

Most of the on-stage conversation focused on art, with the lack of more in-depth political discussion notable given the scale of the CDU’s recent losses.

On Sept. 6, the far-right AfD won 43.8 percent in Saxony-Anhalt, more than doubling its 2021 result, while Merz’s CDU fell to 17.2 percent — its worst-ever showing in the eastern state.

On Sunday, the far-right AfD won around 38 percent of the vote in northeastern Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, beating Merz’s CDU by a hefty margin, which suffered its worst-ever result in postwar Germany and crashed out of the state parliament. In Berlin, the CDU finished behind The Left.

Merz called the latest defeats a “disaster” and pledged to overhaul the CDU’s platform, structure and public image. An ARD-DeutschlandTrend poll earlier this month found just 13 percent of voters satisfied with Merz’s work — a historically low rating.

Merkel then turned to the question of how politicians can reconnect with voters.

“We have to acknowledge that the question of how to maintain a connection with citizens and potential voters has changed dramatically,” she said. If politicians want to spread positive messages, she added, they must show the public “what guides my thinking, where I have doubts and what I have considered.”

World.title: Finland’s Stubb warns Europe not to ‘overreact’ to Russian threats and sabotage
World.content:
“We have to be very careful and understand that Russia is trying to destabilize and scare Europe. And any time we overreact to a hybrid attack, they have actually won the battle in that particular way,” Stubb told POLITICO during an interview on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York.

“We also have to understand that it is not in the interest of Russia nor in the capacity of Russia to go full-scale” with military escalation, Stubb added. “So they will continue to intimidate and we just have to be, as I say, cool, calm and collected in this situation.”

Stubb lauded Germany’s recent decision to attribute responsibility to Russia for the attempted Leipzig drone attack: “That is exactly what you need to do. You need to point the finger and say, we know what you’re doing and these are the consequences.”

In contrast, however, Stubb pointed to the “overreaction” from some intelligence services which “basically say that, well, you’re next” for a Russian invasion.

“We don’t see the evidence of that,” he said, adding: “We think we have to be vigilant and awake. But, you know, we have the longest border in NATO with Russia, it’s half the border. In our intelligence we see that there is activity but no imminent military threat right now.”

Stubb also expressed tentative hopefulness concerning a meeting between U.S. President Donald Trump and his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelenskyy in New York on Tuesday.

Ce samedi, le Rassemblement national a publié un long communiqué pour dénoncer les tentatives d’ingérence et de guerre hybride de Moscou. Une déclaration qui contraste avec la réaction de Jordan Bardella à la sortie de l’Elysée, où Emmanuel Macron avait convié, la veille, les chefs de parti pour évoquer les tensions internationales. Le patron du RN avait alors dénoncé l’absence de propositions sur le carburant, sans s’étendre sur la guerre en Ukraine. Pourquoi une telle correction de tir ? Le lien à la Russie reste-t-il le talon d’Achille d’une formation qui peine à définir une ligne claire, au risque d’alimenter le procès en poutinophilie ?

Marcelo Wesfreid en discute avec Laura Kayali, spécialiste des questions de défense et de géopolitique à POLITICO. N’hésitez pas à vous abonner et à laisser vos commentaires !

World.title: Russia has ‘lost control’ of its oil industry due to Ukraine war, says Trump
World.content:
Trump ended his post with a demand to end the conflict in Ukraine. "This ridiculous and never-ending war with Ukraine must be ended," he said. "The whole World suffers as 25,000 people, mostly soldiers, are being killed each month. What a shame!"

Responding to Trump's message, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on X that his country was ready to stop its attacks on Russia if the Kremlin did the same for Ukraine.

"Ukraine’s energy sector, critical infrastructure, and our food exports must stop being targets for Russia, and this will lead to matching de-escalation steps on our part," he wrote, adding, "the nature of war is now such that the aggressor will suffer as well."

Earlier this month, Trump called on Ukraine to stop targeting Russia's energy infrastructure, saying attacks on the diesel industry were "hurting the world" by causing fuel shortages.

The two men are set to meet in New York Tuesday — a meeting Zelenskyy said "could change a lot," noting that there was "diplomatic momentum" in current talks.

"There are ideas for de-escalation steps and for addressing fundamental security issues – energy security, food security, and the protection of human life," said the Ukrainian president. "We are working together with the American team and are ready to take really serious steps."

World.title: 22 countries back call to keep AI ‘under human control’
World.content:
Neither the U.S. nor China are part of the new declaration. But Finnish President Alexander Stubb, one of the main organizers of the document, told POLITICO that he hopes to create “momentum” and get more actors on board: “I think it will be in the interest of both China and the United States to have some kind of guardrails. And our message here is that we need human intervention, so humans need to be in charge,” he said in an interview.

Referring to the recent cyberattack by rogue AI agents on the Hugging Face platform, the declaration urges to “address these risks” by obliging AI companies “to develop transparent safety protocols, including mandatory pre-deployment testing and independent evaluation, with qualified evaluators granted sufficient access to assess risks.”

Yet the document falls short of calling for slowing down or pausing AI development, with organizers saying they want to focus on managing risks instead.

Alexander Stubb, one of the main organizers of the document, told POLITICO that he hopes to create “momentum” and get more actors on board: “I think it will be in the interest of both China and the United States to have some kind of guardrails. | Alessandro Rampazzo/ AFP via Getty Images

To do that, countries should “further develop and coordinate common standards” and strengthen transparency, “including shared reporting of serious safety incidents.” Moreover, UN member countries should “build on existing international mechanisms and explore creating an international institution” to oversee AI.

Stubb, who spoke to POLITICO at Finland’s consular office in New York, said that “our preference personally” would be to create a new institution similar to the International Atomic Energy Agency “within the U.N. framework.” Yet he added, with a nod to Trump’s skepticism of the United Nations, “we have to leave it open-ended so that people don’t reject it just because it would be within the U.N. framework.”

Norway’s Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, who initiated the declaration together with Stubb and who joined the interview via video, said that, “we would be very encouraged to see both G7 and the upcoming G20 presidency of the United Kingdom take on this ... The U.N. is big, but the G7, G20 is a bit more focused.”

World.title: EU countries fail to reach Russia sanctions list deal, will keep talking
World.content:
Uzbek-born Russian businessman Alisher Usmanov attends the Congress of the Russian Union of Industrialists and Entrepreneurs in Moscow on March 26, 2026. | Pool photo by Maxim Shemetov via AFP/Getty Images

The deal will likely only go ahead if entrepreneurs Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman are removed from the sanctions list.

BRUSSELS — EU countries will meet again Tuesday morning to try to reach a deal that could see two prominent Russian billionaires removed from the bloc’s sanctions list, in exchange for prolonging restrictions on hundreds of others.

Ambassadors from across Europe met in Brussels on Monday to negotiate the renewal of the sanctions framework, but failed to agree despite working late into the evening. France has refused to allow the sanctions framework to proceed unless tycoon Alisher Usmanov is removed. Mikhail Fridman, one of Russia’s wealthiest people, is also slated for removal.

According to three diplomats with knowledge of the talks, who were granted anonymity to speak freely, the deal would see sanctions against more than 3,000 people renewed for the next 36 months — in exchange for the removal of Usmanov and Fridman. Ambassadors are consulting with capitals, but the arrangement is expected to go ahead, the three diplomats said.

World.title: Spanish PM’s wife to face trial over influence peddling, embezzlement allegations
World.content:
The proceedings are the latest in a scandal-riddled year for Socialist leader Sánchez. Former Prime Minister José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero recently faced questions over a €53-million pandemic bailout, while Socialist heavyweight Santos Cerdán was investigated in a public-contract kickback probe involving former minister José Luis Ábalos. Both men deny wrongdoing.

Gómez’s case will now go to a higher court, which must set a hearing date. Spain’s public prosecutor, which says the evidence does not establish a criminal offense, and the defense teams are seeking acquittals. Hazte Oír, an ultra-Catholic group acting as a private prosecutor, is seeking 13 years in prison for Gómez.

Her lawyer, Jaime Campaner, has argued that Hazte Oír’s indictment contains “serious technical defects” that are incompatible with the law and “irremediable” at this stage. He has called for the case to be closed.

World.title: Pope Leo XIV set for first official visit to France, with huge crowds expected in Paris
World.content:
Pope Leo XIV is making his first official visit to France from 25 to 28 September.

 

In the French capital, excitement is building.

According to the police prefecture, up to 250,000 people are expected to line the streets along the route of Leo XIV's procession through the streets of Paris. Around 80,000 people have also bought tickets to attend the youth mass that is set to be held at the Stade de France in Saint-Denis, in the north of the city.

Paris has not welcomed a pope since 2008, when Benedict XVI visited.

“Pope Francis visited Strasbourg, Marseille, and Corsica, which are on the outskirts of France,” said Charles Mercier, director of studies in the history and sociology of Catholicism at the École pratique des hautes études (EPHE) in Paris.

"But coming to the capital is a big event because it hasn’t happened in a long time. It fuels people’s enthusiasm, and I think that’s one of the reasons for the success of this visit.”

Another reason for the enthusiasm is the pontiff’s popularity, which extends far beyond French Catholics. Elected in May 2025, Leo XIV has presented himself as a pope who is connected and attentive to everyone.

Leo XIV will be in Paris and the wider Île-de-France region for two days.

He is due to meet with French President Emmanuel Macron at the Élysée palace on Friday. He is also set to meet with "the authorities, civil society and the diplomatic corps" before heading to UNESCO.

On Sunday, he is expected in Lourdes, where he is due to speak with seven victims of sexual abuse within the Church.

Among them is a former pupil at the nearby school of Notre Dame de Bétharram. In 2024, more than 230 victims filed complaints over corporal punishment and sexual abuse at the Catholic institution in southwestern France.

World.title: Spain seizes two tonnes of cocaine from yacht linked to Balkans drug network
World.content:
The interception of a sailing boat carrying more than two tonnes of cocaine in the Atlantic has led to the dismantling of a logistics network for drug trafficking. The joint military and customs operation off the Galician coast ended with the arrest of the crew on the high seas and of the network's leader in Girona, marking one of the biggest seizures from the drug cartels' maritime routes.

 

Operation Doncella, conducted by Spain's Customs Surveillance Service together with the French customs authorities, resulted in five arrests and the seizure of more than 2,000 kilos of cocaine some 400 miles off Galicia.

The investigation was launched in February in Girona to look into a suspicious yacht.

Boats for Eastern European and Balkan mafias

It focused on a 14-metre yacht flying the Polish flag but some of the paperwork raised questions and it emerged that its owner had been convicted of theft.

The evidence confirmed that the network was supplying foreign-flagged leisure boats to organised crime groups from Eastern Europe and the Balkans. A

fter gathering information in Poland via the Intelligence Centre for Counter-Terrorism and Organised Crime, officers located the yacht in Roses, Girona and kept it under surveillance until 11 July, when it put to sea with its tracking system switched off in order to avoid being monitored.

Five suspects arrested

With help from the US Drug Enforcement Administration, the UK's National Crime Agency and Portugal's Maritime Analysis and Operations Centre for Narcotics, a Spanish patrol vessel tracked and located the smugglers 400 miles off Galicia.

After the boarding operation in the early hours of 14 September, officers found 70 bales containing 2,100 kilos of cocaine stowed across the deck. The operation led to the arrest of four crew members — of Argentinian, Uruguayan, Colombian and Albanian nationality — with the Albanian suspect allegedly responsible for overseeing delivery to buyers in the Balkans.

While the Petrel I was towing the yacht to Vigo, police in Girona arrested the ringleader of the network, a Chilean national in charge of sourcing the vessels. The investigation remains open as officers seek to arrest a man in Barcelona believed to be responsible for the group's surveillance and logistics.

Those charged will appear before the National Court on counts of belonging to an organised criminal group, smuggling and drug trafficking as authorities look to crack dwon on the Atlantic cocaine route.

World.title: Trial of six French Islamic State suspects opens in Baghdad
World.content:
The trial of six French nationals suspected of belonging to the "Islamic State" (IS) group opened in Baghdad on Sunday morning, with the next hearing scheduled for 5 October.

 

They face the death penalty if they are found guilty of crimes "against Iraq and the Iraqi people."

Their lawyers are calling for them to be repatriated to France, arguing that the proceedings are being conducted too quickly and do not give their clients a proper opportunity to mount an adequate defence.

The suspects were part of a group of 47 French nationals transferred last year from Syria to Iraq, where numerous suspected IS members were already being held.

This group included, among others, the man who claimed responsibility for the Nice attack in 2016.

According to investigators, the six men joined IS after travelling via Turkey and then crossing into Syria. They were arrested by Syrian Kurdish forces between 2018 and 2019 during the collapse of the self-proclaimed "caliphate" of Daesh.

After they were transferred to Iraq last year, Iraqi authorities brought charges against them for membership of a terrorist organisation.

Fighters from the jihadist group carried out massacres in Syria and Iraq in 2014, reducing many women and girls to sexual slavery.

Iraq, backed by US-led forces, declared victory over IS in 2017. Two years later, the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces said they had also defeated the group in Syria.

Iraqi courts have handed down hundreds of death sentences and life terms to people convicted of terrorist offences, including foreign fighters.

In 2019, 11 French nationals were sentenced to death before their sentences were commuted to life imprisonment.

Last February, more than 5,700 suspected IS members from over 60 countries were transferred to Iraq by the United States after spending several years in detention in Syria.

Iraq also returned two detained foreign nationals in April to their respective countries, one from Finland and the other from the US, after they were acquitted.

Iraqi PM visits France

The opening of the new trial comes a week after an official visit to France by Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaïdi.

Al-Zaïdi travelled to Paris on 13 and 14 September to "consolidate the strategic partnership and the ties of friendship between France and Iraq," according to the Élysée.

At the end of the visit, the two nations affirmed "their shared vision for strengthening security and stability in the Middle East, based on respect for national sovereignty, non-interference, good neighbourly relations and territorial integrity."

Emmanuel Macron greets the Iraqi Prime Minister, Ali Al-Zaïdi, before a signing ceremony at the Élysée in Paris on Monday 14 September 2026 Photo AP/Thibault Camus

Paris and Baghdad also called for "respect for international law and the use of diplomatic solutions to address the crises and shared threats facing the region."

The Iraqi PM expressed his thanks to France, conveying "his appreciation" for Paris' continued support to Iraq, particularly in the fight "against Daesh terrorism."

France and Iraq also pledged to step up "their cooperation on security and defence" and their shared commitment to "relentlessly combat terrorism and prevent any resurgence of Daesh, with full respect for each other's sovereignty."

World.title: Room rentals rise in Spain driven by soaring flat rents
World.content:
3.2% of Spaniards have rented or looked to rent a room in a shared flat, up from 2.8% a year ago. This is the key finding from the report Profile of people who share housing, produced by Fotocasa Research using data from the first half of 2026, which shows this option is becoming an increasingly common alternative in the rental market.

 

Fotocasa puts this down to a lack of financial leeway rather than to personal preference. "Tenants are not looking to share a flat because it is their first choice, but because the market forces them to adjust their expectations to what they can afford", explains María Matos, head of Research and spokesperson for the platform. "Renting a room has become the plan B for those who cannot secure a conventional tenancy".

Two searches that overlap

The study identifies an overlap between the two markets, but only in one direction. Among those who have rented or looked for a room, 34% have also searched for or rented a whole property in the past 12 months: one in three is aiming for something bigger. In the opposite direction, just 11% of people who have searched for or rented an entire flat have also considered a room.

Demand for rooms and entire homes Fotocasa

Renting entire homes has remained practically stable, with around 10% of the active population in this segment. Taking both markets together, demand for rental housing now reaches 12% of the population, almost half a percentage point more than in 2025, a rise that Fotocasa describes as moderate.

Matos sees those numbers as part of a wider trend: the pressure on renting, she says, "is spreading across the entire market". More and more people need to rent and, "given the lack of supply and prices that are still very high", they are abandoning what they were originally hoping to find.

World.title: Putin's party wins record Duma majority in Kremlin-controlled elections as EU vows sanctions
World.content:
Vladimir Putin's United Russia party has won a record supermajority in parliament, preliminary results showed Monday. The tightly controlled three-day vote excluded every party critical of the Kremlin or the war in Ukraine.

 

Central Election Commission chief Ella Pamfilova said United Russia had secured 355 of the State Duma's 450 seats. That beats its previous record of 343, set in 2016, and is well above the 301 needed to change the constitution. Final results are due later this week.

The Communist Party came second with 40 seats, followed by the nationalist LDPR on 25, New People on 20 and A Just Russia on four. Pamfilova put turnout at more than 59 percent.

It was Russia's first parliamentary election since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Criticism of the war is banned, and Yabloko, the only party calling for an end to the fighting, was barred from running for the national parliament, though it was allowed to stand in some regional votes.

"These indicators, of course, point to the highest level of consolidation within Russian society around the head of state," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said.

United Russia told state media that 49 veterans who fought in Ukraine are expected to enter the Duma for the party.

Voting also took place in occupied parts of Ukraine, including Crimea and the Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson and Zaporizhzhia regions.

On Sunday, the final day of voting, Kyiv hit Moscow with its biggest drone attack of the war, killing two people and setting an oil refinery ablaze. Russia's defence ministry accused Ukraine of trying to disrupt the vote and vowed to intensify strikes on Kyiv.

Russia's 'veneer of democracy'

The EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said the Kremlin had "silenced dissent" and shut out international election monitors.

"The veneer of democracy is all that remains in Russia," she said. "The State Duma elections held by Russia on 18–20 September underscored the continued and deepening erosion of democracy in Russia, taking place in an increasingly authoritarian political environment."

In a statement on behalf of the bloc, Kallas said the EU would impose sanctions on those who organised the vote or stood as candidates in occupied Ukrainian territory.

"The European Union reiterates that it does not and will never recognise either the holding of these so-called “elections” in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine or their results." the statement said.

Britain, Australia, Canada, New Zealand and Norway said in a joint statement that holding the election in occupied areas was a "gross violation" of Ukraine's sovereignty and the UN Charter. They said the vote could not change the status of those territories under international law.

"These sham elections are part of a wider system of occupation: the imposition of Russian administration, law, media, education, language and citizenship, backed by coercion and repression," the statement said.

Ukraine's foreign ministry had earlier called the voting in occupied regions a "farce" and said it would not recognise the results.

The election brought one surprise. In the Novgorod region, where it was allowed on the ballot for regional elections held at the same time, Yabloko won just over six percent of the vote, enough to enter the regional parliament.

Putin's political opponents are in exile, in prison or dead. His main rival, Alexei Navalny, died in an Arctic prison in 2024.
