If an employer does not increase the gross salary and other deductions remain unchanged, the higher tax will reduce the worker’s take-home pay. To keep take-home pay at the same level, an employer may need to increase its labour costs.

Will higher social payments offset the higher tax burden?

Vugar Bayramov, a member of the Milli Majlis Economic Policy Committee, views the expected increase in the share of non-oil revenues to more than 60% positively. He considers this important for budget sustainability. According to him, structural reforms and greater transparency in public procurement could allow the government to allocate additional funds to social needs.

Economist Natig Jafarli said on 8 September, before the publication of the preliminary budget figures, that he expected pensions and salaries for public-sector employees to rise by 8–10%. He stressed that higher social payments sometimes only offset rising prices. This is the economist’s expectation.

Even if such increases take place, it cannot be said that they will offset the additional tax burden on private-sector employees. Higher salaries, pensions and benefits affect different groups of the population.

The preliminary figures point to the following trend: as transfers from the State Oil Fund decline, the government plans to increase tax revenues. What this will mean for citizens will depend on which services receive the additional funding, as well as on how their incomes and everyday expenses change.

Azerbaijan’s 2027 budget

World.title: Azerbaijan security service terrorism case spans five countries – what  is known so far?
World.content:
Azerbaijan security service operation in five countries

Azerbaijan says money collected for religious ceremonies was transferred to terrorist organisations using cryptocurrency. In a statement issued on 18 September, the State Security Service (SSS) said the alleged financing scheme and preparations to assassinate public and religious figures were being investigated as part of the same criminal case.

However, the statement published by the media does not specify the amount of money involved, the organisations alleged to have received it, or the five countries where the operations were carried out.

Information available from open sources does not allow the scale of the case to be independently verified. Available reports largely repeat the account provided by the agency conducting the investigation.

Charges brought

The SSS named the defendants as Vugar Abdullayev, Jalal Hajiyev, Javid Aliyev, Nijat Ahmadov, Nazim Aliyev, Ilkin Hasanzade, Aykhan Huseynov, Elshan Asgarov, Fakhraddin Imanov, Nail Rasulov and Elgun Ismayilov. Although the statement says 10 people were detained, it lists 11 defendants. The reason for the discrepancy is not explained.

They have been charged under Criminal Code articles relating to financing terrorism, forming a criminal organisation, preparing an assassination attempt against a state or public figure, and other offences. According to the SSS, a court ordered the defendants to be remanded in custody.

Link between two strands of case

In the SSS account, Jalal Hajiyev’s name appears both in connection with the alleged assassination plot and the financing scheme. The agency says Vugar Abdullayev and other defendants gathered information about the movements and security arrangements of the alleged targets. Hajiyev, meanwhile, is alleged to have used his contacts abroad to arrange money transfers to people involved in armed conflicts, as well as to terrorist organisations.

Although the two strands are being investigated as part of the same case, the SSS does not specify how they are linked financially. Were the funds allegedly transferred abroad used to finance preparations for the assassination attempts in Azerbaijan? Although some of the same individuals feature in both strands of the case, no evidence has been presented to establish a link between the movement of funds and the planning of the alleged attacks.

How was money traced?

According to the SSS, the funds were collected through fake s posted on social media, purportedly seeking donations for religious ceremonies. The agency says investigators obtained evidence showing where the money came from and how it was transferred.

To independently assess these claims, key evidence would include an archive of the s, payment details, transaction dates and information about the recipients. It is also unclear whether those who transferred the money knew its alleged true purpose or were themselves deceived – a distinction that could imply different degrees of responsibility.

The reference to cryptocurrency alone does not explain how the alleged financing scheme worked. The SSS does not say which digital assets were used, who controlled the addresses involved in the transactions, or how investigators established links between the recipients and terrorist organisations.

A 2023 report by the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) describes the risks of social media fundraising and the use of virtual assets for terrorist financing. It also highlights the difficulty of proving that funds were intended for terrorist purposes and stresses the importance of protecting legitimate charitable activity.

International experience suggests that the mechanism described by the SSS is possible in principle. However, the allegations against specific individuals would need to be supported by evidence in the criminal case. So far, that evidence has not been made public.

World.title: Abkhaz punk rock: TOM SQUARE leader Salima Sagaria tells her story – VIDEO
World.content:
Punk rock in Abkhazia

This story is about a rare phenomenon: Abkhaz punk. Salima Sagaria and her band TOM SQUARE could be described as unique.

Salima began her career in pop music and turned to punk several years ago.

“People say different things to me. Many are supportive and say they are glad that this kind of music has finally appeared in Abkhazia. But there is also a lot of hate. At the beginning of the year, I posted a clip from my new song online. I wasn’t wearing any make-up, I was in ordinary clothes at home, just sitting there and shaking my hair around. For some reason, that really shocked a lot of people. I received threats and was even cursed.

“Our latest track is about exactly that: why so many people are afraid of change, and why our society does not want to move forward and change. This attachment to tradition also manifests itself in preventing creative people from expressing themselves,” Salima says.

“But I’m going to keep going, releasing new tracks and mixing different styles. I want to bring traditional instruments and choir into punk rock. I like introducing something new.”

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: How Nick Daicos won the Brownlow Medal
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Coming into the night, the 2026 Brownlow Medal count held little intrigue about who the winner would be.

Few — if any — in the footballing world thought there was anyone who could seriously challenge Nick Daicos for the award.

But there was still one person who was in shock: Daicos, himself.

"I can't believe I'm the Brownlow medallist to be honest," Daicos said at the award ceremony in Melbourne.

The count was close until about the halfway mark, before Daicos pulled away from the pack as the season progressed.

With his 47 votes last night, Daicos has earned more votes in the last four years than any other player has in any five-year period.

Daicos earned more votes than three entire clubs. He collected 63 per cent of Collingwood's votes for the evening.

He racked up record after record: the most votes in one year, most consecutive games with three votes (six), the most games with three votes (13).

It wasn't just a win, it was domination.

With the win, Daicos joins Tom Mitchell, Gary Ablett Jr and Ben Cousins as father-son selections who have claimed the Brownlow Medal (Jobe Watson's 2012 victory was rescinded).

Daicos time

Plenty has been written about what makes Daicos special.

Coaches and opposition players talk about his elusiveness, vision and ability to make something out of what seems like nothing.

And then there is his competitiveness.

"He hates losing," Magpies great Scott Pendlebury said.

"Especially at table tennis. Whenever we travel on the road, he always tries to get a re-match."

That competitive drive is often what turns good into great, and great into legendary.

But words pale into insignificance compared to watching the best of Daicos in full flight.

Players like Daicos stand out due to the highlights they create.

Teams spend more time trying to get Daicos off balance than any other player in the competition.

It hasn't seemed to have an effect yet.

No matter what teams throw at Daicos, he still has an unerring habit of getting the ball and letting his imagination run wild.

That drive was forged from his early days as a player, often being one of the slightest on the field when he played up in age at both the Greythorn Falcons and the Kew Rovers.

When Daicos moved to Carey Grammar for year 10, he was thrust immediately into the first team to compete in the prestigious APS football competition.

His teammates were no slouches either, with Daicos playing alongside the likes of Noah Anderson and last year's Brownlow medallist, Matt Rowell.

No player in the AFL was more important in getting his team in scoring positions than Daicos was this year.

Daicos thrived at winning the ball when no-one had clear control.

He has an innate ability to track the ball before anyone else, working smarter and not harder.

Daicos also has a scary ability to render his direct opponents as traffic cones.

The Magpies look to get Daicos the ball as much as possible, and he repays them with territory.

Few can match his combination of skill, speed and footy intelligence.

Although Collingwood fell short this year, hopes are higher for 2027 with additional reinforcements.

Family zone

Throughout football's history, geography has shaped the make-up of teams to a great extent.

Teams recruited from specific regions. The fortunes of clubs rose and fell based on the growth of different geographic areas.

Urban expansion fuelled Hawthorn's rise, while weak and depopulating zones condemned other clubs to near extinction.

There was one exception to the geography-based dictation of the footy landscape: the sons of former players.

The father-son rule was introduced in 1949 to ensure players such as Ron Barassi could continue on the legacy of their fathers at their clubs regardless of geography.

These days, the role of geography has inverted and it now dictates where all the father-son selections are.

The family zone for Victorian footy now runs through south-east Melbourne.

This was the former recruiting area for Hawthorn, otherwise known as the Family Club.

The ranks of father-son selections are littered with schools and clubs based in the most desirable parts of Melbourne, often far from the origins of their fathers' careers.

For example, the Silvangi and Daicos offspring played their junior footy at the Greythorn Falcons.

That's only a stone's throw from Collingwood captain Darcy Moore's junior club of Ivanhoe.

Nor is it far from where Mitchell or Watson first honed their craft.

The eastern side of Melbourne has increasingly become a powerhouse in junior footy as well, with Sandringham, Oakleigh and the Eastern Ranges dominating the AFL's Talent League in recent seasons.

Brownlow's changing face

A major change took place to the fabric of the Brownlow Medal this year.

Umpires gained access to a select group of 17 statistics before voting. Daicos excelled in several of these measures.

This may rob part of what made the Brownlow so special.

Umpires have a unique perspective. They're also party to the intangibles, such as on-field demeanour, respect and sportsmanship.

This year's votes aligned more closely to the results of the AFL Coaches Association award than ever before, according to Wheelo Ratings.

Coaches pore over key numbers throughout their games and now umpires can rely on some of the same figures to adjudge best afield as well.

Supplying data may condition umpires to discard insights gleaned in the heat of the action, turning them instead into just another spin on the same cold distant observations.

Defenders are already suffering even more than they traditionally do, while midfielders, who often accumulate high "count" stats, get a larger share of the spoils.

Rucks also outperformed their expected output this year, likely benefiting from the inclusion of hit-outs.

This will likely serve to further intensify a growing trend towards vote concentration in disposal-accumulating midfielders.

The leaderboard for career-long average votes is strewn liberally with current players, with previous leaders Haydn Bunton and Graham Moss only playing the prime vote-earning part of their careers in the VFL.

If this trend continues, Daicos will soon break Patrick Dangerfield and Ablett Jr's record for most career votes, at least until the next star enters the scene.

But all of that is for the future.

All that is important now is that the inevitable ascension of Daicos to the pinnacle of the game has taken place.

World.title: Smart glasses to be banned from WA public schools
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Smart glasses will be banned from public schools in Western Australia to prevent children from being secretly filmed, the state's education minister has announced.

The devices, which look like ordinary glasses, allow the wearer to capture images, video and audio with the press of a button, and have attracted the nickname "pervert glasses" because it is not always clear when they are in use.

Education Minister Sabine Winton said students, teachers, parents and contractors would be banned from wearing or storing the glasses on school premises from the start of term 4.

Sabine Winton has announced a ban on smart glasses in all WA state schools. (ABC News: Kenith Png)

"Smart glasses may look cool but there's absolutely no place in our schools for them," she said.

"We know the devices are becoming increasingly popular and increasingly accessible and cheap and there is a growing community concern about the risk of careless, criminal and malicious activity."

Cheap smart glasses shockingly hackable Independent testing finds a hacker can access cheap smart glasses without a password.

There is growing support for a ban on the import of low-cost devices that are being used to film people without their consent.

An ABC investigation found the devices were exposing Australians' sensitive data, images and videos to hackers.

It comes after the City of Vincent last week instructed its chief executive officer to prepare a report for the council to consider the privacy and safety concerns stemming from the use of smart glasses in city-owned facilities, including recreational centres and libraries.

The report will consider whether the Perth council's existing laws, which ban the use of devices to record someone without their consent at a community facility, are sufficient, and whether it is necessary to beef up enforcement powers.

Do you know more? Contact Callum Liddelow.

World.title: Birthing among 'flies and trucks' becoming more common in parts of NSW
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

When Shara Kimpton gave birth to her third child five weeks early in 2023, she was in a rest area on the Sturt Highway in the New South Wales Riverina.

She and her mother were on their way to the Griffith Hospital, more than 90 kilometres from home, but the baby was in no mood to wait.

"It was quite the rush and everything was a blur," Ms Kimpton said.

"But I just had to follow my instincts because that was the only thing I had.

"There was lots of flies and trucks going past … out in the elements."

Shara Kimpton says she was forced to give birth among flies and with trucks going past. (Supplied: Shara Kimpton)

Stories like Ms Kimpton's are becoming more common.

Twenty-five years ago, the rate of babies being born before arriving at hospital in NSW was similar whether you lived in a regional or a metropolitan area.

But that figure has long been diverging, with rates since doubling in regional local health districts.

In outer regional and remote areas, it has more than tripled.

Rates are highest on the Central Coast and northern NSW, where one in 67 babies is now born before making it to hospital.

Do you know more about this or have a similar story? Email pezet.lauren@abc.net.au or laurenpezet@proton.me

The NSW Health data includes:

planned homebirths before a midwife arrived

freebirths, which is distinct from a homebirth and occurs without a registered midwife or doctor present, before a hospital presentation

births at home or in transit before a planned hospital birth

There is no breakdown of those categories.

Perinatal social worker and regional maternity advocate Jen Laurie said anecdotally many were those in transit, known as "roadside births".

Ms Laurie has spoken to dozens of women about their birthing experience and through her Bush Babies campaign, lobbying the NSW Government, with many sharing stories of births at rest stops and in toilet blocks.

"I sometimes wonder if it's going to take a catastrophic outcome for somebody to be really creative and start listening and do something about it," she said

Jen Laurie says the regional maternity system is a "networked mess". (ABC News: Peter Sanders)

NSW Health Minister Ryan Park said he wanted to "get that number down" and would consider a target if it was advised by the recently appointed inaugural chief midwife.

"It is still small as a percentage of all births, but every time that happens, it causes concern, particularly for mums and families," he said.

Ms Kimpton said despite her history of quick deliveries, when she fell pregnant again with her fourth child she was not offered an appointment with her local clinic until about halfway through her pregnancy, and was not given any alternative options other than driving in for the delivery.

Homebirth was not an option available to her so she planned to freebirth at home despite the known risks, which can include undetected complications, and then presented to hospital as she did not want to risk giving birth on the side of the road again.

"Our only option is go to your closest local midwifery-included hospital or even further, pretty much for centralised care," she said.

Shara Kimpton opted to give birth to her fourth child at home, fearing another roadside birth. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

In a statement, a Murrumbidgee Local Health District apologised that Griffith Hospital was not able to provide Ms Kimpton with an antenatal visit before the recommended 14 weeks, and that maternity staff aim to provide ongoing support and information for birth and emergency options.

"We continue to listen to and learn from women about their experiences to help us plan and improve the care provided within our maternity services to meet the needs of the local community," the statement said.

Ms Kimpton said if Hay, the closest town to her property, still had a birthing option like it used to, she could have planned to go birth there instead.

The birth certificate for Shara Kimpton's son shows he was born at "Birdcage Rest Area". (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

Birthing options centralised

Ms Laurie said she felt the reason behind the increase was clear.

"The reduction of services and the centralisation of services," she said.

"A lot of these regional rural remote places that are no longer offering birthing previously did."

Dozens of birthing services have closed or been suspended under both Labor and Coalition governments across NSW over recent decades.

Examples of mothballed maternity units include the unit at Parkes, which has lay dormant since 2019 because not enough staff want to work there, but Ryan Park said he was still working towards opening it.

The barely used birthing suite in Parkes remains closed due to a lack of available staff. (ABC Central West: Xanthe Gregory)

There was also Muswellbrook, which closed in 2022, forcing expectant mothers to travel 100km to Maitland.

The Upper Hunter Shire Council has expressed fears Scone could be in a similar situation when its only obstetrician retires at the end of 2026, with recruitment still underway.

The closure of the maternity ward at Yass in 2004 has seen women give birth on the Barton Highway on the way to Canberra.

In Tumut, birthing has been suspended after its only obstetrician was banned from practising at the hospital, with women being sent more than 100km away to Wagga Wagga until the position is filled.

Mr Park acknowledged there had been a "change in the midwifery model" over time with a "focus on safety", which he said also had challenges.

"It has to be a service that operates around the clock, and that's why governments of all persuasions probably over the last 25 years have concentrated those services around major hubs and major hospitals," he said.

"What we've tried to do, and our approach is slightly different, we're trying to get more women to be able to birth as close to where they live as possible.

"We've expanded homebirthing and we've expanded midwifery group practices."

Ryan Park says he wants to see more birthing options closer to home, while balancing resourcing challenges. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

There is strict criteria around location and pregnancy risk for women wanting a homebirth, and midwifery group practices generally provide antenatal and postnatal care.

Mr Park also said more than 300 new midwifery places had been filled since 2023, with half of those in rural and regional areas.

He said there was "more work to do".

" I've made it clear to the department I want the focus on trying to open up these birthing services, but I've got to balance that out with making sure that we've got the staff in place. "

A statewide maternity service plan is also due at the end of the year.

Midwives working in 'pressure cooker'

On the Central Coast, the measured impact of the closure of a private maternity unit last year is not clear as the data only goes up to 2024.

Gosford-based doula and educator Gemma Wilson said with Wyong's maternity ward also closed since 2020, the situation on the Central Coast was "dire".

There is currently only one maternity ward to cater for more than 3,500 births each year.

Gemma Wilson is a doula and educator based in Gosford. (ABC News: Tamara Penniket)

"It's been a bit of a snowball effect that's continued to happen here," she said.

" [Midwives are] trying to provide the best care and do the best that they can, but they are literally working in a pressure cooker right now in that system. "

Ms Wilson said while the federal government had allocated $10 million to provide additional support to Gosford's remaining maternity ward, there had not been much improvement.

Gosford Hospital has the only remaining maternity ward on the Central Coast. (ABC News: Tamar Penniket)

She also said while a publicly funded homebirth service opened on the Central Coast in 2023, it did not counter the impact of losing Wyong's birth centre.

"We have nowhere for women in the north end of the coast to birth at," she said.

NSW Health said while there has been a small increase in the number of women birthing at Gosford Hospital since Gosford Private closed its ward, it was not as much as predicted.

Broader impact

Tim McEwen from the Australian Paramedics Association (NSW) said the data showing an increase in births before arrivals correlates with what paramedics see on the ground.

He also thought a reduction in services was behind the trend.

"In a lot of regional towns there's only one ambulance on duty, and that ambulance may not be in town at the time of the medical emergency," Mr McEwen said.

" So the potential for having no maternity unit and no ambulance or backup ambulance available is really quite a frightening prospect both for the public and us as paramedics. "

In a statement, NSW Health said local health districts were focused on filling midwifery and obstetric vacancies through targeted workforce planning, university partnerships, internal pathway programs and tertiary study subsidies.

"We strongly encourage all pregnant women to consult with registered healthcare providers early in their pregnancy, for personalised advice about the best options for themselves and their baby, including options for pregnancy care and birth location," the statement said.

World.title: Council says there's 'no land' for charity's request for rough sleepers
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

The head of a food charity in far-west New South Wales has been left frustrated after being told there was no council land available to build a homeless camp.

Feeding Friends had asked Broken Hill City Council for a block of council land or an unused building to establish a base for homelessness services, including a food outlet, laundry facilities and a transitional camp.

Broken Hill City Council has indicated no land is available to build a camp for those experiencing homelessness. (ABC News: Declan Gooch)

The charity said it was responding to an "urgent need for secure, stable spaces" in the mining city, where those experiencing homelessness could set up temporary and safe shelters.

While the council voted to investigate whether any land was available, Mayor Tom Kennedy made it clear there was not.

"Initial findings is there is no land," Mr Kennedy said.

"So for Feeding Friends to go any further, they're going to have to acquire land themselves.

"[But] what's been proposed before council requires significant planning … [and] vast public consultation."

Prior to the meeting to discuss the request, some locals raised concerns over the encampment's impact on neighbouring residents and businesses.

Tom Kennedy says extensive public consultation and planning approvals would be needed for a homeless encampment. (ABC Broken Hill: Kristina Rosengren)

Demand is increasing

After five years serving hot meals to those experiencing homelessness in Broken Hill, Feeding Friends president Don Barron said demand for its services were growing amid the cost-of-living crisis.

He said the charity now needed a permanent location for its food services.

"I was very disappointed [land wasn't available]," Mr Barron said.

Don Barron says all levels of government need to come together to address homelessness. (ABC Broken Hill: Bill Ormonde)

"[The need] has certainly grown in the way of young families.

"We have homeless people in Broken Hill that do have children, they still go to school but they're living in cars.

"It's probably a lack of housing which is the main reason why people are living in cars … [also] affordability, the cost of living is just gone out of control."

No 'legal framework' to address homelessness

Derwent Coshott, a senior lecturer in law at Sydney University, said legally establishing a transitional campsite would require planning approvals.

But he said there was another pathway through a policy of non-enforcement, referring to the state government's protocol for homeless people in public places.

"The policies that have been adopted have been permissive, in so far as you kind of just let people camp there and you don't enforce the law to move them on," Dr Coshott said.

Derwent Coshott says there is no proper legal framework to address homelessness in these circumstances. (Supplied: Dr Derwent Coshott)

Feeding Friends could ask the council to not enforce the law against them, he said.

"The risk is, of course, that none of this means that the law might not be enforced against them later on."

However, Dr Coshott said the issue raised broader questions about regulating homelessness in NSW.

"We have a NSW administrative protocol that's effectively saying, 'Look, we don't actually have a law that properly deals with this, so the way we're going to deal with this is by not enforcing the law'," Dr Coshott said.

" That basically tells you where the problem is, in the sense that there is no real proper legal framework to address homelessness in these circumstances. "

For Mr Barron, who knows what it's like to sleep rough, it is about confronting homelessness head-on.

"It's not just local council's problem, it's a three-tier problem — local council, which doesn't have funds to do it, the state government, which does, and the federal government, which does," Mr Barron said.

"We all need to sit down as a three-tier society, and involve the public, of how we can address this issue."

World.title: Coalition weighing options to use super to boost home ownership
World.content:
The Coalition has entered the political fray over super, re-litigating the argument that the retirement savings scheme should be used to help people buy a home — but has stopped short of announcing any policies.

Shadow Housing Minister Andrew Bragg will give a speech later today where he is expected to float ideas about how super could be used to boost home ownership ahead of retirement.

"We don't want to become a nation where renting in retirement becomes mandatory," Senator Bragg told ABC News Radio on Tuesday.

" We want to have a country where people can live in their own house … if their superannuation can help them do that, then we should look at that. "

Senator Bragg said multiple options had been canvassed by the Coalition, including using super as collateral for a loan, or withdrawing a lump sum for a house deposit.

But he said he was not advocating for any particular solutions for now, ahead of a speech he will give at the Financial Services Council later today.

"You could keep the money in the system and it could operate as a collateral or an offset," he told ABC News Radio.

"You could take it out to pay off a mortgage or to pull together a first home loan."

While stressing that the Coalition had not settled on its formal policy, Senator Bragg insisted there was a need to look at different ways super could be used to help people buy their first home.

"I think most people would want their well-paid politicians to be pushing out the boat on some ideas that might be able to help them achieve their goal of home ownership," he said.

Where does super go when you die? Millions of Australians could have no say in who inherits their super. Here's how to check if you're one of them.

The Coalition's policy at the last two elections was to allow people to withdraw $50,000 from their super to put towards a house deposit.

Senator Bragg did not say if the opposition would keep that policy, but admitted a "credible critique" was that it was more likely for people in their mid to late 30s who would have accrued that amount, and therefore the policy would not have significantly helped younger people.

Debate heats up on super

Superannuation has become a political flashpoint in recent weeks, with One Nation releasing a policy that would allow people to divert funds from their super to be able to pay their rent or mortgage.

That policy would permit people to keep 3 per cent of their salary that would otherwise go to super for a three year period — which would be $2,300 per year (or $44 per week) for a person on a $90,500 salary.

Some critics have said the measure could be inflationary in the short term and would impact the compound-interest growth of super savings in the long term.

Labor slammed the One Nation policy and has declared the next election will be a "referendum" on superannuation — a key creation of the Labor Keating government in the 1990s.

Under the government's first home super saver scheme, people can make voluntary contributions to their super, allow it to accrue interest, and later withdraw up to $50,000 of that money as part of a home deposit.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers says the Coalition and One Nation "hate super". (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Treasurer Jim Chalmers said the Coalition and One Nation were "coming after super" and they wanted to "vandalise" the retirement savings scheme.

"They hate super. They always have and they always will," Mr Chalmers told ABC Radio National on Tuesday.

"That would be devastating for people's retirement incomes. It would make people worse off.

"Superannuation is for retirement."

Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson would not comment on whether Shadow Cabinet had seen a proposal of Senator Bragg's ideas.

But he said those ideas were "a welcome part of the conversation" amid an increase of people reaching retirement without owning their home.

"The biggest leading indicator of poverty in retirement is people don't own their own home," he said.

"This is why home ownership is so important, and we need it to take precedence as the primary economic interest for retirement and during your working life."

Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson says the government needs to prioritise housing. (ABC News: Brendan Esposito)

Mr Wilson said housing was a key component in forecasted falling fertility rates signalled in yesterday's Intergenerational Report.

"The reality is, with the cost of housing continuing to rise, there's a direct correlation between that and, of course, family formation," he said.

"Part of the challenge is the government and the Labor Party continue to prioritise superannuation over home ownership, which means people are buying later and at higher price, which means that Australian families are being kneecapped from the start."

Senator Bragg will argue in his speech that in retirement, Australian's are best served by owning a residence as a top priority, and secondly owning financial assets to draw an income or replace the pension in their old age.

He said 12 per cent of Australians' income is going towards providing or overproviding for the latter.

"If Australians can reorient some of their super savings early in life (for example, a loan from super for residence), they can optimise their objectives," he will say.

Nationals leader Matt Canavan said Senator Bragg was a "thought leader" and that the Coalition was formulating its policies ahead of the next election.

"Generally speaking of course, it's our policy that people should have a choice when it comes to how they use their superannuation," he said.

"We do believe that superannuation is an investment for your retirement — that's what it's there for, what it should be used for. Obviously investing in your first home, or any home, is an investment and we'd like to promote that choice."

World.title: Qld bushfire caused by permitted burn jumping containment lines, authorities say
World.content:
A southern Queensland fire that prompted the evacuation of six households was likely caused by a permitted burn that got out of control, according to authorities.

The residents of six rural properties in the Southern Downs are returning to their homes today after deciding to evacuate overnight while firefighters worked to control a nearby bushfire south-west of Stanthorpe.

Emergency crews are monitoring the fire, which continues to burn near Murphy Crossing Road at Nundubbermere, about 230 kilometres south-west of Brisbane.

Cenedra Rogers says the bushfire got within 3 kilometres of her property. (Supplied: Cenedra Rogers)

Rural Fire Service Queensland Chief Superintendent Shaun Toohey said the fire was caused by a permitted burn that jumped containment lines several weeks ago.

Mr Toohey said the property owner had been helping crews work to the contain the fire.

"Unfortunately, with the conditions we have down there a fire on the landscape is going to have a couple of weeks to exhaust itself," he said.

"It's an accidental piece that's occurred, but [I'm] really thankful for the work that property owner has done with our crews over the last fortnight."

Southern Downs Regional Council Mayor Melissa Hamilton said while there were no reports of property damage, the drought-affected region was bracing for a difficult bushfire season.

"That is a reminder for people to be incredibly cautious," she said.

"The window for permitted burns is no doubt closing very fast.

"It is an absolute warning as we are now entering our fire season.

"It is dry and we are completely reliant on weather conditions at the moment with a number of fires around the region."

Residents prepared as fire spread

Nundubbermere resident Cenedra Rogers said she decided not to evacuate after emergency services visited her yesterday.

Ms Rogers said she had experienced fires in the area recently and was prepared to leave if directed by authorities.

"We decided to stay just because we have our full faith in the firies. If it got bad, they would probably leave and we would follow them," Ms Rogers said.

She said she watched the situation closely as burnt leaves fell from the sky.

She believes the blaze spread to a neighbouring property.

"We climbed up the hill to have a look and we could see flames leaping into the air from the treetops, which was a bit scary," she said.

"It just came closer and closer and closer until the firies started back-burning and trying to do whatever they could to push it away," Ms Rogers said.

Drought pushes farmers to the brink Nearly a month after vast swathes of Queensland were drought declared, pastures are bare, rivers have stopped running, and hay sheds sit empty.

She said the wind changed direction at about 3am today, pushing the fire away from her home.

"I woke up to see more trucks up the street and the fire moving away from us," she said.

"The winds changed, which is really nice."

Ms Rogers said she worked to protect her home, hosing down the structure and the ground.

"Everything is just bone dry. We were just trying to get a little bit of moisture into the air and into the ground where we've got leaf litter and sticks," she said.

The Bureau of Meteorology forecasts Stanthorpe will reach a top of 23 degrees Celsius on Tuesday following temperatures in excess of 30C in recent days.

World.title: Man linked to wife's suspected murder charged with bribing officials
World.content:
A Queensland man is accused of bribing Bangladeshi officials to remove his name from police records as detectives investigate his estranged wife's suspected murder.

Awlad Hossain, 51, has been charged with bribing a foreign public official, which carries a maximum penalty of 10 years’ imprisonment. Mr Hossain has not yet appeared before court.

The ABC revealed last April that the Australian Federal Police (AFP) was investigating the suspected murder of Mr Hossain's estranged wife, Rehana Parvin, an Australian citizen and mother of five, whose body was found in a small village in Bangladesh in September 2024.

Mother-of-five Rehana Parvin, whose body has been discovered in a small Bangladeshi village two months after she disappeared (Supplied)

Bangladeshi police have issued an arrest warrant for Mr Hossain over her death, but he has not been charged in relation to it, in either Bangladesh or Australia.

AFP officers arrested Mr Hossain on Tuesday and executed search warrants at homes in Goodna and Redbank Plains, where they seized an electronic device.

Investigators also searched financial institutions in Sydney and Brisbane, seizing international funds transfer and bank records.

The ABC understands the AFP will allege that between September 2024 and September 2026, Mr Hossain conspired with people in Bangladesh to influence the Bangladeshi investigation, arranging the transfer of about $90,000 so it could be used to bribe public officials, including to have his name struck from police records.

Foreign bribery first

This is the first time the AFP has put an allegation of foreign bribery of a public official for personal advantage before the court.

Advice provided by Bangladeshi authorities to the AFP suggested the cause of Ms Parvin's death was suspicious. Separate Bangladesh and Australian Federal Police investigations remain ongoing.

Rehana Parvin was an Australian citizen.

AFP Commander Stephen Jay said any attempt to corrupt investigative processes, whether in Australia or overseas, was a serious criminal matter.

"The AFP takes allegations of bribery and corruption seriously, particularly where the alleged conduct is intended to influence the outcome of a serious criminal investigation," Commander Jay said.

"Anyone who attempts to buy influence or interfere with the administration of justice should expect to be held accountable.

"We will continue to work closely with our domestic and international partners regarding this investigation."

World.title: Police investigate possible organised crime links after 11yo shot in face
World.content:
Police are investigating whether men present at the time an 11-year-old boy was shot in the head at a north-west Sydney home had links to organised crime, the ABC understands.

The child was treated for wounds to the face and neck and remains in a critical condition in hospital, following the incident at a Norwest home about 5pm on Monday.

An 18-year-old man has been charged with concealing a serious indictable offence, with two other men, both aged 18, released from custody after being questioned by police.

Police are investigating possible organised crime links. (ABC News)

A 43-year-old woman was also present at the time of the shooting, with another person not yet located.

It is understood investigators are looking into whether the men inside the unit have links to organised crime.

Police on Monday night had said there was no evidence to suggest the incident was related to underworld tensions.

"We have nothing to suggest that it is organised crime-related, but we will conduct a very thorough investigation into this," NSW Police Superintendent Naomi Moore said.

"For those that are obviously fearful on the streets out here at the moment, we are content that we are doing a very thorough investigation here."

She said the boy's mother was with him in hospital and was "distressed, as any parent would be".

Superintendent Moore said police had not yet recovered the firearm.

'Horrible event'

Emergency vehicles were at the scene on Monday afternoon. (ABC News)

A resident at the unit block said police could be seen searching a nearby park and creek after the shooting.

"They had cordoned off the whole park at that time, and they were searching … until late in the night, I believe," he said.

Premier Chris Minns on Tuesday described the incident as an "incredibly distressing situation".

"It's also a very a tragic reminder of how dangerous guns are, often the people who are the victims of guns are innocent people," he said.

World.title: ‘Need a hazmat suit’: Virgin flight attendants are sick of cleaning dirty planes
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesAviation ‘Need a hazmat suit’: Virgin flight attendants are sick of cleaning dirty planes Chris Zappone September 22, 2026 — 11:57am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Virgin Australia flight attendants are demanding the return of dedicated cleaning crews as mess left behind by passengers and gruelling turnaround duties leave staff working up to 10 hours without a break. According to the Flight Attendants’ Association of Australia (FAAA), cabin conditions have deteriorated to the point where staff practically “need a hazmat suit”. Virgin Australia crew are required to clean up planes after flights. “The insufficient catering offer onboard leads passengers to bring their own food onboard,” said one Virgin crew member, who asked not to be named. “From chips to lollies and mushed-up fruit in the carpets, the amount of cleaning is increasing.” Virgin requires the cabin crew to perform deep cleans between journeys, adding strain to their workload. After cleaning planes, the Virgin crew, who have won awards for their quality of service, must then serve food to passengers on subsequent flights.



Related Article Updated

Aviation New planes, fuel hedging shield Virgin from oil price shock Virgin was contacted for comment. The FAAA is now pushing to reinstate professional cleaners between flights to relieve overburdened staff and maintain hygiene standards. FAAA industrial relations manager Steven Reed said: “It used to be ‘tidy the cabin, fluff the cushions, make sure there’s nothing in the seat pockets, and cross the seatbelts, ready for the next passengers coming on’. “Now some of the state of the aircraft is such that they almost need a hazmat suit to clean it up.”



A number of Virgin flights to overseas destinations such as Bali and Fiji have been marked by excessively rowdy passengers, who add even further strain to the crew and leave cabins in disarray. “It’s gone beyond what was entitled, and obviously the FAAA on behalf of its members is pushing really hard to get cabin cleaners back on the aircraft between flights,” Reed said. The association recognises the need for crew to sometimes work “longer and harder” days – but it says they need better pay and more say over which shifts they take up. Reed said that after cleaning cabins, the same crew will serve food on the subsequent flight. In March, Virgin’s crew won the World’s Best Airlines Award for the eighth year in a row in the AirlineRatings.com World’s Best Airlines Awards 2026. The airline is also in the process of taking delivery of new Boeing 737-8s this year.



Related Article Aviation ‘Nothing to retire on’: Fired Qantas workers get $35 million payout Virgin Australia said on Friday that it would add nearly 4000 seats on flights between Perth and Melbourne, and 1000 seats between Brisbane and Melbourne, to help Fremantle Dockers and Brisbane Lions fans attend the grand final next weekend. Both Virgin and Qantas have been criticised for lifting the price on return tickets to Melbourne for the AFL grand final. On Monday, Virgin was charging $1728 for a Brisbane-Melbourne flight, almost triple the cost of the same flight two weeks later, Bloomberg reported. Qantas’ cheapest Brisbane-Melbourne return airfare was $1658. Both are about triple the price of the same route two weeks later. Reed said that “flight attendants are just exhausted from doing 10-, 12-, 14-hour days”. The union wants to see pay raises for Virgin crew and a reduction of shift times to nine hours and 45 minutes, as they stood before COVID, from the current elevated 10 hours. World.title: Beau Lamarre-Condon trial live updates: Former NSW Police officer says he acted in self-defence as trial continues over alleged murders of Jesse Baird, Luke Davies
World.content:
Hello and welcome to our live coverage of Beau Lamarre-Condon’s double murder trial in the NSW Supreme Court.

The former police officer has pleaded not guilty to murdering Sydney couple Jesse Baird, 26, and Luke Davies, 29, in the eastern suburbs on February 19, 2024.

Beau Lamarre-Condon (left) is accused of murdering Jesse Baird and Luke Davies.

He has also pleaded not guilty to one count of aggravated breaking and entering into Baird’s Paddington home in August 2023 and stealing a mobile phone and wallet belonging to Baird.

A 15-person jury has been empanelled for the trial, which is expected to run for up to 12 weeks. In the event all 15 jurors are still present at the end of the trial, a ballot will be conducted to reduce their number to 12.

Yesterday, Crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield, SC, started delivering his opening address to the jury. This sets out the Crown’s case and is not evidence, but it is a guide to the evidence the prosecution expects to call in the months ahead.

Lamarre-Condon is entitled to the presumption of innocence and his barrister John Stratton, SC, will deliver an opening address today after Hatfield finishes his remarks.

During his opening yesterday, Hatfield alleged that Lamarre-Condon developed an “an obsessive and jealous infatuation” with Baird after a short relationship that started in late 2022 and was ended for the first time by Baird in April 2023.

After a brief resumption of their relationship later that year, it was “firmly and irretrievably ended” by Baird in November 2023, the Crown says.

The Crown case is that the murder of Baird was premeditated but that he killed Davies, Baird’s new boyfriend, to eliminate a witness to his crime.

World.title: The pretence of Trump running the most transparent White House ever is over
World.content:
Analysis WorldNorth AmericaTrump's White House The pretence of Trump running the most transparent White House ever is over Michael Koziol September 22, 2026 — 11:51am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

New York: The Trump administration likes to pride itself on running “the most transparent administration in history”. And until this week, it had a semblance of a point. Donald Trump, who grew his profile by starring on The Apprentice, was the television president. No president loved TV more, and surely no president was more adept at deploying it for his own benefit. The media boycott in response to Trump’s media ban has prompted the president to rebrand the White House streaming channel as “Trump TV”. AP But say what you will, access to Trump was unparalleled. He welcomed cameras into the Oval Office almost every day, and spoke so often that even members of the media wished for less. Even this correspondent, as a foreigner representing an overseas media outlet, was able to show up to the South Lawn of the White House and question the US president every time he departed on the Marine One helicopter.



It was a marked improvement in access, especially compared to Joe Biden – who, amid his evident decline, was hidden away from the media. Related Article Trump's White House Trump launches ‘Trump TV’ channel after networks boycott him Trump loved – and still loves – pointing out this contrast. But his boasting always missed a key point: whatever access Trump may have granted, it was to a diminishing pool of serious journalists, and to an increasing crop of partisan hacks. From the start, the press office run by Karoline Leavitt granted pole position in the White House press briefing room to so-called “new media” outlets – almost always right-wing podcasters and influencers whose querying of the president was a riff on “why are you so great?” and “why are the Democrats so awful?” Trump’s banning of CNN and MS NOW from the White House reportedly came after his aide, Natalie Harp, showed him unfavourable coverage. Bloomberg



Slowly but surely, these charlatans took over. The White House assumed control of the daily press “pool” – the small team that gets to go into the Oval Office – and gave more and more slots to the right-wing fringe media. Their inane questions would not elicit new information, but gave Trump a free kick to promote his agenda and disparage his political enemies. Earlier this year, pool positions for foreign journalists were largely abolished. The excuse for this was a rivalry between two competing foreign media groups – which did exist – but the cumulative impact was to exclude the foreign press from the most powerful office in the world, and to give those spots to yet more right-wing goons. Now, Trump has banished CNN, Politico and MS NOW (formerly MSNBC), some of the few remaining serious media outlets able to question the president on matters of import. Other news organisations are boycotting Trump in solidarity, a commendable move, but one that ultimately reduces the presence of capable reporters in the room. TV channels take a stand against the ban by Donald Trump. Bloomberg Solidarity does not come naturally to the American press corps. Journalists rarely back each other up, and are usually more than happy to move on to some other issue rather than demand answers on the issue of the day. This time, however, even Fox News has joined the resistance, which should tell you all you need to know.

World.title: ‘I want to set them on fire’: ARIA-nominated musician’s alleged threats to ex-partner
World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWCourts ‘I want to set them on fire’: ARIA-nominated musician’s alleged threats to ex-partner Amber Schultz September 22, 2026 — 11:50am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Warning: This story contains graphic content. An ARIA-nominated musician and Olympian has been issued an apprehended violence order after it was alleged in court that he told a woman he had dreams about pouring petrol on his ex-partner and setting her and her current partner alight. The AVO protects the ex-partner, her current partner and two others in the home. Musician Paul Greene pictured outside Nowra Local Court for an AVO appearance earlier this year. Sam Mooy It is the second AVO issued to folk singer-songwriter Paul Greene in the past year, both protecting former partners.



In November, Greene’s most recent partner Mary* was protected by a two-year AVO in Nowra Local Court. That order was made by consent and without admissions from Greene. Days after that AVO was issued, Mary reached out to Jess*, who had been in an earlier long-term relationship with Greene, claiming he had made comments that scared her. Greene allegedly told her he could ride up to Jess’ home disguised in his motorcycle gear, and knew how long he would serve in jail if he was convicted of double homicide, saying it would be “worth it”. It is the second AVO Greene has been issued in the past 12 months, both protecting ex-partners. Sam Mooy “[He] used to go really dark and talk about how he wanted to take you and [your current partner] out, and he wouldn’t care if he went to jail,” Mary texted her.



“It used to freak me out, but I never thought he actually would, but now I’m not so sure. I’m worried about you guys.” Mary said Greene had begun drinking heavily and taking drugs, which had been a trigger for his alleged domestic violence against Jess while they were in a relationship. A third woman also told police Greene spoke of dreams he had about killing Jess and her current partner, saying he “wanted to set them on fire by pouring gasoline on them and lighting them on fire”. The woman also said Greene told her he “want[ed] to slit their throats”, burn their house down and “see them in pain”.



The AVO, which states that police have concerns about the escalating nature of the threats, was issued in Nowra Court last Monday, prohibiting Greene from going within 500 metres of Jess’ home or work, contacting her, or threatening her. Related Article Courts ARIA-nominated musician and Olympian accused of domestic abuse The AVO was made by consent. It took nine months for the final order to be made following a series of delays and adjournments. In one instance, Jess spent the day waiting to give video-link evidence from a police station, only for the case to be adjourned without her being called. Greene was also charged with breaching the interim AVO after making a call to Jess’ phone. He was found not guilty, with the judge unconvinced the call was intentional.



Greene represented Australia in the 400m sprint at the 1996 Atlanta Olympic Games, as well as the 1990, 1994 and 1996 Commonwealth Games. Since retiring from athletics, he has become well known within the music industry and in the wider Shoalhaven area. He has performed with Midnight Oil’s Rob Hirst as Hirst & Greene, with Paul Greene & The Other Colours at the National Folk Festival, and at a Greens council election event. This year, he was nominated by the council for a Shoalhaven Australia Day Citizen of the Year Award. A petition to revoke his nomination garnered more than 500 signatures. He recently joined the long-running rock band vSpy vSpy for a tour in October, represented by Laneway Music. *Names changed for privacy

World.title: The five Brownlow looks everyone’s still talking about
World.content:
LifestyleFashionBrownlow Medal The five Brownlow looks everyone’s still talking about Courtney Thompson September 22, 2026 — 11:49am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

You needn’t be sitting at Crown Melbourne’s breakfast buffet to know there’s more than a few hangovers being nursed after last night’s Brownlow Medal. Collingwood midfielder Nick Daicos took home the top gong, while his partner Arlette Amor won both best dressed and best Carolyn Bassett-Kennedy cosplay in her understated white Effie Kats gown. Now that the bronzer has settled, these are the five Brownlow looks people can’t stop talking about the morning after. 1. Tayla Brown Tayla Brown wearing an embellished Cassandra Renee dress at the 2026 Brownlow. WireImage



A widely circulated dress from the Brownlow has been Tayla Brown’s embellished gown by bridal experts Cassandra Renee. As the cheap-shot headlines tell you, the dress could have been created by an AI chatbot from a “Brownlow fashion” prompt: the racer back tank style left the sides wide open and left her back exposed, while the splits at the hem allowed for a flash of thigh. But what’s lost here is how great Brown looked. Stylist Meggy Smith kept the beauty and accessories minimal to let the dress shine (literally), drawing comparisons to celebrities like Zoë Kravitz at the 2021 Met Gala. 2. Bailey Smith Bailey Smith wearing a custom YSG Tailors tuxedo at the 2026 Brownlow. AFL Photos



Just like your perennially single louche uncle who always rocks up to the family function late, Bailey Smith waltzed onto the Brownlow red carpet just as it was wrapping up. Dressed in a bespoke YSG Tailors soft tan tuxedo with a peak lapel and oversized trouser, the Geelong midfielder chose to accessorise with a pair of reflective sunglasses. You wouldn’t know it from Smith’s refusal to adhere to a designated schedule, but he was more than fashionably prepared for the event, having not one look to choose from, but three. “We can have something nailed down in our first consultation, and within half an hour of me leaving the meeting Bailey will have sent me another two concepts,” says Ryan McIntyre, YSG Tailors co-founder and director. “Bailey definitely has input, but he’s not always 100 per cent sure what’s going to work,” McIntyre says. “He has to trust the process a little bit.” 3. Brooke Bailey Brooke Bailey in a Oglia-Loro Couture gown at the 2026 Brownlow. WireImage



Brooke Bailey’s Oglia-Loro Couture look started with the hand-beaded fringe tulle fabric that shimmied as she entered the gala with partner, the recently retired Dion Prestia. “I had a beautiful piece of hand-beaded tulle and Paul said, ‘I have someone who this is perfect for,’ says designer Sam Oglialoro, explaining the process of creating the sculpted, strapless gown with stylist, Paul Versace. “It’s giving that whole era of the naked dress,” Versace adds. 4. Paris Bishop Paris Bishop, partner of Sam Durham of the Bombers, in a jaw-dropping crystal gown by Alin Le’Kal. Getty Images



Fresh off the plane from LA, model and partner to Essendon player Sam Durham Paris Bishop seemed to glow as she floated down the Brownlow red carpet in her custom Alin Le’Kal outfit. Styled by Lana Wilkinson, the champagne-hued corset and fishtail skirt featured hand-beaded crystal embellishments designed to accentuate her complexion. “We wanted to have that little bit of an LA tizz through it, which I think suits the glow that she’s got going on,” says Le’Kal of the look that left a touch of skin exposed at Bishop’s lower back where the corset and skirt met. “At the Brownlow, the girls can go a bit sexier than the Logies or other red carpets. I wanted to really do that well.” 5. Chloe Serong Chloe Serong in a custom Atalie Studios gown at the 2026 Brownlow. Getty Images



Looking pretty in ombre pink, Chloe Serong opted for a striking Atalie Studios creation to accompany husband Fremantle Dockers star Caleb Serong. The strapless gown was one of the more creative to walk the carpet, with an architectural neckline and rectangle cut-out at the chest. The beading embellishments were hand-dyed to resemble the inside of a dark fruit – say, like a pomegranate or blackberry. “More people are looking for an escape into surrealism or fantasy through fashion,” says couturier Grace Presow. “So my approach to each design is very deeply strategic and imaginative.” Juicy, indeed! World.title: Prince Harry in talks to make Diana documentary
World.content:
WorldEuropePrince Harry Prince Harry in talks to make Diana documentary Victoria Ward and Hannah Furness September 22, 2026 — 11:35am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: Prince Harry is in talks to make a documentary about his mother, Diana, Princess of Wales. The London Telegraph understands that the Duke of Sussex wants to mark the 30th anniversary of Diana’s death, on August 31 next year, by honouring her legacy “in the most meaningful way”. Prince Harry appeared at the 2026 WellChild Awards in London on Monday night. Aaron Chown/Pool PA via AP He has approached several friends and relatives of his late mother, including her brother, Earl Spencer, to ask whether they would take part in a documentary. However, the earl, writing in his new memoir, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, said he chose to write the book to avoid being a “talking head” in one of many productions planned about his sister, fearing they would follow a “flawed” agenda.



Diana holds toddler Prince Harry during a visit to Spain in 1987. AP The earl made a series of claims in his book concerning the King, including disparaging remarks the latter is alleged to have made about the princess in the days after her death. The duke’s decision to make a personal documentary is likely to infuriate the Prince of Wales, who has silently endured high-profile revelations about his family life from his brother in recent years. A source close to Prince Harry told the Telegraph: “The duke has discussed a number of possible projects to mark the 30th anniversary of his mother Diana, Princess of Wales’s passing. “Nothing has been finalised or confirmed, and he is still considering the most meaningful way to honour her legacy during this important anniversary year.”



Such a program would be produced by the Sussexes’ Archewell Productions and would probably be bought by Netflix, which has a “first look” deal with Harry and Meghan. It will be viewed by some as a power move in the battle for the princess’s legacy. Kensington Palace has not commented on how Prince William might mark the anniversary. Nine years ago, the brothers joined forces to contribute to two documentaries about their mother to mark the 20th anniversary of her death, but such a collaboration now appears inconceivable. ‘The truth is difficult’ In writing his memoir, published on Tuesday, the earl, 62, ensured he was first out of the blocks in the latest race to tell his late sister’s story. He told The Telegraph it deserved to be told “honestly, however uncomfortable for others”.



He said: “I was an eyewitness to history, and where the truth is difficult, I haven’t shied away from it. Earl Spencer has made a series of disclosures about his sister and her troubled life ahead of his book publication. PA Images via Getty Images “I did not consult any members of my family about the content of the book, as I did not want to implicate them in my authorial decisions, or to be constrained by them. I hope readers will see the book for what it is: an honest account.” Neither Prince William nor Prince Harry were given any indication about the book’s contents. Similarly, the earl is not thought to have consulted his sisters, Lady Sarah McCorquodale and Lady Jane Fellowes, about their memories, choosing instead to create an entirely personal record. The official christening photo of Archie, the first son of Harry and Meghan.



The memoir has already prompted a fierce war of words with Buckingham Palace about comments attributed to the King, who was the Prince of Wales when Diana died in Paris aged 36. In the book, the earl claims that in the aftermath of her death, the King told him “rest assured, we’ll forget her soon enough”, and spoke to the earl with a “giddy tone”, like a “lottery winner”. The palace swiftly responded with a rare statement suggesting the earl’s memory was false. A spokesman said the King was “mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss”. Spencer (centre) walks behind Diana’s coffin at her 1997 funeral, flanked by (L-R) the late Prince Philip, Duke of Edinburgh, Prince William, Prince Harry and Charles, then-prince of Wales. Reuters The earl then accused the King of “gaslighting” him and being “astonishingly provocative”. In turn, royal sources accused the earl of “peddling what little remains” of the princess’s privacy and getting out his “crested carving knives” for the King.



Earl Spencer, who is expected to donate a portion of the memoir’s proceeds to charity, said he believed he had a duty to record his version of events. Related Article Royal family Harry and Meghan need protection to avoid Diana’s ordeal, Earl Spencer says He said: “Writing around Diana’s life has been heavily mythologised, and much of what’s been written about her has been notable for its inaccuracy. “The 30th anniversary of her death is approaching; I am in my 60s now, and I feel the passage of time more sharply than I once did. I don’t want to reach the end of my own life having left my sister’s story to be told by people who never knew her.” He added: “It is a personal account of my sister, Diana. It is not only her story, it is my story; a book which will stand the test of time.”



The earl continued: “As a historian, I believe Diana’s story deserves to be told honestly, however uncomfortable for others, and because silence has its own cost. I made the decision to write it a year ago, as I was being approached to take part in other people’s projects about her.” In his book, he revealed that he had declined “endless, repeated” requests to contribute to documentaries about the princess, including from “Diana’s biographer Andrew Morton, and from Tony Blair’s [former] spin doctor, Alastair Campbell”. He said he had decided to “tell things how I remember them” instead of following “an agenda set by some TV producer I will never meet”. The Duke and Duchess of Sussex are adjusting to life back in the UK after six years in the US. Instagram@Meghan On Monday evening, Prince Harry made his third public appearance since moving back to the UK, attending the annual WellChild Awards in central London. He ignored a series of questions about his family as he was whisked inside the Royal Lancaster Hotel.



The duke said there was “not a dry eye in the house” at the ceremony, which celebrates children living with complex medical needs and their families, who “give it everything they’ve got every single day”. Related Article Royal family Harry and Meghan’s battle to be accepted into Cotswolds high society He added: “To all the mums and dads – most of us will never truly know the emotional ups and downs of your day. But I sincerely hope that you take strength from nights like this. And while we may not know the detail of your day, in this room and beyond, we recognise the commitment of your care and all that comes with it.” Harry and William have both spoken publicly about their mother, and have given their daughters Diana as a middle name. Their wives, Meghan and Catherine, regularly wear jewellery she owned. However, Harry is more often associated with the princess through his own efforts to follow publicly in her footsteps. Last year, he visited Angola, where he was pictured walking through a minefield, just as his mother had in 1997.

World.title: ‘Need a hazmat suit’: Virgin flight attendants are sick of cleaning dirty planes
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesAviation ‘Need a hazmat suit’: Virgin flight attendants are sick of cleaning dirty planes Chris Zappone September 22, 2026 — 11:57am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Virgin Australia flight attendants are demanding the return of dedicated cleaning crews as mess left behind by passengers and gruelling turnaround duties leave staff working up to 10 hours without a break. According to the Flight Attendants’ Association of Australia (FAAA), cabin conditions have deteriorated to the point where staff practically “need a hazmat suit”. Virgin Australia crew are required to clean up planes after flights. “The insufficient catering offer onboard leads passengers to bring their own food onboard,” said one Virgin crew member, who asked not to be named. “From chips to lollies and mushed-up fruit in the carpets, the amount of cleaning is increasing.” Virgin requires the cabin crew to perform deep cleans between journeys, adding strain to their workload. After cleaning planes, the Virgin crew, who have won awards for their quality of service, must then serve food to passengers on subsequent flights.



Related Article Updated

Aviation New planes, fuel hedging shield Virgin from oil price shock Virgin was contacted for comment. The FAAA is now pushing to reinstate professional cleaners between flights to relieve overburdened staff and maintain hygiene standards. FAAA industrial relations manager Steven Reed said: “It used to be ‘tidy the cabin, fluff the cushions, make sure there’s nothing in the seat pockets, and cross the seatbelts, ready for the next passengers coming on’. “Now some of the state of the aircraft is such that they almost need a hazmat suit to clean it up.”



A number of Virgin flights to overseas destinations such as Bali and Fiji have been marked by excessively rowdy passengers, who add even further strain to the crew and leave cabins in disarray. “It’s gone beyond what was entitled, and obviously the FAAA on behalf of its members is pushing really hard to get cabin cleaners back on the aircraft between flights,” Reed said. The association recognises the need for crew to sometimes work “longer and harder” days – but it says they need better pay and more say over which shifts they take up. Reed said that after cleaning cabins, the same crew will serve food on the subsequent flight. In March, Virgin’s crew won the World’s Best Airlines Award for the eighth year in a row in the AirlineRatings.com World’s Best Airlines Awards 2026. The airline is also in the process of taking delivery of new Boeing 737-8s this year.



Related Article Aviation ‘Nothing to retire on’: Fired Qantas workers get $35 million payout Virgin Australia said on Friday that it would add nearly 4000 seats on flights between Perth and Melbourne, and 1000 seats between Brisbane and Melbourne, to help Fremantle Dockers and Brisbane Lions fans attend the grand final next weekend. Both Virgin and Qantas have been criticised for lifting the price on return tickets to Melbourne for the AFL grand final. On Monday, Virgin was charging $1728 for a Brisbane-Melbourne flight, almost triple the cost of the same flight two weeks later, Bloomberg reported. Qantas’ cheapest Brisbane-Melbourne return airfare was $1658. Both are about triple the price of the same route two weeks later. Reed said that “flight attendants are just exhausted from doing 10-, 12-, 14-hour days”. The union wants to see pay raises for Virgin crew and a reduction of shift times to nine hours and 45 minutes, as they stood before COVID, from the current elevated 10 hours. World.title: Beau Lamarre-Condon trial live updates: Former NSW Police officer says he acted in self-defence as trial continues over alleged murders of Jesse Baird, Luke Davies
World.content:
Hello and welcome to our live coverage of Beau Lamarre-Condon’s double murder trial in the NSW Supreme Court.

The former police officer has pleaded not guilty to murdering Sydney couple Jesse Baird, 26, and Luke Davies, 29, in the eastern suburbs on February 19, 2024.

Beau Lamarre-Condon (left) is accused of murdering Jesse Baird and Luke Davies.

He has also pleaded not guilty to one count of aggravated breaking and entering into Baird’s Paddington home in August 2023 and stealing a mobile phone and wallet belonging to Baird.

A 15-person jury has been empanelled for the trial, which is expected to run for up to 12 weeks. In the event all 15 jurors are still present at the end of the trial, a ballot will be conducted to reduce their number to 12.

Yesterday, Crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield, SC, started delivering his opening address to the jury. This sets out the Crown’s case and is not evidence, but it is a guide to the evidence the prosecution expects to call in the months ahead.

Lamarre-Condon is entitled to the presumption of innocence and his barrister John Stratton, SC, will deliver an opening address today after Hatfield finishes his remarks.

During his opening yesterday, Hatfield alleged that Lamarre-Condon developed an “an obsessive and jealous infatuation” with Baird after a short relationship that started in late 2022 and was ended for the first time by Baird in April 2023.

After a brief resumption of their relationship later that year, it was “firmly and irretrievably ended” by Baird in November 2023, the Crown says.

The Crown case is that the murder of Baird was premeditated but that he killed Davies, Baird’s new boyfriend, to eliminate a witness to his crime.
