World.title: The pretence of Trump running the most transparent White House ever is over
World.content:
Analysis WorldNorth AmericaTrump's White House The pretence of Trump running the most transparent White House ever is over Michael Koziol September 22, 2026 — 11:51am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

New York: The Trump administration likes to pride itself on running “the most transparent administration in history”. And until this week, it had a semblance of a point. Donald Trump, who grew his profile by starring on The Apprentice, was the television president. No president loved TV more, and surely no president was more adept at deploying it for his own benefit. The media boycott in response to Trump’s media ban has prompted the president to rebrand the White House streaming channel as “Trump TV”. AP But say what you will, access to Trump was unparalleled. He welcomed cameras into the Oval Office almost every day, and spoke so often that even members of the media wished for less. Even this correspondent, as a foreigner representing an overseas media outlet, was able to show up to the South Lawn of the White House and question the US president every time he departed on the Marine One helicopter.



It was a marked improvement in access, especially compared to Joe Biden – who, amid his evident decline, was hidden away from the media. Related Article Trump's White House Trump launches ‘Trump TV’ channel after networks boycott him Trump loved – and still loves – pointing out this contrast. But his boasting always missed a key point: whatever access Trump may have granted, it was to a diminishing pool of serious journalists, and to an increasing crop of partisan hacks. From the start, the press office run by Karoline Leavitt granted pole position in the White House press briefing room to so-called “new media” outlets – almost always right-wing podcasters and influencers whose querying of the president was a riff on “why are you so great?” and “why are the Democrats so awful?” Trump’s banning of CNN and MS NOW from the White House reportedly came after his aide, Natalie Harp, showed him unfavourable coverage. Bloomberg



Slowly but surely, these charlatans took over. The White House assumed control of the daily press “pool” – the small team that gets to go into the Oval Office – and gave more and more slots to the right-wing fringe media. Their inane questions would not elicit new information, but gave Trump a free kick to promote his agenda and disparage his political enemies. Earlier this year, pool positions for foreign journalists were largely abolished. The excuse for this was a rivalry between two competing foreign media groups – which did exist – but the cumulative impact was to exclude the foreign press from the most powerful office in the world, and to give those spots to yet more right-wing goons. Now, Trump has banished CNN, Politico and MS NOW (formerly MSNBC), some of the few remaining serious media outlets able to question the president on matters of import. Other news organisations are boycotting Trump in solidarity, a commendable move, but one that ultimately reduces the presence of capable reporters in the room. TV channels take a stand against the ban by Donald Trump. Bloomberg Solidarity does not come naturally to the American press corps. Journalists rarely back each other up, and are usually more than happy to move on to some other issue rather than demand answers on the issue of the day. This time, however, even Fox News has joined the resistance, which should tell you all you need to know.

World.title: ‘I want to set them on fire’: ARIA-nominated musician’s alleged threats to ex-partner
World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWCourts ‘I want to set them on fire’: ARIA-nominated musician’s alleged threats to ex-partner Amber Schultz September 22, 2026 — 11:50am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Warning: This story contains graphic content. An ARIA-nominated musician and Olympian has been issued an apprehended violence order after it was alleged in court that he told a woman he had dreams about pouring petrol on his ex-partner and setting her and her current partner alight. The AVO protects the ex-partner, her current partner and two others in the home. Musician Paul Greene pictured outside Nowra Local Court for an AVO appearance earlier this year. Sam Mooy It is the second AVO issued to folk singer-songwriter Paul Greene in the past year, both protecting former partners.



In November, Greene’s most recent partner Mary* was protected by a two-year AVO in Nowra Local Court. That order was made by consent and without admissions from Greene. Days after that AVO was issued, Mary reached out to Jess*, who had been in an earlier long-term relationship with Greene, claiming he had made comments that scared her. Greene allegedly told her he could ride up to Jess’ home disguised in his motorcycle gear, and knew how long he would serve in jail if he was convicted of double homicide, saying it would be “worth it”. It is the second AVO Greene has been issued in the past 12 months, both protecting ex-partners. Sam Mooy “[He] used to go really dark and talk about how he wanted to take you and [your current partner] out, and he wouldn’t care if he went to jail,” Mary texted her.



“It used to freak me out, but I never thought he actually would, but now I’m not so sure. I’m worried about you guys.” Mary said Greene had begun drinking heavily and taking drugs, which had been a trigger for his alleged domestic violence against Jess while they were in a relationship. A third woman also told police Greene spoke of dreams he had about killing Jess and her current partner, saying he “wanted to set them on fire by pouring gasoline on them and lighting them on fire”. The woman also said Greene told her he “want[ed] to slit their throats”, burn their house down and “see them in pain”.



The AVO, which states that police have concerns about the escalating nature of the threats, was issued in Nowra Court last Monday, prohibiting Greene from going within 500 metres of Jess’ home or work, contacting her, or threatening her. Related Article Courts ARIA-nominated musician and Olympian accused of domestic abuse The AVO was made by consent. It took nine months for the final order to be made following a series of delays and adjournments. In one instance, Jess spent the day waiting to give video-link evidence from a police station, only for the case to be adjourned without her being called. Greene was also charged with breaching the interim AVO after making a call to Jess’ phone. He was found not guilty, with the judge unconvinced the call was intentional.



Greene represented Australia in the 400m sprint at the 1996 Atlanta Olympic Games, as well as the 1990, 1994 and 1996 Commonwealth Games. Since retiring from athletics, he has become well known within the music industry and in the wider Shoalhaven area. He has performed with Midnight Oil’s Rob Hirst as Hirst & Greene, with Paul Greene & The Other Colours at the National Folk Festival, and at a Greens council election event. This year, he was nominated by the council for a Shoalhaven Australia Day Citizen of the Year Award. A petition to revoke his nomination garnered more than 500 signatures. He recently joined the long-running rock band vSpy vSpy for a tour in October, represented by Laneway Music. *Names changed for privacy

World.title: The five Brownlow looks everyone’s still talking about
World.content:
LifestyleFashionBrownlow Medal The five Brownlow looks everyone’s still talking about Courtney Thompson September 22, 2026 — 11:49am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

You needn’t be sitting at Crown Melbourne’s breakfast buffet to know there’s more than a few hangovers being nursed after last night’s Brownlow Medal. Collingwood midfielder Nick Daicos took home the top gong, while his partner Arlette Amor won both best dressed and best Carolyn Bassett-Kennedy cosplay in her understated white Effie Kats gown. Now that the bronzer has settled, these are the five Brownlow looks people can’t stop talking about the morning after. 1. Tayla Brown Tayla Brown wearing an embellished Cassandra Renee dress at the 2026 Brownlow. WireImage



A widely circulated dress from the Brownlow has been Tayla Brown’s embellished gown by bridal experts Cassandra Renee. As the cheap-shot headlines tell you, the dress could have been created by an AI chatbot from a “Brownlow fashion” prompt: the racer back tank style left the sides wide open and left her back exposed, while the splits at the hem allowed for a flash of thigh. But what’s lost here is how great Brown looked. Stylist Meggy Smith kept the beauty and accessories minimal to let the dress shine (literally), drawing comparisons to celebrities like Zoë Kravitz at the 2021 Met Gala. 2. Bailey Smith Bailey Smith wearing a custom YSG Tailors tuxedo at the 2026 Brownlow. AFL Photos



Just like your perennially single louche uncle who always rocks up to the family function late, Bailey Smith waltzed onto the Brownlow red carpet just as it was wrapping up. Dressed in a bespoke YSG Tailors soft tan tuxedo with a peak lapel and oversized trouser, the Geelong midfielder chose to accessorise with a pair of reflective sunglasses. You wouldn’t know it from Smith’s refusal to adhere to a designated schedule, but he was more than fashionably prepared for the event, having not one look to choose from, but three. “We can have something nailed down in our first consultation, and within half an hour of me leaving the meeting Bailey will have sent me another two concepts,” says Ryan McIntyre, YSG Tailors co-founder and director. “Bailey definitely has input, but he’s not always 100 per cent sure what’s going to work,” McIntyre says. “He has to trust the process a little bit.” 3. Brooke Bailey Brooke Bailey in a Oglia-Loro Couture gown at the 2026 Brownlow. WireImage



Brooke Bailey’s Oglia-Loro Couture look started with the hand-beaded fringe tulle fabric that shimmied as she entered the gala with partner, the recently retired Dion Prestia. “I had a beautiful piece of hand-beaded tulle and Paul said, ‘I have someone who this is perfect for,’ says designer Sam Oglialoro, explaining the process of creating the sculpted, strapless gown with stylist, Paul Versace. “It’s giving that whole era of the naked dress,” Versace adds. 4. Paris Bishop Paris Bishop, partner of Sam Durham of the Bombers, in a jaw-dropping crystal gown by Alin Le’Kal. Getty Images



Fresh off the plane from LA, model and partner to Essendon player Sam Durham Paris Bishop seemed to glow as she floated down the Brownlow red carpet in her custom Alin Le’Kal outfit. Styled by Lana Wilkinson, the champagne-hued corset and fishtail skirt featured hand-beaded crystal embellishments designed to accentuate her complexion. “We wanted to have that little bit of an LA tizz through it, which I think suits the glow that she’s got going on,” says Le’Kal of the look that left a touch of skin exposed at Bishop’s lower back where the corset and skirt met. “At the Brownlow, the girls can go a bit sexier than the Logies or other red carpets. I wanted to really do that well.” 5. Chloe Serong Chloe Serong in a custom Atalie Studios gown at the 2026 Brownlow. Getty Images



Looking pretty in ombre pink, Chloe Serong opted for a striking Atalie Studios creation to accompany husband Fremantle Dockers star Caleb Serong. The strapless gown was one of the more creative to walk the carpet, with an architectural neckline and rectangle cut-out at the chest. The beading embellishments were hand-dyed to resemble the inside of a dark fruit – say, like a pomegranate or blackberry. “More people are looking for an escape into surrealism or fantasy through fashion,” says couturier Grace Presow. “So my approach to each design is very deeply strategic and imaginative.” Juicy, indeed! World.title: Prince Harry in talks to make Diana documentary
World.content:
WorldEuropePrince Harry Prince Harry in talks to make Diana documentary Victoria Ward and Hannah Furness September 22, 2026 — 11:35am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: Prince Harry is in talks to make a documentary about his mother, Diana, Princess of Wales. The London Telegraph understands that the Duke of Sussex wants to mark the 30th anniversary of Diana’s death, on August 31 next year, by honouring her legacy “in the most meaningful way”. Prince Harry appeared at the 2026 WellChild Awards in London on Monday night. Aaron Chown/Pool PA via AP He has approached several friends and relatives of his late mother, including her brother, Earl Spencer, to ask whether they would take part in a documentary. However, the earl, writing in his new memoir, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, said he chose to write the book to avoid being a “talking head” in one of many productions planned about his sister, fearing they would follow a “flawed” agenda.



Diana holds toddler Prince Harry during a visit to Spain in 1987. AP The earl made a series of claims in his book concerning the King, including disparaging remarks the latter is alleged to have made about the princess in the days after her death. The duke’s decision to make a personal documentary is likely to infuriate the Prince of Wales, who has silently endured high-profile revelations about his family life from his brother in recent years. A source close to Prince Harry told the Telegraph: “The duke has discussed a number of possible projects to mark the 30th anniversary of his mother Diana, Princess of Wales’s passing. “Nothing has been finalised or confirmed, and he is still considering the most meaningful way to honour her legacy during this important anniversary year.”



Such a program would be produced by the Sussexes’ Archewell Productions and would probably be bought by Netflix, which has a “first look” deal with Harry and Meghan. It will be viewed by some as a power move in the battle for the princess’s legacy. Kensington Palace has not commented on how Prince William might mark the anniversary. Nine years ago, the brothers joined forces to contribute to two documentaries about their mother to mark the 20th anniversary of her death, but such a collaboration now appears inconceivable. ‘The truth is difficult’ In writing his memoir, published on Tuesday, the earl, 62, ensured he was first out of the blocks in the latest race to tell his late sister’s story. He told The Telegraph it deserved to be told “honestly, however uncomfortable for others”.



He said: “I was an eyewitness to history, and where the truth is difficult, I haven’t shied away from it. Earl Spencer has made a series of disclosures about his sister and her troubled life ahead of his book publication. PA Images via Getty Images “I did not consult any members of my family about the content of the book, as I did not want to implicate them in my authorial decisions, or to be constrained by them. I hope readers will see the book for what it is: an honest account.” Neither Prince William nor Prince Harry were given any indication about the book’s contents. Similarly, the earl is not thought to have consulted his sisters, Lady Sarah McCorquodale and Lady Jane Fellowes, about their memories, choosing instead to create an entirely personal record. The official christening photo of Archie, the first son of Harry and Meghan.



The memoir has already prompted a fierce war of words with Buckingham Palace about comments attributed to the King, who was the Prince of Wales when Diana died in Paris aged 36. In the book, the earl claims that in the aftermath of her death, the King told him “rest assured, we’ll forget her soon enough”, and spoke to the earl with a “giddy tone”, like a “lottery winner”. The palace swiftly responded with a rare statement suggesting the earl’s memory was false. A spokesman said the King was “mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss”. Spencer (centre) walks behind Diana’s coffin at her 1997 funeral, flanked by (L-R) the late Prince Philip, Duke of Edinburgh, Prince William, Prince Harry and Charles, then-prince of Wales. Reuters The earl then accused the King of “gaslighting” him and being “astonishingly provocative”. In turn, royal sources accused the earl of “peddling what little remains” of the princess’s privacy and getting out his “crested carving knives” for the King.



Earl Spencer, who is expected to donate a portion of the memoir’s proceeds to charity, said he believed he had a duty to record his version of events. Related Article Royal family Harry and Meghan need protection to avoid Diana’s ordeal, Earl Spencer says He said: “Writing around Diana’s life has been heavily mythologised, and much of what’s been written about her has been notable for its inaccuracy. “The 30th anniversary of her death is approaching; I am in my 60s now, and I feel the passage of time more sharply than I once did. I don’t want to reach the end of my own life having left my sister’s story to be told by people who never knew her.” He added: “It is a personal account of my sister, Diana. It is not only her story, it is my story; a book which will stand the test of time.”



The earl continued: “As a historian, I believe Diana’s story deserves to be told honestly, however uncomfortable for others, and because silence has its own cost. I made the decision to write it a year ago, as I was being approached to take part in other people’s projects about her.” In his book, he revealed that he had declined “endless, repeated” requests to contribute to documentaries about the princess, including from “Diana’s biographer Andrew Morton, and from Tony Blair’s [former] spin doctor, Alastair Campbell”. He said he had decided to “tell things how I remember them” instead of following “an agenda set by some TV producer I will never meet”. The Duke and Duchess of Sussex are adjusting to life back in the UK after six years in the US. Instagram@Meghan On Monday evening, Prince Harry made his third public appearance since moving back to the UK, attending the annual WellChild Awards in central London. He ignored a series of questions about his family as he was whisked inside the Royal Lancaster Hotel.



The duke said there was “not a dry eye in the house” at the ceremony, which celebrates children living with complex medical needs and their families, who “give it everything they’ve got every single day”. Related Article Royal family Harry and Meghan’s battle to be accepted into Cotswolds high society He added: “To all the mums and dads – most of us will never truly know the emotional ups and downs of your day. But I sincerely hope that you take strength from nights like this. And while we may not know the detail of your day, in this room and beyond, we recognise the commitment of your care and all that comes with it.” Harry and William have both spoken publicly about their mother, and have given their daughters Diana as a middle name. Their wives, Meghan and Catherine, regularly wear jewellery she owned. However, Harry is more often associated with the princess through his own efforts to follow publicly in her footsteps. Last year, he visited Angola, where he was pictured walking through a minefield, just as his mother had in 1997.

World.title: Tarakihi catch limits reduce to 10 per person nationwide
World.content:
Fisheries Minister Shane Jones says tarakihi catch limits will be reduced, with a nationwide recreational fishing limit of 10 per person.

Commercial limits for the eastern fishery are being reduced by 20 percent, and the western fishery by 55 percent.

Jones said he has considered the latest science and catch information, uncertainty about future stocks of young fish, and the effects of use of the fishery in making the decision.

"These measures will immediately reduce fishing pressure on these tarakihi stocks and put them on more positive trajectories, while allowing a lower level of fishing to continue.

Limits have been increased for snapper and trevally on the North Island's east coast, leatherjacket on the South Island's east and south coast, and frostfish and blue mackerel in deep water.

Fisheries Minister Shane Jones. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Butterfish catch limits have also been reduced, with a five-per-person recreational limit.

Seafood NZ chief executive Lisa Futschek said the quota management system was working as intended.

"This process matters. Sustainable fisheries management isn't about catch limits remaining static; it is about making changes when the evidence shows they are needed."

The company's general manager for inshore fisheries Tiff Bock said they supported decisions to ensure tarakihi stocks continued to rebuild.

"Industry has been actively rebuilding east coast tarakihi since 2018 through catch reductions, avoidance measures, gear changes, improved monitoring and significant investment in research. We remain committed to rebuilding the stocks."

Catch limit changes:

Inshore

Snapper, increase - SNA 2 - East Cape, Hawke's Bay, and Wellington

Trevally, increase - TRE 2 - East Cape, Hawke's Bay, and Wellington

Leatherjacket, increase - LEA 3 - east coast South Island, Southland

East Coast tarakihi, decrease - TAR 1E, 2, 3, 7E - east coasts North and South Island

West Coast tarakihi, decrease - TAR 1W, 7W, 8 - West coasts North and South Island

Stargazer, decrease - STA 7 - West Coast and top of the South Island

Butterfish, decrease - BUT 7 - West Coast and top of the South Island

Shortfin eel, decrease - SFE 13 - Te Waihora (Lake Ellesmere)

Elephant fish, decrease - ELE 3 and 5 - east coast South Island, Southland, and Sub-Antarctic

Ling, decrease - LIN 1 - Northland, Auckland, Waikato, and Bay of Plenty

Pāua, decrease - PAU 5D - Southland and Otago

Deepwater

Blue mackerel, increase - EMA 7 - west coast North Island, West Coast South Island

Gemfish, increase - SKI 3 - east coast South Island, Chatham Islands

World.title: Middlemore Hospital staff declare healthcare 'crisis'
World.content:
More than 200 healthcare professionals at Auckland's Middlemore Hospital have signed a letter warning they are in a crisis, calling on Health New Zealand to prioritise patient and staff safety.

Health New Zealand told RNZ it was reviewing the concerns raised by staff, noting that patient safety and staff wellbeing were the organisation's highest priorities.

The letter from Middlemore Hospital staff backs a state of emergency recently declared by workers at North Shore Hospital's emergency department and raises concerns about chronic understaffing, overcrowding and staff being asked to work while sick.

"We are in a crisis," the letter says.

It comes after nurses in Middlemore Hospital's emergency department told RNZ they had been asked to come to work despite calling in sick.

The healthcare workers say the requests are putting both staff and patients at risk and are a consequence of chronic understaffing.

"When we call to advise we are unfit to work, we do not expect to be coerced, bullied or emotionally blackmailed into working," the letter says.

"Recently, staff working in the Middlemore emergency department are being asked to come into work sick.

"This endangers the safety and wellbeing of both staff and the patients we see and is a disturbing consequence of the chronic short staffing we have been expected to work through. This increase in risk was predictable and completely avoidable."

The workers say the emergency department regularly operates over capacity, at times reaching about 400 patient representations when its capacity is 150.

"This winter, Middlemore emergency department has routinely operated at 200 percent over capacity, peaking closer to 250 percent over capacity at times," the letter says.

They claim the situation is being driven by a recruitment freeze and chronic understaffing.

The letter also says the conditions breach workers' rights under their employment agreements, as well as the rights of workers and patients in the Emergency Department under the Health and Safety at Work Act 2015.

"We are exhausted, burnt out and we and our families are carrying the burden that should sit with Te Whatu Ora. Our immune systems are compromised, and we are more likely to be unwell," the letter says.

"We cannot continue to simply accept this when the consequences are patients being exposed to preventable harm. Or accept continued breaches of our rights to safe work."

The healthcare workers are calling on Health New Zealand to act immediately.

One of their demands is the recruitment of 40 additional nursing full-time equivalent positions they claim have already been identified through the Care Capacity Demand Management process without further delay.

They also want Health New Zealand to commit to culturally appropriate nurse-to-patient ratios that reflect patient acuity and demand.

Another demand is for Health New Zealand to stop asking staff to work while sick.

Anne Daniels, president of New Zealand Nurses Organisation Supplied

New Zealand Nurses Organisation president Anne Daniels said the collective letter suggested that healthcare workers had exhausted other options.

"This public letter is a very, very clear declaration that none of the things that are supposed to work in terms of going through the system have worked and they've been left with no choice," Daniels said.

She said it was "extremely heartbreaking" to see the situation at Middlemore Hospital, describing it as being the direct result of "deliberate underfunding" of the health system.

Daniels said the government and nursing employers needed to focus on filling nursing gaps, and that the workforce could do little about staffing levels other than demand that vacancies be filled.

"The accountability is with the government and employers," she said.

Daniels said no nurse should be coerced into working if they were sick.

Earlier this month, nurses at Middlemore Hospital told RNZ they had been asked to work despite calling in sick.

"When I called the [hospital] sick line, they told me to take paracetamol and come to work," one nurse told RNZ.

Another nurse said they had been asked to wear an N95 mask and come to work.

Daniels said such practices were unacceptable.

"The nurses are choosing to do the right thing and stay away from work," she said.

"If they are being threatened or if they feel that they're being coerced, they must come to the union, and we will stand up with them and beside them and push back on this because it is totally unacceptable."

Vanessa Thornton, group director of operations for Counties Manukau, told RNZ that patient safety and staff wellbeing were Health New Zealand's highest priorities.

"We are reviewing the concerns raised by staff, including those relating to workload, capacity and workforce pressures, and are engaging with clinical, operational and nursing leaders, alongside staff representatives, to better understand the issues and identify any actions required," Thornton said.

"We remain focused on maintaining safe care for patients while supporting the wellbeing of our staff."

Thornton said Health New Zealand did not expect staff who were unwell to attend work, and managers were expected to support staff to stay home when sick.

She said Middlemore Hospital's emergency department continued to experience high demand and that staffing requirements, workforce needs and service capacity were regularly reviewed to ensure the hospital could provide safe, high-quality care.

RNZ asked Health New Zealand whether Middlemore Hospital's emergency department was currently understaffed, how many nursing FTE vacancies remained and whether it would recruit the 40 nursing FTEs requested by staff.

"We remain committed to recruiting into vacant roles and supporting our frontline teams," Thornton said.

She said Health New Zealand took its obligations under employment and health and safety legislation seriously and would continue working closely with staff and their representatives to address the concerns raised.

"We recognise the significant pressure our emergency department teams have faced over winter, and we thank staff for their ongoing commitment to caring for patients and whānau," Thornton said.

World.title: Labour rejects claims of hypocrisy around its interest deductibility policy
World.content:
Audio player for " Labour leader Chris Hipkins discusses landlord tax decision " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/politics_election-2026/1519045%2Flabour-rejects-claims-of-hypocrisy-around-its-interest-deductibility-policy

Labour leader Chris Hipkins discusses landlord tax decision Morning Report Download MP3 9m

Labour is defending against claims of hypocrisy around its policy on interest deductibility, saying the party is simply maintaining the status quo.

National says the party is being "slippery" and the promise not to reverse the changes cannot be trusted.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins' claims that the move had been foreshadowed as early as last October appear to be in doubt.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6405391480112

Speaking to reporters after the prime minister's post-Cabinet media briefing on Monday, he ruled out changes to interest deductibility, which currently allows landlords to claim tax deductions for the interest on their residential investment properties.

He later confirmed to reporters that stance had been backed by the full Labour caucus, and pushed back at suggestions of mistruth being "just ridiculous".

"We said at the time that before the election we would make a final decision around interest deductibility. That's exactly what we've done."

Finance Spokesperson Barbara Edmonds said the announcement of the capital gains tax meant "the settings have changed, and we have changed our decision".

Government cries foul

National leader Christopher Luxon said Labour could not be trusted on tax, giving the example that Chris Hipkins had said in a debate at the last election the party was not committing to a capital gains tax "and now he's doing a CGT".

"Think about who he's going to be in business with if he ever gets there with Chlöe Swarbrick and Opportunity Party, I mean, like honestly, it's just they spent three years attacking us on a landlord tax and blaming everything on ... cuts for landlords, as they keep saying.

"Hipkins cannot be trusted on tax. Period. I mean, this is a guy that stood up in a debate and said, 'I will not introduce a CGT in my time,' and lo and behold, he wants to introduce a CGT".

National's finance spokesperson Nicola Willis said Labour's rule-out could not be believed "when every interview I've been with a Labour MP over the past few years they've railed against that policy.

"Chris Hipkins is slippery and unreliable, and frankly hypocritical," she said.

On whether that stance had been foreshadowed, she said "of course it wasn't ... what's been foreshadowed is Labour constantly saying that one of the reasons the cost of living has been challenging in New Zealand is our policy on interest deductibility".

Campaign chair Simeon Brown said Labour had changed its position at the 11th hour, and "I think they're acting out of desperation".

Frontbencher Chris Bishop said it was "humiliating, and I think you can't trust these guys on it, and anyone who believes they actually won't reintroduce interest deductibility changes, I think, is dreaming. They will."

ACT leader David Seymour said Hipkins was "clearly doing a bit of a Captain Panic-pants this election, and if I was responsible for his portfolio of policies and ideas, I'd be panicking too".

'Foreshadowing' claims dubious

On Monday, Hipkins said the party "did foreshadow when we announced a capital gains tax that that was changing our thinking around how we would look at interest deductibility in the future".

He doubled down under questioning from Morning Report host John Campbell on Tuesday.

"You should have been at the press conference where we answered quite a range of questions on it, John, where we said we'd make a final decision around how to treat interest deductibility before the election, but that it would change because of the introduction of a capital gains tax," he said.

However, a transcript of that announcement shows just one question on interest deductibility, with Hipkins saying "we'll set out any additional or any other changes around tax closer to the election".

Edmonds at the time laid out separate deductibility measures - improvements to a home would be exempt from a CGT, and she was yet to decide on depreciation.

She also said that if property owners "move away from revenue account property, they won't be able to deduct expenses".

Other than that, no mention was made of interest deductibility rules during the nearly one hour media conference.

Edmonds on Tuesday said at the time, the party had still been considering "holding costs".

"That's what they're called in the tax technical world. So if you look back to the tax working group, it did recommend that holding costs such as rates, insurance, interest costs should be deductible."

She said it was a "timing issue" and the matter had been under consideration since October.

The policy document includes one line stating that "as per the Tax Working Group recommendations, holding costs like rates and interest are not deductible from the capital gain".

They said the reason it had been announced before the pre-election economic and fiscal update due out this week was that the decision had been made.

Labour has been pushing back on questions about how much its policy to rule out fuel tax increases for the next three years would cost, and Edmonds said the difference there was that "interest deductibility is already in the books, so we know what the cost is".

World.title: Senior official appearing to try hide information being taken 'very seriously'
World.content:
The Ombudsman and Public Service Commissioner are looking into a senior official seemingly trying to "subvert" the Official Information Act, the Education Minister says.

Leaked footage given to the New Zealand Herald shows senior Ministry of Education official Catherine Law telling staff not to put information shared with the minister's office in writing and reminding them it was "OIA-able" - referencing the Official Information Act.

Speaking to media, Erica Stanford said she was confident her Secretary of Education had the situation "in hand".

"She's already talked to the Public Service Commission, she's already talked to the Ombudsman, and she's already looking into the matter and taking it very seriously, as I expect that she would do."

Education Minister Erica Stanford. RNZ / Mark Papalii

Stanford denied instructing officials to subvert the OIA process.

"We take our obligations extremely seriously, and as I said, this is a matter for the Secretary of Education and her staff.

"My political staff and I have not seen the documents that she was talking about."

Asked if there was a culture where officials were trying to hide information so they did not embarrass her, Stanford said she hoped "that's not the case".

"I've always made sure that the Secretary of Education understands that we are abiding by the Official Information Act, and I've made that clear again yesterday."

Labour leader and former education minister Chris Hipkins said circumventing transparency laws was "inexcusable".

"Ultimately, ministers sign off the curriculum so there's there's nothing that should be secret here.

"There should be a transparent process around that, and trying to circumvent that so that you can make edits to the curriculum without anybody knowing that's what you're doing seems bizarre, secretive, and just inexcusable." he said.

World.title: Stocktake of IT projects at MBIE finds some deficiencies in controls
World.content:
A stocktake of half a billion dollars of IT projects at MBIE sparked by a bungled immigration initiative the ministry misled MPs about has found some deficiencies in controls.

But the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment says it is assured its broader technology portfolio was "operating as intended" and reassured there were "no surprises" in the findings.

The newly released stocktake was done in July and released on Monday after an immigration project bungle that cost taxpayers at least $39 million.

"I am reassured by the fact that there were no surprises in these findings, but there are some things we can do better," said deputy secretary of corporate and digital shared services Paul Stocks in a statement.

Covering 70 projects, the stocktake found core oversight and control were generally in place but too patchy.

Among the 31 bigger projects that have to have formal controls, nine rated a negative 'red', six a less-bad 'amber', 15 'green' or OK - and one has been shut down.

The stocktake recommended fixes to be in place by the end of the month and MBIE says they are, and it was working on more.

"Over the next year, we will strengthen central oversight, improve technology investment capability and reporting, and clarify accountability across our technology portfolio," Stocks said.

The stocktake done by the ministry and checked by an outside consultant said all the IT initiatives were operating within the right Cabinet, Treasury and ministerial approval and delegation limits.

It found "good practices" throughout the portfolio with a majority of projects having effective controls, clear governance and robust reporting back.

"However, variability exists in how project progress is measured, aggregated and reported."

This plus some old ways of presenting information made it difficult to monitor some of them compared to others.

The finances were mostly reported on properly but in limited instances "reduced financial transparency" and weaknesses in how the expected benefits from an IT project were assessed, made it harder to keep track and ensure a project was affordable.

A quarter of projects were behind on delivery and the rest largely on track.

"Inconsistencies in reporting, financial transparency, benefits management, portfolio classification and governance visibility reduce confidence in the extent to which emerging delivery concerns are consistently identified, escalated, understood and acted upon."

A small number of more complex projects - three of them are worth over $20m each, though 39 were small and under $250,000 each - already had greater assessment controls in place, the nine-page stocktake said.

World.title: Labour candidate Warrick Cleine withdraws nomination
World.content:
A top Labour candidate has withdrawn from the election, with the party leader saying his circumstances have changed.

Last week, Chris Hipkins said Vietnam-based Warrick Cleine who was ranked 30 on Labour's list, was intending to relocate to New Zealand for the election campaign.

Supplied

"He'll certainly be joining us on the campaign trail in New Zealand," Hipkins said last Monday about Cleine who is the chief executive of consulting firm KPMG's Vietnam and Cambodia division.

Hipkins said Cleine had indicated he would move back to New Zealand when he put his name forward for selection for the Labour Party.

Asked again about Cleine on Tuesday this week, Hipkins said Cleine was no longer able to commit to the campaign, so had withdrawn his nomination.

"I understand that," Hipkins said, adding that he respected the decision.

"My understanding is that when he put his name forward, he was intending to come back to New Zealand to campaign, he's no longer in a position to do that, and so he's withdrawn his candidacy."

Hipkins rejected the suggestion Cleine may have been calculating his chances of getting into parliament according to recent polls. He also rejected Labour had been mucked around by the decision.

World.title: Formula 1 agrees to shorter races in 2027
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Formula 1 has approved a 15 kilometre reduction in official race distances starting next season.

The change means the total distance will be cut from 305 to 290 kilometres.

The Formula 1 Commission finalised the decision in London.

"In line with the refinements to the power unit regulations to be introduced in 2027 on fuel flow, a reduction in the total race distance from 305km to 290km was approved, corresponding to a reduction of two or three laps," a statement read.

Aussie F1 GP loses season-opening honour Melbourne's Australian Grand Prix will not have the privilege of opening the 2027 Formula 1 season, but it will boast two races in its biggest weekend yet.

The power unit regulations favour increased engine power over hybrid electrical output.

To better handle rain delays and red flags, the commission has also abolished the strict three-hour overall event cap.

While the two-hour maximum of active racing time remains, the change gives organisers flexibility to complete full race distances.

Another objective ‌is to give spectators the best possible chance ‌to enjoy a full race when disruptions occur.

Practice sessions will also gain added flexibility to extend following stoppages.

AP/Reuters

World.title: Lions 'praying' Neale gets off but confident they will cope if ban stands
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Brisbane Lions players are confident they can cover the potential absence of Lachie Neale in the grand final, with the two-time Brownlow medallist facing a one-match ban.

Neale and the Lions will challenge the suspension at the AFL tribunal on Tuesday evening.

The 33-year-old has been charged with striking Hawthorn's Jack Ginnivan in last Saturday night's preliminary final.

Neale facing grand final ban The Lions will contest a one-match suspension handed to Lachie Neale, which would rule the two-time premiership captain out of the AFL grand final.

If the suspension is upheld, Neale will miss Saturday's grand final against Fremantle at the MCG.

Lions teammate Jarrod Berry said it would be a blow to lose Neale.

But he said the Lions were equipped to overcome any adversity.

"One of our best traits is being able to deal with that [adversity]," Berry said.

"We do it well and there's no point putting energy into it until we know the result.

"We'll be sitting tight and praying that he gets off. But if he doesn't, we'll face it when it comes."

Neale's gut punch on Ginnivan was graded as intentional conduct, medium impact and body contact by match review officer Michael Christian.

There is damning vision showing Neale guilty of the behind-play strike and numerous precedents this season of other players being banned for one match for similar incidents.

But the Lions are set to argue the suspension should be downgraded to a fine.

They will cite a fresh clause that allowed Collingwood great Scott Pendlebury to avoid a suspension in March.

Clause that could save Neale The Brisbane Lions will challenge Neale's one-game suspension for striking Hawthorn's Jack Ginnivan in last Saturday night's preliminary final.

Pendlebury was given a one-match ban for rough conduct for a bump on Adelaide's Josh Worrell.

He was found guilty by the tribunal but the sanction was downgraded to a $3,000 fine due to "compelling and exceptional circumstances", a clause open to the tribunal that will be central to Neale's case.

The relevant clause states: "Players will not automatically receive a reduced sanction for a good record.

"However, if a classifiable offence is contested or referred to the tribunal, a player with an exemplary record may argue that their good record constitutes exceptional and compelling circumstances."

The Magpies successfully argued the clause applied to Pendlebury, who had never previously faced the tribunal in his storied 21-year career.

Neale also has not previously appeared before the tribunal in his 320-match career.

He is also a dual Brownlow medallist and premiership captain, plus a four-time All Australian.

Geelong coach Chris Scott does not agree with the provision.

"Seriously, when we're starting to say, 'There's a rule for you because you've done good things for the game,' it's almost implying that other people haven't done a good job," Scott said on Fox Footy.

But Scott added: "I know his record is exceptional, but aside from that, I just like to see them play.

"I actually think that's going to be hard to defend personally, but my hope is that he does play."

AAP

World.title: Banned Swan falls well short in Brownlow Medal vote
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

The AFL has avoided the unwanted scenario of one of Sydney's suspended players winning the Brownlow Medal, with Isaac Heeney finishing outside the count's top five.

The league had a contingency plan in place if Heeney had won the game's highest individual honour.

But Nick Daicos's record-breaking number of votes, and prolific polling from Bailey Smith and Marcus Bontempelli, meant the plan never needed to come into play.

Daicos wins first Brownlow Nick Daicos breaks Patrick Cripps's record in the 3-2-1 voting era by winning the first Brownlow Medal of his career.

Heeney, and Swans teammates Chad Warner and Nick Blakey were among the notable absences from Monday night's awards ceremony.

Along with Riley Bice and James Jordon, they have been absent from Sydney's headquarters since being suspended by the club in August.

The five were stood down for breaching club standards following a post-match incident at the Pullman Hotel in East Melbourne.

Those suspensions are separate to a police investigation into sexual assault allegations, with Victoria Police flagging an update is not expected until late October.

No charges have been laid and the ABC is not suggesting any wrongdoing on the part of the five suspended players.

Daicos rewrites history with Brownlow win Nick Daicos's stardom has always had an inevitability to it, and his maiden Brownlow Medal triumph is the latest example of him fulfilling his immense promise.

The five players were ruled ineligible for All-Australian honours and were not invited to the Brownlow Medal function in Melbourne.

But they remained eligible for the award.

Brodie Grundy, Charlie Curnow, Dane Rampe, Logan McDonald and Tom McCartin were among those on hand for the Swans.

Once the count started, Heeney was the only player considered a genuine contender.

Heeney did not poll until round four, when he landed two votes, and claimed three votes against Gold Coast in Gather Round.

Warner polled for the first time in round four, while Blakey claimed three votes in round six.

Heeney claimed three consecutive three-vote performances to rise into the top four of the count at one point.

But his best performances were not enough to come close to Daicos's record-setting mark of 47 votes.

Heeney finished equal-eighth on 26 votes, ahead of teammate Errol Gulden (17), who ended the season with five consecutive best-afield performances.

AAP

World.title: Brownlow simply latest chapter as Daicos continues rewriting AFL history
World.content:
When Nathan Buckley's decade-long tenure as Collingwood coach came to an end midway through 2021, there was a silver lining for the club amid the painful exit of the club legend.

Buckley's tenure had seen the Pies flirt with winning a premiership in 2018 and 2019 before ultimately failing, but by the time he wrapped up, Collingwood seemed well out of the premiership window.

The silver lining came in the form of a player who was yet to set foot on an AFL field: Nick Daicos, then a teenager touted as a generational prospect years before he was eligible to be drafted.

Daicos wins first Brownlow Medal and sets new modern-day voting record Nick Daicos breaks Patrick Cripps's record in the 3-2-1 voting era by winning the first Brownlow Medal of his career.

The AFL world was no stranger to the Daicos surname due to the exploits of Nick's famous father, Peter, who was immortalised at Collingwood as a member of the club's 1990 premiership side.

You did not need to be a Collingwood fanatic to know about Nick Daicos. Everyone around the game knew the kid was on his way because of his prolific exploits at the junior levels.

The weight of expectation that comes with the level of hype Daicos had as a draft prospect can prove crippling. Unfortunately, years of evidence support this.

Sometimes even the most hyped prospects can take time to fit into the AFL system, and it makes sense. These are boys coming to a man's game.

The more rigorous training regimes, expanded playbooks, media commitments, dietary requirements, and everything else that comes with being an AFL player can be too much. That is even before we get to the pace of the game being completely different.

Nick Daicos with his parents. (Getty Images / AFL Photos: Michael Willson)

That hasn't been the case with Daicos, who, as an audacious Nike advert claimed on the morning of the Brownlow count, has proven it inevitable from day one.

From his first game, Daicos showed an ability to bend the game to his will in ways not seen in teenagers, and we have all been blessed to witness it.

Daicos's arrival helped catapult Collingwood from second-last in 2021 to fourth in his first season in the AFL.

Collingwood fell one point short of a grand final appearance in Daicos's debut season, but went all the way in his second.

After collecting boatloads of the football across halfback while occasionally dipping his toes in the midfield as a rookie, Daicos supercharged the Pies engine room in 2023, helping them claim the flag, and he has not looked back since.

Daicos helped propel Collingwood to a premiership in just his second season in the AFL. (AFL Photos via Getty Images: Dylan Burns)

From very early on in Daicos's career, the Brownlow win appeared to be a question of when rather than if, but it was the one accolade he was frustratingly made to wait on.

Daicos followed up his premiership by polling a ridiculous 38 votes in 2024, the most by any player in the league's history up until that point, only for that year's winner, Patrick Cripps, to poll 45.

Last year, he was again a seemingly unbackable favourite before being stunned by Gold Coast's Matt Rowell.

Missing out on a Brownlow after being among the favourites for a few years can be something that follows you.

Marcus Bontempelli, despite being widely considered the best player of his generation, has yet to win the prestigious medal.

Bulldogs star Marcus Bontempelli's career is an example of just how hard Brownlow Medals are to come by. (Getty Images: Michael Willson)

Buckley was famously made to wait year after year before eventually breaking through in 2003, his 11th season, while Gary Ablett Jr was even denied by his own teammate before his maiden Brownlow triumph. It is almost a rite of passage if you're an all-timer.

Despite Bontempelli, Zak Butters and Bailey Smith all challenging him at various points during the count, Daicos would not be denied this year.

Almost in revenge for the previous two seasons, this year, Daicos turned in an individual season that would ultimately prove impossible to ignore for the umpires.

Daicos broke Cripps's record with 47 votes and set a few more records along the way.

He is now the only player in league history to poll over 30 votes in three consecutive seasons, the only player to put together six straight three-vote games, and the only player to put together 13 three-vote games in a single season.

Daicos celebrates his Brownlow triumph with his parents after the count. (Getty Images: Morgan Hancock)

Given the ease with which Daicos has played from his first contest in the AFL four seasons ago, it was surprising to talk about the weight of expectation actually weighing on him after winning his elusive first Brownlow.

You get the sense that the weight of expectation might be the only thing that is capable of slowing him down, because efforts from his AFL counterparts to do so have so far proven futile.

For a player so metronomic and seemingly superhuman on the field, it was refreshing to hear Daicos admit he too deals with nerves and struggles with criticism, just like the rest of us.

Daicos admitted to the Brownlow win being a relief after being denied for so many years as a favourite, even saying he had given up trusting in betting markets.

Daicos is likely to put together more dominant seasons now that the weight of winning a Brownlow is no more. (Getty Images: Daniel Carson)

Now that the Brownlow box has been ticked off, it is frightening to think of what an unburdened Daicos could potentially achieve.

Still just 23 years of age, Daicos has gone from being the precocious youngster to one of Collingwood's veterans, and he will act as the bridge from one era of Collingwood premiership contention to the next, just as Scott Pendlebury did.

He seems good enough to single-handedly wrench Collingwood's premiership window open for as long as he wants.

Daicos has the chance to eclipse Scott Pendlebury (right) as Collingwood's greatest-ever player. (Getty Images: Morgan Hancock)

Adding premierships to his 2023 triumph will be at the top of Daicos's to-do list, and the hope will be that in the process of achieving that goal, his resume ultimately becomes undeniable.

The chance to be Collingwood's greatest player is in play. The chance to be the greatest player in league history is as well, as premature as that shout may seem.

The records Daicos set with his maiden Brownlow win will eventually be just another footnote for a player who is poised to rewrite the game's history books.

Like the commercial said: inevitable.

World.title: Thirteen-year-old surfer breaking records as first Indigenous world champ
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Leihani Zoric almost didn't compete in El Salvador, but now the 13-year-old is the youngest International Surfing Association (ISA) Under 18 World Junior Champion in history.

"When I went over there, I was extremely sick," Zoric told ABC Weekend Breakfast.

"I wasn't even going to go, my mum and dad were like, 'Leihani don't go, you're that sick'."

But the teenager was committed.

"I was like, 'no, I'm going to go. I believe that I can go all the way'," she told her parents.

And all the way she went, using visualisation to help her through.

"I wrote it down about 1,000 times [and] I said to myself, 'I'm going to become this year's Under 18 ISA gold medallist'," Zoric said.

"So, when it happened, I was like, oh my God, this is crazy."

Zoric, from Byron Bay in northern NSW, is the youngest ever surfer to win the ISA Under 18 World Championship. (Supplied: Surfing Australia)

Across more than a week of competition, Zoric was part of a 12-strong Australian team that went head-to-head with the world's best junior surfers.

She competed three age divisions above her own, to take out the title.

"It feels amazing," Zoric said.

"I'm really proud of myself for all my hard work and effort I've put in, and all the people that have helped me along the way."

It comes after a stand-out year so far, which includes winning the Junior Girls and Open Women's divisions at the 2026 Indigenous Surfing Titles.

She's now back home not only as a World Champion, but a history maker.

And she's taking it all in her stride, with a maturity that's beyond her years.

"I'm just so grateful to have been able to go to El Salvador and represent my culture and my country as best as I can," she said.

Loading Instagram content

Creating a proud history

Zoric, from Byron Bay in northern New South Wales, is also the first Indigenous world champion surfer at any level.

"I'm really proud to have represented my Yued mob over in Western Australia," she said.

"We have such important history in our culture and I feel like [that] has really shaped me as a person."

Zoric first got a feel for surfing at two days old, when her dad put her on a surfboard in the shallows at Broken Head.

From then on, she just loved the water.

Thirteen-year-old Zoric has had a stellar year, also winning the Open Women's division at the 2026 Indigenous Surfing Titles. (Supplied: Surfing Australia)

She takes inspiration from Soli Bailey, the first pro surfer to compete under the Aboriginal flag in the World Surfing League, and Cathy Freeman.

"Having those people inspire me has definitely made me want to be like them one day," she said.

Along with looking up to others, Zoric wants to be a positive role model herself.

When she's not in the water, she's busy creating connection, with things like Lei's Lu'au, a community day celebrating girls and women in surfing.

Loading Instagram content

"I hope that I inspire, not just as an athlete, but being a good person and always caring about others, being encouraging and just having a positive attitude all the time," she said.

"Bringing people up and lifting their spirits and attitudes and just [making] them feel like they belong here in this world.

"Because everybody is important and special in their own unique ways."

Locana Cullen (Under 16 men's) and Lucy Darragh (Under 16 women's) also claimed individual golds at the World Junior Championships, with Australia winning three out of the four divisions.

The Australians also won their third consecutive team gold at the event.

World.title: NRL set to axe ref Klein after controversial semifinal ending
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

The NRL is reportedly set to axe top referee Ashley Klein for the preliminary finals after admitting the Warriors were wrongly denied a crucial late penalty in their 12-10 semifinal loss to Newcastle.

NRL officials today confirmed the Warriors should have been awarded a penalty for an escort infringement by the Knights' Tyson Frizell with a minute left in yesterday's Eden Park thriller.

Had the penalty been awarded, the Warriors would have had the chance to level at 12-12 via a penalty goal from just to the side of the posts and send the match to extra time.

NRL investigating Eden Park incident The NRL is threatening to ban spectators who threw projectiles at referee Ashley Klein, with the league's integrity unit investigating the aftermath of Sunday's semifinal in Auckland.

But the call was instead missed on the field, with the bunker unable to review the play, despite a stoppage for an injury soon afterwards.

A comprehensive NRL review of Newcastle's 12-10 semifinal did, however, back the bunker over two other contentious calls.

First, it was deemed that bunker official Chris Butler was right to rule that Warriors centre Ali Leiataua got a thumb to a ball before it went to ground late in the match.

The NRL also supported the bunker's decision to stick with the on-field call of a strip against Warrior Te Maire Martin.

But it is the non-call on Frizell that will annoy the Warriors most.

The Newcastle veteran appeared to get in the way of Leka Halasima as he chased through on a kick in the Warriors' last attacking raid.

Given the seconds that would have come off the clock while the Warriors lined up the shot, there would probably not have been time for a restart.

"I thought they were trying to find ways to take it off us," Warriors coach Andrew Webster said after the game.

Projectiles thrown at ref as Knights win Projectiles have been thrown at the NRL refereeing crew following Newcastle's upset semifinal win over the New Zealand Warriors.

"The last one, two points would have drawn the game, he is going across Leka, pretending to try and catch the ball which they've told us you can't do."

AAP understands Klein will pay for the error by losing his spot in the preliminary finals, with Grant Atkins or Gerard Sutton likely to be called up.

Klein has overseen every game of the past five State of Origin series and two of the last four grand finals.

He had been expected to referee last year's decider, before losing out to Atkins following 18 penalties in a Melbourne-Cronulla preliminary final.

Meanwhile, the NRL have threatened bans for fans who threw projectiles at Klein as he walked off Eden Park on Sunday night.

Vision showed a mass of bottles and rubbish being thrown at the long-time official, with Warriors great Shaun Johnson labelling the fans' behaviour "embarrassing".

AAP

World.title: Daicos wins first Brownlow Medal and sets voting record
World.content:
Collingwood superstar Nick Daicos has finally claimed his first Brownlow Medal in a runaway victory with a record-breaking 47 votes.

The 23-year-old surged to a perfect nine votes from his first three games, led from round 11, then registered six consecutive best-on-ground performances between rounds 15 and 20 to seal victory by round 21.

Daicos won the AFL's greatest individual honour from Geelong star Bailey Smith (36) and Western Bulldogs champion Marcus Bontempelli (34).

The Magpie had 13 three-vote performances and beat the previous votes record of 45 set by Carlton champion Patrick Cripps in 2024.

Daicos, the son of Magpies great Peter Daicos, conceded he was relieved, having finally prevailed after runner-up finishes in the past two seasons, a third placing in 2023 and an eighth place in his debut year of 2022.

"I've just learned not to trust the the betting markets, to be honest," Daicos said at Monday night's vote count.

"But no, there is (relief).

"It's a massive award, and I'm so privileged to be up here. And yeah, I can't believe I'm a Brownlow medallist, to be honest."

The dynamic midfielder had already snared the AFL Players Association and AFL Coaches Association player-of-the-year awards this season.

It was the fourth consecutive year that Daicos was favourite, and with the umpires able to consult statistics for the first time, the star Magpie was irresistible.

Nick Daicos and partner Arlette Amor. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

Daicos averaged 34.9 disposals, 5.7 clearances, 6.7 inside-50s and 1.1 goals.

The brilliant playmaker was edged out by Gold Coast's Matt Rowell last year and Cripps the year before, when Daicos polled 38 votes.

Daicos, the Collingwood vice-captain who's widely expected to be named skipper next season, is the club's first Brownlow medallist since Dane Swan in 2011.

Bontempelli and Smith were the next best performers ahead of Melbourne skipper Max Gawn (28), Brisbane star Will Ashcroft (27), Carlton's two-time winner Patrick Cripps (27) and North Melbourne's Harry Sheezel (27).

Port Adelaide superstar Zak Butters, set to join Bontempelli at the Bulldogs next season, was among the contenders before his late-season ankle injury and finished on 26.

Sydney's Charlie Curnow, Collingwood's Nick Daicos, Geelong's Bailey Smith and Collingwood's Josh Daicos. (Getty Images: Michael Wilson/AFL Photos)

Banned Sydney stars Isaac Heeney and Chad Warner weren't in the room as they polled 26 and 12 votes respectively.

Brisbane's Conor McKenna won goal of the year while Hawthorn dynamo Nick Watson was awarded mark of the year.

AAP

Tech.title: A cut cable disrupted hundreds of flights across the US
Tech.content:
is a senior editor who has obsessed over headlines and internet speeds since 2011. He previously worked as an advocate for the National Park System.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Hundreds of flights were cancelled or delayed on Monday after construction crews in New Jersey accidentally cut a Verizon fiber cable used for air traffic control.

FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said that a circuit failure led to the discovery of the severed fiber cable, ABC News reports. The outage hammered airports across the Northeast, causing ground stops at all three major New York City airports.

In a statement to CNBC, Verizon said that it bore “no responsibility for this incident,” putting the blame on “construction contractors working in the area” that “dug up and cut our cable.”

Ironically, it looks like trains make have taken out the planes, but fingers are still being pointed. US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said an Amtrak crew accidentally cut the line, but AP reports that Amtrak blames a New Jersey Transit crew for the disruption. “This incident occurred on New Jersey Transit property and involved a New Jersey Transit contractor,” an Amtrak spokesperson told NBC4.

As of Monday evening, Duffy said that “the telecom lines have been repaired, and all airport operations in the Northeast are resuming,” but cautioned that it will take “some time to clear all existing delays.” According to FlightAware, there were over 1,000 canceled flights today in the US

Tech.title: Amazon wants to help the Colorado River, but we still don’t know how much water the company uses
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Amazon plans to spend $20 million on water conservation projects along the Colorado River, a crucial but dwindling water supply for 40 million people in the Western US.

The initiative comes as Amazon and other tech companies face mounting scrutiny over how much water their data centers use. Amazon has a goal of becoming water positive — replenishing more water than it uses — by the end of the decade. It recently disclosed some information about its water use, but we still have an incomplete picture of the company’s impact as a whole.

Amazon announced the launch of a Colorado River Basin Collaborative today, with a mission to “create one of the biggest corporate water conservation efforts for a single U.S. watershed.” It expects to raise $100 million over two years — including the $20 million investment from its own coffers — for water conservation efforts.

The Colorado River brings water to 40 million people

Stretching 1,400 miles, the Colorado River brings water to 40 million people across seven states in the Western US and and two states in Mexico. The waterway has faced “unprecedented” drought over the last 26 years, according to the US Bureau of Reclamation. Decades of overuse on top of human-caused climate change have exacerbated the problem. To cope, the US Department of the Interior finalized a plan in August imposing steep water cuts on Arizona, Nevada, and California.

As the first stop for most goods the US imports from Asia, California is home to more Amazon warehouses than any other state. In Orange County, California, Amazon pledged $2.2 million over the next three years to help detect and patch up leaks. That effort is ultimately supposed to conserve 189 million gallons of water each year, according to Amazon.

As part of the newly announced collaborative, other companies can contract independently with conservation projects they choose. The United Nations-backed Water Resilience Coalition will vet projects. Amazon is also joining the Water Resilience Coalition, which includes Microsoft, Meta, and other brands across a range of sectors.

Tech companies are facing waves of resistance against new AI data centers. AI was estimated to use between 312.5 billion and 764.6 billion liters of water in 2025, according to one estimate, about as much water as people consume globally in water bottles. In Arizona, Colorado River water cuts are expected to raise utility rates, and some residents fear data centers could make things worse.

In June, Amazon disclosed that its data centers used 2.5 billion gallons of water globally in 2025, including those it owns, leases, or shares. Data centers Amazon owns and operates directly reduced their water consumption by 2 percent in 2025 compared to the year prior, according to the company. It attributes gains to a 52 percent improvement in water efficiency since 2021. The company says it uses 0.12 liters of water per kilowatt-hour of electricity, claiming that’s about seven times more efficient than the industry average for data centers.

Amazon’s annual sustainability report shares water use per unit of power (l/kwh) for its data centers since 2021, but not the company’s total water use over that time period. Sustainability experts and environmental advocates caution against assessing a company’s sustainability by efficiency measurements alone. The more efficient a technology becomes, the more resources it might ultimately consume as companies start using it more, according to an economic concept called Jevons paradox. That makes it important to track how much water a company is using overall, as well as how much it needs in each place it operates during demand peaks when supply is most limited.

For comparison, Microsoft’s latest sustainability report discloses its data centers’ total water use since 2020, while Google’s report shares water use for global operations since 2021 with a breakdown by location. All three tech giants have had to abandon data center projects after facing community opposition, Reuters reports. Unlike other tech companies, Amazon’s warehouses also have a massive physical footprint that isn’t reflected in the company’s data center disclosures.

A Guardian investigation in 2025 alleges that Amazon obscured how much water the company uses by deciding not to account for how much it takes to generate electricity, considered a “secondary” water use. Concerned about “reputational risk,” executives decided to only address “primary” water use at its facilities when calculating progress toward sustainability goals. The numbers Amazon recently shared about its data center water use also exclude water consumption stemming from electricity generation.

While data centers often use water for cooling systems, a majority of a data center’s water footprint stems from this “secondary use.” Power plants need water to cool equipment and turn turbines using steam, and in 2021, Amazon used 10.5 billion gallons (39.7 billion liters) of water in 2021, according to the Guardian report citing an internal leaked document. That’s about as much as 95,000 US households consume.

In an email to The Verge, Amazon spokesperson Margaret Callahan says the Guardian report “relied on cherry-picked data from an outdated document that misrepresents our water strategy — making the conclusions fundamentally wrong and misleading” and that a “document’s existence doesn’t guarantee its accuracy or finality.”

Callahan didn’t provide more data on how much water Amazon has used in total over the years. She pointed out that the company is 75 percent toward its goal of becoming water positive, returning 3 gallons for every 4 that it used last year.

In its announcement today, Kara Hurst, chief sustainability officer at Amazon, compares the new Colorado River initiative to the company’s previous climate targets.

”Through the Climate Pledge, we’ve seen what happens when companies tackle a problem together: progress accelerates. We’re bringing that same model to the Colorado River because water and climate are deeply connected,” Hurst says.

Amazon’s carbon footprint, however, grew 16 percent in 2025 — a trend happening across the tech industry as companies race to make advances in AI.

Tech.title: California tightens rules on AI data center energy and water use
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom has signed seven bills designed to prevent AI data centers from passing utility costs onto residents, as reported earlier by the Los Angeles Times. The package of laws requires the California Public Utilities Commission to introduce a new rate classification for data centers while forcing them to pay for upgrades to local power grids and water systems.

Other bills included in the package will require proposed data centers to disclose their estimated water use to local governments, along with information about energy efficiency and drought planning. They must also meet certain energy, water, and fuel consumption requirements before qualifying for a streamlined approval process. Last week, Newsom signed an executive order to speed up the creation of an AI “kill switch.”

Related Gavin Newsom is pushing for an AI kill switch

“While the Trump administration moves toward deregulation, communities are left to deal with the consequences — higher electricity demand, grid constraints, water use, and pollution,” Newsom says in the press release. “With these laws, we are ensuring that Californians remain in the driver’s seat — and that those profiting from data centers aren’t doing so at our expense.”

Tech.title: GM can’t ‘bring back’ Apple CarPlay because it never left
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Last week, GM announced a new software experience for its upcoming Chevy Silverado and GMC Sierra trucks, including a new look for Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, the popular phone mirroring systems that the automaker made a big deal about removing from its electric vehicles in 2023.

Naturally, this led to some confusion about whether GM was “bringing back” CarPlay and Android Auto to its vehicles. Yahoo Finance reported it that way, calling it an “about-face” by the automaker, while Apple Insider’s headline boasted that GM “cave[d]” on its decision to remove the interface from its gas-powered vehicles. Even The Verge’s own commenters were a bit flummoxed about what was going on.

It’s certainly true that GM has not offered phone projection in any of its electric vehicles for the past three years. That means no CarPlay or Android Auto in the Chevy Equinox, Blazer, Bolt, and Silverado EVs; Cadillac Lyriq, Optiq, Vistiq, and Escalade IQ; or GMC Sierra and Hummer SUV and Truck EVs.

All of those vehicles have Google software products embedded in their systems, like Maps and Gemini. That’s because GM builds its operating system on top of Android Automotive, which is often called Google Automotive Services or GAS when bundled with the full suite of native apps. But if you’re hoping to plug in your phone, or connect wirelessly, and see the familiar app layout on the infotainment screen of a GM electric vehicle, you’ll be sorely disappointed.

The same can’t be said about GM’s many gas-powered trucks and SUVs. GM never disabled phone projection in its best-selling ICE models. Tens of thousands of owners of GM-branded vehicles regularly project their phones’ displays on their vehicles’ infotainment screens without any issue. And now CarPlay and Android Auto are both getting spiffy new picture-in-picture upgrades in the Chevy Silverado and GMC Sierra, a sign that perhaps GM is learning to co-exist with phone mirroring.

GM is partly responsible for the confusion. In an October 2025 appearance on Decoder, GM CEO Mary Barra defended the company’s decision to prohibit CarPlay in its electric vehicles and indicated that the policy would eventually extend to GM’s gasoline-powered lineup as well.

Everyone freaked out for a second time. Removing phone projection in EVs was one thing, but many truck and SUV owners were understandably incensed about the prospect of losing the capability in their beloved GM-branded vehicles. But a few days later, GM seemed to walk back that statement, clarifying to a number of outlets that Apple CarPlay and Android Auto would remain available in its gas-powered vehicles “for the foreseeable future.” Last week’s announcement of a new software experience in the Silverado and Sierra trucks would seem to be included in that “foreseeable future.”

Allow me to add some further reporting here. For the Silverado/Sierra announcement, I spoke to Colin McCormick, group product manager for Google built-in, projection, and profiles at GM. Here’s what he had to say about how GM’s position on phone projection has evolved over the years:

And so the way that I look at this is that we were one of the early adopters of CarPlay and Android Auto when it first came out. And we do have a small segment of EVs right now that don’t offer that, but there is a large majority of our vehicles that do offer that. And our big position on this is that it shouldn’t be two competing systems. So as we work together with Apple and Google to provide solutions that we think are best for the customer, this is what we’re representing in this new UI design. So I think we’re landing in a spot where … we don’t have a customer that has to decide, ‘Oh, I’m going to use projection,’ or, ‘Oh, I want to use the native system.’ That’s our sweet spot for us. And that’s where we want to live.

GM most likely realizes that its position on CarPlay and Android Auto isn’t popular. People really like mirroring their phones! It’s clean, it’s familiar, and it’s (mostly) dependable. The same can’t be said for most modern cars’ native software. Even the ones that are really well designed, like Rivian and Tesla, still struggle with some core functions like profile logins and messages. And you can find plenty of owners of both brands that would give their firstborn child for the ability to mirror their phone.

CarPlay and Android Auto aren’t perfect. They have dependability problems and connectivity problems aplenty. But they are worlds better than the majority of the native operating systems in cars today — most of which are just trash. Yes, they’re getting better. And GM is not wrong in thinking it can offer a better experience. But people get testy when you take away their choices.

So GM is finding ways to coexist with CarPlay and Android Auto. It doesn’t want to lose more customers over it, which is why we’re getting this most recent solution that includes picture-in-picture phone projection. GM thinks this solves the “two competing systems” problem, as mentioned by McCormick. But what it really does is get it out of the corner it backed itself into over phone mirroring.
